m: showing great skill and flair; complete or perfect in every respect
x: Even in a crowded kitchen, my aunt is a consummate host who remembers every guest's favorite dish.
Our new project manager is a consummate professional, calm under pressure and meticulous about deadlines.
Professor Rahman explained quantum mechanics with consummate skill, making even the hardest ideas seem simple.
Critics praised the veteran diplomat's consummate handling of the tense negotiations between the two countries.
She played the role of the loving daughter with such consummate ease that no one suspected her resentment.
tc: Though he had never trained formally, the violinist played with such ______ artistry that seasoned musicians assumed he had studied for decades.
The contrast with 'never trained formally' and the reaction of 'seasoned musicians' show the blank must mean supremely skilled.
se: Colleagues admired the ______ skill with which she calmed the angry client.
masterly
Both 'consummate' and 'masterly' describe skill of the highest level, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: to break or violate a law, rule, or agreement; to conflict with
x: Parking on the sidewalk outside the market contravenes city rules, but few drivers ever get fined.
Sharing client data with an outside vendor would contravene our company's privacy policy.
The university warned that submitting a purchased essay contravenes its code of academic integrity.
Environmental groups argue that the new factory contravenes regulations protecting the river from industrial waste.
He felt that marrying without his parents' blessing would contravene everything they had taught him about family.
tc: Rather than obeying the ceasefire agreement, the rebels continued to ______ its terms by launching attacks at night.
'Rather than obeying' signals the opposite of obedience, so the blank must mean violate.
se: Any company that tries to ______ the new safety standards will face heavy fines.
violate
Both 'contravene' and 'violate' mean to break a rule, and the threat of fines fits either word equally.

m: stubbornly or willfully disobedient to authority
x: The contumacious teenager ignored every curfew his parents set and simply laughed at their warnings.
HR finally dismissed the contumacious employee who refused, again and again, to follow safety procedures.
The judge fined the contumacious witness for repeatedly refusing to answer questions in court.
Historians describe the province as contumacious, resisting every order sent from the distant capital.
Her contumacious attitude toward her mentor eventually cost her a friendship she valued deeply.
tc: Unlike his compliant classmates, Imran was openly ______, refusing every instruction the headmaster gave.
'Unlike his compliant classmates' and 'refusing every instruction' point to a word meaning stubbornly disobedient.
se: The court has little patience for ______ defendants who ignore its orders.
defiant
Both 'contumacious' and 'defiant' describe people who openly resist authority, so the meaning stays the same.

m: friendly, lively, and enjoyable, especially in a social setting
x: Saturday dinners at my grandmother's house are always convivial, full of laughter, gossip and too much biryani.
The office party was surprisingly convivial, and even the shyest interns ended up dancing.
After the seminar, the professor invited us for a convivial evening of tea and conversation.
Local leaders hoped the festival's convivial atmosphere would ease tensions between the two communities.
His convivial nature made him easy to love, though it sometimes hid how lonely he felt.
tc: Far from the stiff, formal gathering she had feared, the reunion was warm and ______, with old friends laughing late into the night.
'Far from the stiff, formal gathering' sets up a contrast, and 'warm' and 'laughing' show the blank means friendly and lively.
se: The host's ______ manner put every guest at ease within minutes.
genial
Both 'convivial' and 'genial' describe a warm, friendly manner, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: capable of being corrected, reformed, or improved
x: My little brother's messy habits are annoying, but I think they are corrigible with patience.
Our manager believes most mistakes by new staff are corrigible if they are caught early.
The teacher insisted that weak grammar is entirely corrigible through daily reading and writing practice.
Reformers argue that young offenders are corrigible and deserve rehabilitation rather than long prison sentences.
She refused to give up on him, convinced that his temper was a corrigible flaw rather than a fixed trait.
tc: Unlike his hardened older brother, who seemed beyond help, the boy was still young and ______, so the counselor remained hopeful.
The contrast with someone 'beyond help' and the counselor's hope show the blank means capable of being reformed.
se: The coach saw the rookie's sloppy footwork as ______, not as a permanent weakness.
correctable
Both 'corrigible' and 'correctable' mean able to be fixed, which contrasts with 'permanent weakness' in the same way.

m: contemptibly lacking in courage; cowardly
x: It was craven of me to blame the broken vase on the cat instead of admitting the truth.
Staff were disgusted by the director's craven refusal to defend his team in front of the board.
The historian condemned the scholars who made craven compromises to please the regime.
Editorials called the government's silence on the attacks a craven betrayal of its own citizens.
She felt craven for ending the relationship by text message rather than facing him in person.
tc: While his comrades stood their ground, the soldier's ______ flight from the battlefield shamed his entire regiment.
The contrast with comrades who 'stood their ground' and the resulting shame show the blank means cowardly.
se: Voters were angered by the senator's ______ refusal to criticize the powerful lobby.
cowardly
Both 'craven' and 'cowardly' describe a refusal driven by lack of courage, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: belief in or acceptance of something as true
x: I don't give much credence to the rumors my neighbors spread about each other.
The latest sales figures lend credence to the manager's argument that the campaign is working.
New fossil evidence has given credence to the theory that birds descended from dinosaurs.
Police initially gave little credence to the witness, but her story later proved accurate.
After years of broken promises, she could no longer give any credence to his apologies.
tc: The scientist's wild claims gained no ______ among her peers, who dismissed them as unsupported by any data.
Peers who 'dismissed' the claims clearly did not believe them, so the blank means acceptance as true.
se: The leaked emails lent ______ to the journalist's claims of corruption.
credibility
'Lent credence to' and 'lent credibility to' both mean made the claims more believable.

m: showing fearlessness and determination in the face of danger or difficulty
x: Our dauntless neighbor waded through knee-deep monsoon water to deliver medicine to an elderly couple.
Despite three rejected proposals, the dauntless engineer kept refining her design until the client approved it.
The dauntless researchers continued their fieldwork in the Arctic even after a storm destroyed their camp.
Reporters praised the dauntless firefighters who entered the burning building again and again.
His dauntless optimism after the divorce surprised friends who had expected him to fall apart.
tc: Though the mountain had claimed many lives, the ______ climbers pressed on toward the summit without hesitation.
'Though the mountain had claimed many lives' contrasts with pressing on 'without hesitation', so the blank means fearless.
se: The ______ journalist kept reporting from the war zone despite repeated threats.
intrepid
Both 'dauntless' and 'intrepid' mean fearless, which explains why she kept working despite threats.

m: to show that a widely held idea or belief is false or exaggerated
x: My cousin loves to debunk the health myths that spread in our family WhatsApp group.
In the meeting, Farah calmly debunked the claim that remote staff were less productive.
The article debunks the popular belief that we use only ten percent of our brains.
Fact-checkers worked overnight to debunk false reports about the election results.
Therapy helped him debunk the old belief that he was unworthy of love.
tc: Rather than confirming the popular legend, the historian's research served to ______ it completely.
'Rather than confirming' signals the opposite, so the blank means to prove the legend false.
se: Scientists quickly moved to ______ the viral claim that the vaccine altered human DNA.
refute
Both 'debunk' and 'refute' mean to prove a claim false, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: to kill, destroy, or remove a large proportion of something
x: Last year's flood decimated our village's rice crop, leaving many families without food for months.
Budget cuts have decimated the research department, which lost half its staff in a year.
Overfishing has decimated cod populations in the North Atlantic over the past century.
Disease brought by European settlers decimated indigenous communities across the Americas.
The scandal decimated his confidence, and he avoided speaking in public for years.
tc: The pesticide was meant to protect crops, but it killed so many bees that it threatened to ______ the entire local population.
'Killed so many bees' shows the blank must mean destroy a large part of the population.
se: Officials feared the epidemic would ______ the town's already small population.
devastate
Both 'decimate' and 'devastate' mean to destroy a large part of something, so the meaning is the same.

m: to publicly criticize or condemn something as bad or wrong
x: My father decries the endless honking in Dhaka traffic every time we drive anywhere.
Several employees decried the new policy as unfair to those with young children.
Many academics decry the growing pressure to publish quickly rather than carefully.
Human rights groups decried the arrest of peaceful protesters outside parliament.
She often decried her own lack of patience but never seemed able to change it.
tc: Rather than praising the reforms, opposition leaders rushed to ______ them as a threat to free speech.
'Rather than praising' and 'a threat to free speech' show the blank means to condemn publicly.
se: Teachers continue to ______ the cuts to school funding at every public meeting.
condemn
Both 'decry' and 'condemn' mean to criticize something publicly and strongly.

m: no longer existing, operating, or functioning
x: We finally threw out the defunct washing machine that had been sitting on the balcony for years.
Many of my old emails went to a defunct company address that nobody checks anymore.
The library still holds journals from defunct publishers that closed decades ago.
The defunct coal mine is now being converted into a museum about the region's history.
Their friendship felt defunct long before either of them admitted it out loud.
tc: The airline once carried millions of passengers, but after years of losses it is now ______ and its planes sit idle.
'Years of losses' and planes that 'sit idle' show the airline no longer operates.
se: The ______ satellite has been drifting silently in orbit since its batteries failed.
inoperative
Both 'defunct' and 'inoperative' describe something that no longer works, which matches the failed batteries.

m: to do something one considers beneath one's dignity; to condescend
x: My teenage sister barely deigned to look up from her phone when I said hello.
The senior partner finally deigned to answer my email after I had sent three reminders.
The famous professor rarely deigned to attend undergraduate seminars, preferring to teach only doctoral students.
The minister did not deign to respond to the villagers' petition about the broken bridge.
He spoke to me as if he were deigning to share his wisdom with a child.
tc: So arrogant was the celebrity chef that he would not even ______ to taste the dishes prepared by his junior cooks.
'So arrogant' explains why he felt tasting their food was beneath him, so the blank means condescend.
se: The haughty official would not ______ to speak with ordinary citizens.
condescend
Both 'deign' and 'condescend' mean to do something one considers beneath oneself, which fits 'haughty'.

m: a leader who wins support by exploiting people's emotions and prejudices rather than using reason
x: My grandfather warned us never to trust a demagogue who promises to solve every problem overnight.
In the debate club, Tariq played the demagogue so convincingly that the audience cheered his absurd claims.
The history lecture examined how demagogues in the 1930s exploited economic despair.
Analysts fear that rising inequality creates fertile ground for demagogues who blame immigrants for everything.
She was disappointed when her idealistic friend began talking like a demagogue, stirring up anger instead of offering solutions.
tc: Rather than offering reasoned policies, the candidate played the classic ______, stoking fear and anger to win votes.
'Rather than offering reasoned policies' and 'stoking fear and anger' define a leader who exploits emotion.
se: Historians remember him as the ______ who rose to power by inflaming ethnic hatred.
rabble-rouser
Both 'demagogue' and 'rabble-rouser' describe a leader who stirs up crowds through emotion and prejudice.

m: the final part of a story or situation, in which matters are explained or resolved
x: We stayed up past midnight just to watch the denouement of our favorite TV drama.
The denouement of the six-month merger talks came when both boards finally signed the agreement.
Our literature professor argued that the novel's denouement feels rushed compared with its brilliant opening.
The long trial reached its denouement when the jury returned a verdict of not guilty.
Their stormy romance had a surprisingly gentle denouement: they parted as close friends.
tc: After two hours of mounting suspense, the play's ______, in which every mystery is finally resolved, left the audience satisfied.
The phrase 'in which every mystery is finally resolved' defines the blank as the resolving final part of a story.
se: Readers loved the novel's ______, which tied up every loose thread.
resolution
Both 'denouement' and 'resolution' mean the part of a story where loose ends are settled.

m: to express disapproval of; also, to play down or belittle
x: My mother deprecates the habit of scrolling through phones at the dinner table.
Senior engineers deprecated the plan to skip testing just to meet the deadline.
The journal's editors deprecate the use of vague, inflated language in research papers.
Several religious leaders deprecated the violence and urged calm across the city.
He tends to deprecate his own achievements, which quietly frustrates the friends who admire him.
tc: Though many colleagues praised the shortcut, the cautious auditor continued to ______ it as risky and unprofessional.
'Though many colleagues praised' sets up a contrast, so the auditor must disapprove of the shortcut.
se: Doctors ______ the practice of prescribing antibiotics for common colds.
deplore
Both 'deprecate' and 'deplore' mean to express strong disapproval of a practice.

m: a ruler who holds absolute power and usually uses it cruelly
x: My uncle runs his household like a despot, deciding everything from dinner to his children's careers.
Employees called the new CEO a petty despot who punished anyone who questioned him.
The seminar compared how ancient despots used monuments to project their power.
After decades under a despot, the country is struggling to build democratic institutions.
She left the relationship once she realized her partner had become a jealous little despot.
tc: Unlike his predecessor, who shared power with an elected council, the new king ruled as the kind of ______ who tolerated no dissent.
The contrast with sharing power and the phrase 'tolerated no dissent' show the blank means an absolute ruler.
se: The ______ jailed every journalist who dared to criticize his regime.
tyrant
Both 'despot' and 'tyrant' mean a cruel ruler with absolute power, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: extremely poor and lacking basic necessities such as food and shelter
x: After the river swallowed their land, the family was left destitute and moved to a slum in Dhaka.
The charity's staff work long hours providing meals for destitute workers who lost their jobs.
Her thesis examines how destitute widows survived in nineteenth-century London.
The war has left millions destitute, without food, shelter or clean water.
Even when they were destitute, my grandparents shared whatever little food they had with neighbors.
tc: Once one of the richest merchants in the city, he died ______, without even enough money for his own funeral.
The contrast with 'richest merchants' and 'without even enough money' show the blank means extremely poor.
se: The shelter provides free beds for ______ families who have nowhere else to go.
impoverished
Both 'destitute' and 'impoverished' describe families in severe poverty, giving the same meaning.

m: intended to teach, especially in a preachy or moralizing way
x: My uncle has a didactic habit of turning every family dinner into a lecture on saving money.
The training video was so didactic that employees started mocking it during the session.
Many children's books from the Victorian era were openly didactic, teaching obedience and thrift.
Critics found the documentary too didactic, preaching to viewers instead of letting the facts speak.
She disliked his didactic tone, which made even friendly advice sound like a reprimand.
tc: The author hoped to entertain readers, but her novel's constant moral lessons made it feel heavily ______.
'Constant moral lessons' contrasted with the aim to entertain show the blank means preachy and instructive.
se: The film's ______ tone irritated audiences who resented being lectured.
preachy
Both 'didactic' and 'preachy' describe a lecturing tone, which matches audiences who 'resented being lectured'.

m: spread out rather than concentrated; (of writing or speech) wordy and unfocused
x: The diffuse light of a monsoon afternoon made our living room feel calm and gray.
Responsibility for the project is so diffuse that nobody knows who should approve the budget.
My supervisor said my thesis introduction was too diffuse and asked me to cut it in half.
Scientists say the pollution is diffuse, coming from thousands of small sources rather than one factory.
Her grief was diffuse, a quiet sadness that colored everything rather than a sharp pain.
tc: Rather than making one sharp argument, the essay was ______, wandering from point to point without ever reaching a conclusion.
'Rather than making one sharp argument' and 'wandering from point to point' show the blank means unfocused and rambling.
se: Support for the reform is ______, spread across many small groups with no clear leader.
scattered
Both 'diffuse' and 'scattered' mean spread out rather than concentrated, which the rest of the sentence confirms.

m: to make someone feel uneasy, embarrassed, or confused
x: My aunt's questions about my salary always discomfit me at family weddings.
The interviewer's long silences were clearly meant to discomfit the candidates.
Students were discomfited when the professor asked them to defend their answers in front of the class.
The leaked documents discomfited officials who had denied any knowledge of the scheme.
His sudden confession of love discomfited her, and she quickly changed the subject.
tc: The lawyer hoped her sharp, unexpected questions would ______ the witness, who had seemed calm and confident until then.
The witness 'had seemed calm and confident', so the lawyer's aim was the opposite: to make him uneasy.
se: Nothing seemed to ______ the speaker, not even hecklers shouting from the back row.
fluster
Both 'discomfit' and 'fluster' mean to make someone flustered or uneasy, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: a feeling of worry, anxiety, or unease
x: There was growing disquiet in our house as my brother's exam results were delayed again.
The layoffs caused widespread disquiet among staff who feared they would be next.
Researchers expressed disquiet about how the data had been collected.
The court's decision has caused public disquiet over the independence of the judiciary.
She tried to hide her disquiet when her husband did not call from the airport.
tc: Although the doctor assured her the test was routine, she could not shake her ______ as she waited for the results.
'Although the doctor assured her' signals contrast, so she still felt worried; the blank means unease.
se: News of the factory closure spread ______ throughout the small town.
anxiety
Both 'disquiet' and 'anxiety' name the worry that bad news spreads through a community.

m: the formal ending or breaking up of an organization, partnership, or assembly
x: My parents felt relieved after the dissolution of their old business partnership, which had caused years of arguments.
The board voted for the dissolution of the committee once its work was finished.
Our history course covers the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991.
The president announced the dissolution of parliament and called fresh elections.
The slow dissolution of their marriage left both of them exhausted and sad.
tc: Once a powerful federation, the alliance weakened year by year until its final ______ in 1990, when every member state left.
'Weakened year by year' and 'every member state left' show the blank means the formal breaking up of the alliance.
se: The partners agreed to the ______ of the firm after a decade of disputes.
breakup
Both 'dissolution' and 'breakup' mean the ending of the partnership, so the meaning stays the same.

m: relating to women, especially the female side of a family
x: On the distaff side of my family, almost every woman became a teacher.
The company's distaff employees formed a network to push for equal pay and promotion.
Her research traces property inheritance along the distaff line in medieval England.
The magazine profiled the distaff branch of the famous political dynasty, long overshadowed by its men.
He felt closest to his distaff relatives, especially the aunts who had raised him.
tc: Although the family's men were famous, it was the ______ side, his mother's sisters and grandmother, who shaped his character.
The contrast with 'the family's men' and the restatement 'his mother's sisters and grandmother' show the blank means female.
se: He inherited the farm through the ______ line, from his mother's family.
maternal
Both 'distaff' and 'maternal' refer to the mother's side, which the phrase 'his mother's family' confirms.

m: to be indecisive and hesitate instead of acting
x: Stop dithering over the menu and just order the biryani before the kitchen closes.
Management dithered for months about the new software, and our competitors moved ahead.
I dithered between engineering and economics until the admission deadline had almost passed.
Critics accused the government of dithering while the flood waters rose.
She dithered for weeks about whether to tell him how she felt.
tc: Unlike her decisive sister, who chose a university within a day, Mina tended to ______ for weeks over even small choices.
The contrast with 'her decisive sister' shows the blank means to be indecisive.
se: If we ______ any longer, someone else will buy the apartment.
hesitate
Both 'dither' and 'hesitate' mean to delay a decision, and the risk of losing the apartment fits either.

m: to deprive of or rid oneself of something, such as power, possessions, or investments
x: Before moving abroad, we had to divest ourselves of most of our furniture and books.
The company plans to divest its loss-making cement division by next year.
Several universities have voted to divest from fossil fuel companies.
The new law divests local councils of their power to approve building permits.
Moving to a new city helped her divest herself of painful memories.
tc: Upon becoming a monk, he chose to ______ himself of every possession, keeping only a robe and a bowl.
'Keeping only a robe and a bowl' shows he got rid of everything else, so the blank means strip or rid.
se: The reform aims to ______ the old aristocracy of its remaining privileges.
strip
Both 'divest ... of' and 'strip ... of' mean to take something away, giving the same meaning.

m: showing stubborn, determined persistence
x: Through dogged practice every evening, my little cousin finally learned to bowl a decent off-spinner.
Her dogged pursuit of the missing invoice saved the company thousands of dollars.
Years of dogged research eventually led the team to the gene responsible for the disease.
Dogged reporting by a local newspaper exposed corruption in the city's water department.
He showed dogged loyalty to his friend, even when everyone else had turned against him.
tc: Though she failed the exam twice, her ______ persistence paid off when she passed with distinction on the third attempt.
Continuing after two failures until success shows the blank means stubbornly determined.
se: It took ______ effort over many years to clear the backlog of cases.
tenacious
Both 'dogged' and 'tenacious' describe persistent, determined effort over a long time.

m: temporarily inactive or asleep, but capable of becoming active again
x: My interest in painting had been dormant for years until my daughter bought me a set of brushes.
The project lay dormant for months until a new client revived it.
Seeds can remain dormant in the soil for decades before conditions allow them to sprout.
Scientists warn that the volcano, though dormant, could erupt again within the next century.
Old feelings of jealousy, long dormant, returned when she saw him with someone new.
tc: The virus can stay ______ in the body for years before suddenly becoming active and causing symptoms.
'Before suddenly becoming active' shows the virus was inactive until then.
se: The bank closed her account because it had been ______ for over five years.
inactive
Both 'dormant' and 'inactive' describe an account that has not been used, so the meaning is the same.

m: excessively harsh and severe, especially of laws or punishments
x: My parents' draconian curfew meant I had to be home by eight, even on weekends.
Staff complained that the new attendance rules were draconian and punished people for minor delays.
Under the university's draconian policy, an assignment submitted even one minute late receives zero.
Human rights groups condemned the draconian law that bans peaceful public protest.
She felt his draconian rules about money made their marriage feel like a prison.
tc: Critics said the punishment was far too ______: twenty years in prison for stealing a loaf of bread.
The colon introduces an example of extreme harshness, so the blank means excessively severe.
se: The government introduced ______ measures to limit the freedom of the press.
harsh
Both 'draconian' and 'harsh' describe severe measures, so the sentence means the same.

m: deceitfulness; saying or doing one thing while secretly intending another
x: I was shocked by the duplicity of a friend who praised my cooking but mocked it behind my back.
The manager's duplicity came to light when emails showed he had promised the same promotion to two people.
The novel explores the duplicity of a scientist who fakes his data to win funding.
The investigation exposed the company's duplicity in claiming its products were environmentally safe.
After discovering his duplicity, she wondered whether anything he had told her was true.
tc: The spy's ______ was so complete that even his own family never suspected he was working for both sides.
Secretly 'working for both sides' without anyone suspecting is the definition of deceitfulness.
se: Voters were angered by the candidate's ______ in making opposite promises to different groups.
deceit
Both 'duplicity' and 'deceit' mean dishonest double-dealing, which 'opposite promises' illustrates.

m: to instruct and improve someone morally or intellectually
x: My grandfather's stories about the Liberation War were meant to edify as well as entertain us.
The ethics workshop was meant to edify new managers, but most of them spent it checking emails.
A good textbook should edify students rather than simply drill facts into them.
Public television was founded to edify viewers, not merely to sell advertising.
She found that long conversations with her mentor edified her far more than any lecture.
tc: The museum's aim is not just to entertain visitors but to ______ them, leaving them wiser than when they arrived.
'Leaving them wiser' restates the meaning of the blank: to instruct and improve.
se: The preacher's sermons were intended to ______ the congregation.
enlighten
Both 'edify' and 'enlighten' mean to instruct and improve people's understanding.

m: to erase or wipe out; to make oneself inconspicuous
x: Years of rain had effaced the names carved on the old graves in our village.
No amount of public relations could efface the damage the scandal did to the firm's reputation.
Some historians accuse the regime of trying to efface entire communities from the official record.
The new government moved quickly to efface every statue and symbol of the old dictatorship.
She tended to efface herself at parties, standing quietly in a corner while others talked.
tc: Nothing could ______ the memory of that terrible night; it stayed vivid in her mind for decades.
The memory 'stayed vivid', so nothing could wipe it out; the blank means erase.
se: The authorities tried to ______ every trace of the protest from the city walls.
erase
Both 'efface' and 'erase' mean to remove every trace of something.

m: expressing feelings such as gratitude or approval in an unrestrained, gushing way
x: My aunt is so effusive that she hugs everyone at the door, including the delivery man.
The client sent an effusive thank-you email after we delivered the project early.
The reviewer was effusive in her praise of the young scientist's first book.
Officials gave an effusive welcome to the foreign delegation at the airport.
He felt slightly embarrassed by her effusive declarations of love on their second date.
tc: Unlike her reserved husband, who merely nodded, Laila was ______, thanking the host again and again with tears in her eyes.
The contrast with 'her reserved husband' and repeated tearful thanks show the blank means gushing.
se: The coach was ______ in his praise of the young bowler.
lavish
'Effusive in his praise' and 'lavish in his praise' both mean praising generously and openly.

m: believing that all people are equal and deserve equal rights and opportunities
x: In our egalitarian household, everyone takes turns washing the dishes, including my father.
The startup prides itself on an egalitarian culture where interns can challenge the founders.
The professor argued that Scandinavian school systems are among the most egalitarian in the world.
Activists are campaigning for a more egalitarian society in which wealth is fairly shared.
She wanted an egalitarian marriage in which both partners shared careers and childcare equally.
tc: Unlike the rigidly hierarchical firms of the past, the new company is strongly ______, with no private offices and equal pay bands.
The contrast with 'rigidly hierarchical' and the details about equal pay show the blank means committed to equality.
se: The commune was founded on ______ principles, with every member owning an equal share.
democratic
Both 'egalitarian' and 'democratic' describe principles of equality among members.

m: expressing sadness or mourning, especially for something lost or past
x: My father grew elegiac whenever he talked about the village pond where he swam as a boy.
The CEO's farewell speech was oddly elegiac, as if he were mourning the company itself.
The poet's later work is elegiac, lamenting the loss of the countryside to industry.
The documentary takes an elegiac look at the last days of the city's old cinemas.
Her letters became elegiac after her best friend moved overseas for good.
tc: The concert ended not with a triumphant march but with ______ music, a slow lament for the friends the composer had lost.
The contrast with 'triumphant' and the restatement 'a slow lament' show the blank means mournful.
se: The novel's ______ final chapter mourns a way of life that has vanished forever.
mournful
Both 'elegiac' and 'mournful' describe writing full of sorrow for something lost.

m: to make something more attractive by adding details or decoration, often untrue ones
x: My uncle always embellishes his fishing stories, so the fish gets bigger every time.
She was warned not to embellish her resume with skills she did not actually have.
The historian argued that later writers had embellished the king's victories with invented details.
The journalist was fired for embellishing quotes in several front-page stories.
He embellished the card with tiny hand-drawn flowers for his wife's birthday.
tc: Rather than reporting the facts plainly, the witness tended to ______ her account with dramatic details she could not have seen.
'Rather than reporting the facts plainly' and 'dramatic details' show the blank means to add exaggerated details.
se: Fishermen are known to ______ their stories, adding a few inches to every catch.
exaggerate
Both 'embellish' and 'exaggerate' mean to make a story sound more impressive than the truth.

m: soothing; intended to calm anger and avoid confrontation
x: My mother's emollient words calmed my father before he could start shouting at the plumber.
The manager adopted an emollient tone in the meeting to cool the dispute between two teams.
Dermatologists recommend an emollient cream for people with dry, cracked skin.
The minister's emollient statement did little to calm the furious protesters.
After their argument, he sent her an emollient message apologizing for his harsh words.
tc: Instead of responding harshly to the angry critics, the spokesperson's reply was soft and ______, designed to calm tempers.
The contrast with 'responding harshly' and 'designed to calm tempers' show the blank means soothing.
se: The diplomat's ______ remarks helped ease tensions between the two delegations.
conciliatory
Both 'emollient' and 'conciliatory' describe words meant to calm and reduce conflict.

m: to burden or weigh down, making movement or progress difficult
x: Encumbered with three suitcases, my mother struggled through the crowded railway station.
Endless paperwork encumbers our team and slows down every new project.
Students who are encumbered with heavy loans often choose jobs they dislike.
The economy remains encumbered by debts left over from the previous government.
She did not want to encumber her friends with her problems, so she kept quiet.
tc: Hikers are advised to pack light, since heavy gear will only ______ them on the steep mountain trail.
'Pack light' and 'heavy gear' show the blank means to weigh down or hinder.
se: Strict regulations ______ small businesses and discourage new investment.
hamper
Both 'encumber' and 'hamper' mean to hold back or burden, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: a state of deep hostility or mutual hatred
x: The enmity between the two neighbors started over a mango tree and lasted thirty years.
Enmity grew in the office after the manager publicly favored one team over another.
Scholars still debate the origins of the enmity between the two ancient city-states.
Decades of enmity between the nations made the peace treaty seem almost impossible.
She felt no enmity toward her ex-husband, only a quiet sadness.
tc: Once close friends, the two writers developed such bitter ______ after a public quarrel that they never spoke again.
The change from 'close friends' to never speaking again shows the blank means hostility.
se: Years of ______ between the rival clans ended with an unexpected marriage.
hostility
Both 'enmity' and 'hostility' mean deep mutual hatred, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to ask someone earnestly or anxiously to do something; to beg
x: My little sister entreated our parents to let her keep the stray kitten.
The team leader entreated everyone to submit their reports before the holiday weekend.
Our professor entreated us not to copy answers from the internet.
Aid workers entreated wealthy nations to send emergency food to the flood-hit region.
He entreated her to stay, but she had already packed her bags.
tc: Rather than ordering his soldiers to fight, the old general chose to ______ them, pleading with them to defend their homes.
'Rather than ordering' and 'pleading' show the blank means to ask earnestly.
se: The mother continued to ______ the judge to show mercy to her son.
implore
Both 'entreat' and 'implore' mean to beg earnestly, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a descriptive word or phrase attached to a person's name; also, an abusive word or insult
x: My grandfather earned the epithet 'the walking clock' because he was never late for anything.
Colleagues gave her the epithet 'the Fixer' after she rescued three failing projects.
Homer often uses fixed epithets, such as 'rosy-fingered Dawn', to describe recurring figures.
The candidate was condemned for hurling ethnic epithets at protesters during a rally.
In the heat of their argument, he shouted an epithet he immediately regretted.
tc: Alexander's military conquests earned him the ______ 'the Great', a title still attached to his name.
'A title still attached to his name' restates the blank: a descriptive phrase added to a name.
se: Fans gave the batsman the ______ 'the Wall' because he was so hard to dismiss.
nickname
Both 'epithet' and 'nickname' mean a descriptive name attached to a person.

m: unpredictable and irregular in behavior or pattern
x: Our electricity supply has been erratic all summer, cutting out several times a day.
His erratic attendance at work finally led to a warning from HR.
The experiment produced erratic results, so the team checked the equipment for faults.
Climate scientists link the region's increasingly erratic monsoon to rising ocean temperatures.
She grew tired of his erratic moods, never knowing whether he would be loving or cold.
tc: Unlike his steady, predictable brother, Rafi was ______ on the field: brilliant one week and terrible the next.
The contrast with 'steady, predictable' and the swing from brilliant to terrible show the blank means unpredictable.
se: The patient's ______ heartbeat worried the doctors.
irregular
Both 'erratic' and 'irregular' describe a heartbeat without a steady pattern.

m: used as an artificial and usually inferior substitute for something real
x: During the shortage, we drank an ersatz coffee made from roasted barley.
The new office's ersatz wood paneling fooled no one; it was obviously plastic.
Critics dismissed the film as ersatz history, full of invented scenes and costumes.
The mall's ersatz Venetian canals attract tourists who have never seen the real thing.
He offered ersatz sympathy, but she could tell he did not really care.
tc: Far from being genuine leather, the bag was made of a cheap, ______ material that cracked within weeks.
'Far from being genuine' and 'cheap' show the blank means an inferior artificial substitute.
se: The restaurant serves ______ Italian food that no real Italian would recognize.
fake
Both 'ersatz' and 'fake' describe an imitation that is not the real thing.

m: quickly fading or disappearing; lasting a very short time
x: The evanescent smell of rain on dry soil is my favorite part of the first monsoon shower.
Startup success can be evanescent: a company admired one year may vanish the next.
Physicists study evanescent particles that exist for only a tiny fraction of a second.
Social media fame is often evanescent, lasting only until the next viral video.
Their evanescent romance lasted just one summer, but she remembered it for years.
tc: The rainbow was ______, vanishing within seconds before anyone could take a photograph.
'Vanishing within seconds' defines the blank as quickly fading.
se: Poets have long celebrated the ______ beauty of cherry blossoms, which last only a few days.
fleeting
Both 'evanescent' and 'fleeting' mean short-lived, matching blossoms that 'last only a few days'.

m: demanding great effort, care, skill, or precision
x: My grandmother is an exacting cook who insists on grinding every spice by hand.
Our exacting new boss expects every report to be checked three times before it reaches her.
The lab maintains exacting standards so that other teams can reproduce its results.
Surgeons must meet exacting requirements before they are allowed to operate unsupervised.
He found it hard to love such an exacting father, who praised nothing less than perfection.
tc: The editor was so ______ that she would reject an entire article over a single misplaced comma.
Rejecting an article over one comma shows the blank means extremely demanding and precise.
se: The job has ______ physical requirements that few applicants can meet.
demanding
Both 'exacting' and 'demanding' describe requirements that are hard to satisfy.

m: to criticize someone or something very severely
x: My father excoriated the electricity company after our power was cut for the third time in a day.
In a furious email, the director excoriated the sales team for missing its targets yet again.
The reviewer excoriated the paper's methodology, calling its conclusions entirely unsupported.
Newspapers excoriated the mayor for ignoring warnings about the collapsing bridge.
She excoriated herself for months after forgetting her best friend's wedding.
tc: Far from offering gentle feedback, the critic chose to ______ the novel, calling it the worst book of the decade.
'Far from offering gentle feedback' and 'the worst book of the decade' show the blank means to criticize harshly.
se: Opposition leaders were quick to ______ the government for its slow response to the floods.
castigate
Both 'excoriate' and 'castigate' mean to criticize severely, so the meaning is the same.

m: to strongly encourage or urge someone to do something
x: Every morning, my mother exhorts me to eat breakfast before rushing off to class.
The manager exhorted the team to give one final push before the product launch.
Our supervisor exhorted us to read widely beyond our own narrow field.
Health officials exhorted residents to boil drinking water during the outbreak.
In his letters, her father exhorted her never to lose faith in herself.
tc: Seeing his tired players slow down, the coach began to ______ them from the sideline, shouting at them to keep running.
'Shouting at them to keep running' restates the blank: to urge strongly.
se: Leaders continued to ______ citizens to stay calm during the crisis.
urge
Both 'exhort' and 'urge' mean to strongly encourage people to do something.

m: unreasonably high, especially of prices or costs
x: Rickshaw pullers in Dhaka often charge exorbitant fares when it rains heavily.
The consultant's fee seemed exorbitant for just two days of work.
Many students cannot afford the exorbitant cost of new textbooks, so they share photocopies instead.
Patient groups are protesting the exorbitant prices that drug companies charge for life-saving medicines.
He spent an exorbitant amount on her birthday gift, hoping to win her back.
tc: Most families could not afford the apartments, whose rents were ______, often three times the average monthly salary.
'Could not afford' and 'three times the average monthly salary' show the blank means unreasonably high.
se: The hotel charges ______ prices for bottled water.
extortionate
Both 'exorbitant' and 'extortionate' describe prices that are unfairly high.

m: to speak or write at great length or in great detail about a subject
x: At dinner, my uncle expatiated on the merits of his new car until everyone was bored.
During the meeting, the director expatiated on company values for nearly an hour.
The professor loves to expatiate on Victorian poetry, often running well past the lecture time.
In his memoir, the retired general expatiates on battles that most readers have long forgotten.
She could expatiate for hours on her childhood in Sylhet, recalling every tea garden and river.
tc: Rather than summarizing briefly, the speaker continued to ______ on the topic for two full hours.
The contrast with 'summarizing briefly' and 'two full hours' show the blank means to speak at great length.
se: Given the chance, he will ______ on his theories of economics for hours.
expound
Both 'expatiate on' and 'expound on' mean to talk about a subject in great detail.

m: to analyze and explain an idea or text in detail
x: My sister patiently explicated the rules of cricket to her confused American friend.
The analyst explicated the quarterly figures so clearly that even the sales staff understood them.
Each student must explicate a short poem, explaining its imagery line by line.
The scientist wrote a book explicating climate models for a general audience.
He tried to explicate his feelings in a long letter, but it only confused her more.
tc: The poem is so dense that readers need a scholar to ______ it, explaining each obscure reference in detail.
'Explaining each obscure reference in detail' restates the blank: to analyze and explain.
se: The professor spent an entire lecture trying to ______ the philosopher's difficult argument.
elucidate
Both 'explicate' and 'elucidate' mean to explain something difficult clearly and in detail.

m: to erase or remove something completely, especially an unwanted record or memory
x: After paying the fine, she asked the court to expunge the old charge from her record.
HR agreed to expunge the unfair warning from his personnel file once the investigation cleared him.
The editor expunged every reference to the disputed study before the textbook went to print.
No apology could fully expunge the memory of that humiliating evening from his mind.
Activists are campaigning to expunge the records of people convicted under the old colonial-era law.
tc: The judge ordered the clerk to ______ the offensive remark from the transcript so that no trace of it would remain.
'So that no trace of it would remain' restates the meaning: to remove completely.
se: He hoped the new evidence would persuade the court to ______ the conviction from his record.
erase
Both 'expunge' and 'erase' mean to remove the conviction entirely, giving the same meaning.

m: spoken or done without preparation; improvised on the spot
x: Asked to say a few words at the wedding, he gave a short extemporaneous toast that made everyone laugh.
Her extemporaneous answers in the client meeting impressed the partners more than her polished slides did.
The debate club trains students in extemporaneous speaking, giving them only two minutes to prepare.
The minister's extemporaneous remarks at the rally caused far more controversy than his scripted speech.
His extemporaneous apology felt more sincere than any carefully written letter could have.
tc: Having lost his notes moments before going on stage, the speaker had no choice but to deliver ______ remarks.
Losing his notes means he had to speak without preparation.
se: The comedian's funniest moments were ______, prompted by shouts from the audience rather than by her script.
improvised
Both 'extemporaneous' and 'improvised' describe material made up on the spot, matching 'rather than by her script'.

m: too simple; superficial and ignoring the real complexity of an issue
x: Blaming phones for every problem young people face is a facile explanation that ignores deeper causes.
The consultant's report offered facile solutions that fell apart as soon as the finance team examined them.
My professor circled my conclusion and wrote, 'Too facile; what about the counterarguments?'
Calling Dhaka's traffic simply a matter of too many cars is a facile analysis of a complex urban problem.
She was tired of his facile reassurances that everything would work out without any effort on his part.
tc: Far from being ______, the author's argument carefully weighs the competing economic, cultural and historical factors.
'Far from' combined with 'carefully weighs' the factors shows the blank means oversimplified.
se: Critics dismissed the film's ______ message that love alone can solve poverty.
simplistic
Both 'facile' and 'simplistic' criticize the message as naively oversimplified.

m: imaginative but unrealistic; existing only in the imagination
x: My little nephew told a fanciful story about a dragon living in our water tank.
The startup's revenue projections were so fanciful that the investors stopped reading after the first page.
Historians now regard the old legend of the city's founding as largely fanciful.
Early claims that the new drug could reverse ageing turned out to be fanciful.
She had fanciful ideas about marriage, imagining it would feel like a never-ending honeymoon.
tc: The engineer rejected the design as ______, pointing out that no known material could withstand such pressure.
'No known material could withstand' it shows the design was unrealistic.
se: The notion that the project could be finished in a week was dismissed as ______ by everyone on the team.
unrealistic
Both 'fanciful' and 'unrealistic' mean the idea had no basis in reality.

m: intense and passionate feeling or enthusiasm
x: Fans celebrated the cricket victory with such fervor that the streets of Dhaka stayed noisy until dawn.
The new manager brought a fervor to the sales team that had been missing for years.
He spoke about medieval history with a fervor that made even reluctant students pay attention.
Nationalist fervor swept the country in the weeks before the referendum.
She defended her best friend with a fervor that surprised everyone at the table.
tc: Although he had once supported the cause with ______, he now spoke of it with weary indifference.
'Although' sets up a contrast with 'weary indifference', so the blank means passion.
se: The volunteers worked with such ______ that the flood shelter was rebuilt in only three days.
zeal
Both 'fervor' and 'zeal' mean intense enthusiasm, giving the same meaning.

m: smelling extremely unpleasant; stinking
x: After the monsoon flooding, a fetid smell rose from the drains along our street.
Someone had left fish in the office fridge, and by Monday the whole kitchen was fetid.
The researchers waded through fetid swamp water to collect samples of the rare frog.
Residents complained to the city council about the fetid garbage dump next to the school.
He opened the gym bag he had forgotten for a week and recoiled from the fetid odor.
tc: Unlike the fragrant gardens upstairs, the basement was damp and ______, reeking of rotting wood.
The contrast with 'fragrant' and the phrase 'reeking of rotting wood' show the blank means foul-smelling.
se: The ______ air in the abandoned warehouse made the inspectors cover their noses.
foul
Both 'fetid' and 'foul' describe air that smells disgusting.

m: shockingly obvious and offensive; done openly without any attempt to hide wrongdoing
x: Parking in the ambulance bay showed a flagrant disregard for the hospital's rules.
The auditors found flagrant errors in the accounts that no careful accountant could have missed.
Copying an entire paragraph without citation is a flagrant violation of the university's honor code.
The referee sent him off for a flagrant foul on the opposing striker.
Her flagrant lie about where she had been that night ended their friendship.
tc: The violation was neither subtle nor technical but ______, committed openly in front of dozens of witnesses.
'Neither subtle' and 'committed openly' show the blank means shockingly obvious.
se: Firing the whistleblower was a clear and ______ breach of the company's own ethics policy.
blatant
Both 'flagrant' and 'blatant' mean openly and shamelessly wrong.

m: excessively elaborate or ornate, especially in language or style
x: His love letters were so florid that she could hardly find the actual message among the adjectives.
Our manager asked us to replace the florid language in the proposal with plain, direct sentences.
Victorian novels are often criticized for florid prose that modern readers find exhausting.
The architect's florid design, covered in gilded curls and statues, divided the city council.
In his florid speech at the farewell party, he compared his retiring boss to a lighthouse, a mountain and a river.
tc: The editor trimmed the novelist's ______ descriptions, preferring sentences that were plain and spare.
'Preferring sentences that were plain and spare' contrasts with the blank, so it means over-elaborate.
se: Readers found the speech's ______ style tiresome, with every simple point buried under decoration.
ornate
Both 'florid' and 'ornate' describe a style that is excessively decorated.

m: a minor weakness or odd habit in someone's character
x: My grandfather's one foible was insisting on reading the newspaper before anyone else touched it.
Good managers learn to tolerate their team members' foibles as long as the work gets done.
The biography is affectionate, treating the scientist's foibles with gentle humor rather than scorn.
Voters seem willing to forgive a politician's personal foibles but not outright dishonesty.
After ten years of marriage, they laugh about each other's foibles instead of arguing over them.
tc: His habit of humming while he worked was a harmless ______ rather than a serious flaw.
'Harmless' and 'rather than a serious flaw' show the blank means a minor weakness.
se: Everyone has some ______, and his was an inability to leave a crossword unfinished.
quirk
Both 'foible' and 'quirk' mean a small personal oddity.

m: patient self-control; restraint and tolerance when provoked
x: The nursery teacher showed remarkable forbearance as the toddlers spilled paint across the floor.
The bank agreed to a period of forbearance, letting struggling borrowers delay their loan payments.
Thanks to my supervisor's forbearance, I was given an extra month to finish my thesis.
Diplomats urged both sides to exercise forbearance until the ceasefire talks could resume.
She endured her in-laws' constant criticism with a forbearance that her friends found astonishing.
tc: Despite endless provocations from hecklers, the speaker responded with ______, never once raising her voice.
'Never once raising her voice' despite provocation shows the blank means patient restraint.
se: Sharing a small apartment with three noisy roommates required great ______ on her part.
patience
Both 'forbearance' and 'patience' mean calmly tolerating annoyance.

m: direct and outspoken; saying honestly what one thinks
x: My aunt is forthright about everything, including my weight and my career choices.
Investors appreciated the chief executive's forthright admission that the product launch had failed.
The professor gave forthright feedback on my draft, which stung but helped enormously.
The commission's forthright report blamed officials directly for the collapse of the factory building.
I'd rather have a forthright friend who tells me the truth than one who only flatters me.
tc: Instead of giving vague and evasive replies, the witness was ______, answering every question directly.
'Instead of ... evasive' and 'answering every question directly' show the blank means frank.
se: She was refreshingly ______ about her reasons for leaving the company.
candid
Both 'forthright' and 'candid' mean open and honest.

m: excessively flattering or complimentary, to the point of seeming insincere
x: The waiter's fulsome compliments on our choice of wine made us suspect he wanted a bigger tip.
Her fulsome praise of the boss at every meeting was starting to embarrass her colleagues.
Reviewers mocked the author's fulsome dedication to his publisher, which ran to two full pages.
State newspapers printed fulsome tributes to the dictator every single morning.
He found her fulsome thanks for such a small favor a little awkward.
tc: The speech was so excessive and insincere in its flattery that it struck listeners as ______ rather than genuinely appreciative.
'Excessive and insincere in its flattery' defines the blank directly.
se: Embarrassed by the host's ______ flattery, the guest changed the subject as quickly as he could.
unctuous
Both 'fulsome' and 'unctuous' describe flattery that is overdone and insincere.

m: an embarrassing mistake made in a social or public situation
x: Calling my new colleague by the wrong name twice was an embarrassing gaffe.
The press officer spent the afternoon trying to contain the gaffe made during the morning briefing.
In my first seminar, I committed the gaffe of criticizing a paper written by the professor herself.
A single televised gaffe can now go viral and derail an entire election campaign.
At dinner, he made the gaffe of asking her sister when the baby was due.
tc: The diplomat's careless joke about the host country's history was a serious ______ that required a formal apology.
A 'careless joke' that 'required a formal apology' signals an embarrassing public blunder.
se: Forgetting the bride's name during his toast was the biggest ______ of the evening.
blunder
Both 'gaffe' and 'blunder' mean an embarrassing mistake.

m: to shock or excite someone into taking action
x: The broken streetlight finally galvanized our neighbors into forming a residents' association.
Losing the big contract galvanized the sales team, who worked harder than ever that quarter.
The professor's challenge galvanized the class to rethink everything they believed about economics.
News of the factory fire galvanized public support for stricter safety laws.
Her mother's sudden illness galvanized her to finally quit smoking after twenty years.
tc: The coach hoped his fiery halftime speech would ______ the listless players into a second-half comeback.
Turning 'listless players' into a 'comeback' shows the blank means to stir into action.
se: Organizers hoped the documentary would ______ young voters to register before the deadline.
spur
Both 'galvanize' and 'spur' mean to prompt people into action.

m: unpleasantly bright and showy; gaudy
x: He wore a garish orange suit to the wedding and stood out in every photograph.
The new office was painted a garish lime green that gave everyone a headache.
Critics described the museum's renovation as garish, full of neon lights and plastic gold.
Garish billboards now cover the old buildings along the highway into the city.
She found his garish displays of wealth embarrassing rather than impressive.
tc: The designer avoided ______ colors, choosing instead soft, muted tones that calmed the eye.
The contrast with 'soft, muted tones' shows the blank means loud and showy.
se: The restaurant's ______ decor, all flashing lights and bright plastic, put off many diners.
gaudy
Both 'garish' and 'gaudy' mean tastelessly bright and showy.

m: relevant and appropriate to the subject being discussed
x: The judge ruled that the defendant's past was not germane to the current case.
Please keep your comments germane to the agenda so we can finish the meeting on time.
My supervisor told me to cut any material that wasn't germane to my research question.
Questions about funding are germane to any serious debate about public health policy.
His story was charming but hardly germane to our argument about whose turn it was to cook.
tc: The chairperson ruled the question out of order, saying it was not ______ to the matter under debate.
Ruling a question 'out of order' because of its link to the debate shows the blank means relevant.
se: Only evidence that is ______ to the charges will be admitted at trial.
relevant
Both 'germane' and 'relevant' mean directly connected to the charges.

m: done without good reason; uncalled for and unnecessary
x: The film was spoiled by gratuitous violence that added nothing to the story.
His gratuitous comment about her accent during the meeting upset the whole team.
Reviewers criticized the article for gratuitous jargon that obscured its actual findings.
Human rights groups condemned the gratuitous use of force against peaceful protesters.
There was no need for such a gratuitous insult; she had only asked him a simple question.
tc: The editor cut the scene because its cruelty was ______, serving no purpose in the plot.
'Serving no purpose' defines the blank as unnecessary.
se: Many readers felt the ______ swearing in the novel distracted from its serious themes.
unnecessary
Both 'gratuitous' and 'unnecessary' mean the swearing had no real purpose.

m: very severe or serious, causing great harm or suffering
x: Leaving the gas stove on all night could have been a grievous mistake.
Losing our biggest client was a grievous blow to the company's finances.
The inquiry found grievous flaws in the way the exam results had been calculated.
The earthquake caused grievous damage to schools and hospitals across the region.
His mother's death was a grievous loss from which he never fully recovered.
tc: The oversight was not minor at all; it was ______, costing several people their lives.
'Not minor' and 'costing several people their lives' show the blank means extremely serious.
se: The report concluded that the hospital's failures were ______ and had directly led to patient deaths.
grave
Both 'grievous' and 'grave' mean extremely serious in their consequences.

m: idyllically happy and peaceful, usually describing a time in the past
x: She often talks about the halcyon summers she spent at her grandparents' village home.
Older staff remember the halcyon days when the company gave everyone a bonus each December.
My father still describes his student years as the halcyon days of his life.
Economists warn that the halcyon era of cheap borrowing is now over.
In those halcyon early months of their relationship, they never seemed to argue.
tc: Compared with the turbulent years that followed, the period before the war seemed ______ and serene.
The contrast with 'turbulent' and the pairing with 'serene' show the blank means peaceful and happy.
se: He looked back fondly on the ______ days of childhood, free of bills and deadlines.
idyllic
Both 'halcyon' and 'idyllic' describe a happy, untroubled time.

m: stubbornly determined to do what one wants, ignoring advice
x: My headstrong little sister insisted on walking to school alone, despite the pouring rain.
The headstrong new director ignored the board's advice and launched the product early.
As a headstrong student, he refused to change his thesis topic even when his supervisor objected.
Headstrong investors who ignore warning signs often lose the most when the market crashes.
Her parents worried that she was too headstrong to listen to anyone's advice about her future.
tc: Ignoring every warning from his more cautious advisers, the ______ king marched his army into the mountains.
'Ignoring every warning' shows the blank means stubbornly self-willed.
se: The ______ teenager refused to listen to anyone who told her the plan was risky.
stubborn
Both 'headstrong' and 'stubborn' describe someone who refuses to take advice.

m: showing a reckless lack of care or attention to warnings or consequences
x: Heedless of the traffic, the boy ran across the road after his cricket ball.
The company pushed ahead with the merger, heedless of warnings from its own lawyers.
Heedless of the deadline, he spent the whole evening watching football instead of studying.
Heedless development along the coast has destroyed much of the mangrove forest.
She was heedless of her friends' advice and moved in with him after just two weeks.
tc: Though everyone urged caution, he remained ______ of the risks and climbed the cliff without a rope.
'Though everyone urged caution' contrasts with the blank, which means paying no attention.
se: ______ of the storm warnings, the fishermen set out to sea at dawn.
unmindful
Both 'heedless of' and 'unmindful of' mean ignoring the warnings.

m: holding or expressing opinions sharply opposed to accepted or official beliefs
x: At my family's dinner table, preferring coffee to tea is practically heretical.
Suggesting a four-day work week was considered heretical in our office until last year.
Her heretical theory about the origins of the language was rejected by most linguists for decades.
In the seventeenth century, claiming that the Earth moved around the Sun was deemed heretical.
He confessed the heretical opinion that he had never enjoyed the novel everyone else loved.
tc: The economist's views, once dismissed as ______, have now become the accepted orthodoxy.
'Once' contrasts with 'now ... accepted orthodoxy', so the blank means opposed to accepted belief.
se: In a department devoted to classical theory, her ______ approach made her many enemies.
unorthodox
Both 'heretical' and 'unorthodox' mean going against established views.

m: worshipping idols, or showing excessive and uncritical admiration for someone or something
x: Some fans' idolatrous devotion to the band borders on the absurd.
The staff's idolatrous attitude toward the founder made it hard to question any of his decisions.
The historian described the idolatrous cults that flourished in the ancient city.
Critics warned against an idolatrous faith in technology as the answer to every social problem.
His idolatrous admiration for his older brother blinded him to his brother's faults.
tc: The young fan's devotion was so excessive and uncritical that it could only be called ______.
'Excessive and uncritical' devotion defines worship-like admiration.
se: The ______ fans treated the singer almost as a god, cheering wildly at her every word.
adoring
Both 'idolatrous' and 'adoring' describe fans who worship the singer.

m: dishonorable and shameful; not deserving respect
x: Pushing past an old man to get the last seat on the bus felt like an ignoble victory.
He refused to win the promotion by the ignoble tactic of taking credit for others' work.
The paper traces the ignoble history of fraudulent research in the field.
The government's ignoble retreat from its election promises angered many voters.
She was ashamed of the ignoble jealousy she felt when her best friend got engaged.
tc: Far from acting out of noble principle, the senator was driven by ______ motives of greed and revenge.
'Far from ... noble principle' and 'greed and revenge' show the blank means dishonorable.
se: Abandoning his teammates to save himself was an act that many considered deeply ______.
dishonorable
Both 'ignoble' and 'dishonorable' mean shameful and unworthy of respect.

m: forbidden by law, rules or custom
x: Police raided a warehouse storing illicit liquor in the old part of the city.
Two employees were fired for running an illicit side business on company computers.
The university has strict penalties for the illicit sale of exam papers.
Customs officers seized illicit drugs worth millions at the port.
Their illicit affair had been going on for years before his wife discovered it.
tc: Unlike the licensed vendors in the market, these traders dealt in ______ goods smuggled across the border.
The contrast with 'licensed' and the word 'smuggled' show the blank means illegal.
se: The investigation uncovered ______ payments made to customs officials.
illegal
Both 'illicit' and 'illegal' mean the payments broke the law.

m: unchanging over time or impossible to change
x: In our house, Sunday lunch at my grandmother's is an immutable tradition.
The company treats its founding principles as immutable, and they have never been revised.
Physicists once assumed that the laws of nature were immutable across the entire universe.
Constitutional rights should not be treated as immutable if society's needs change.
He believed his feelings for her were immutable, but time proved him wrong.
tc: Unlike fashion, which changes every season, the basic laws of mathematics are ______.
The contrast with fashion that 'changes every season' shows the blank means unchanging.
se: Many religions teach that certain moral truths are ______ and cannot be altered by human opinion.
unchangeable
Both 'immutable' and 'unchangeable' mean the truths can never be altered.

m: flawless; meeting the highest standards
x: The hotel's service was impeccable, from the doorman to the housekeeping staff.
His impeccable record of punctuality earned him the employee of the year award.
The examiners praised the thesis for its impeccable research and clear argument.
Her impeccable English surprised the interviewers, who assumed she must have lived abroad.
He had impeccable manners, always standing up when an elder entered the room.
tc: The pianist's performance was ______; even the harshest critics could not find a single wrong note.
'Could not find a single wrong note' shows the blank means flawless.
se: She has ______ taste in clothes, so I always ask her advice before a big event.
flawless
Both 'impeccable' and 'flawless' mean her taste has no faults.

m: arrogant and domineering; expecting to be obeyed without question
x: With an imperious wave of her hand, the customer sent the soup back to the kitchen.
The new manager's imperious style quickly alienated even the most loyal employees.
The professor answered our questions in an imperious tone that discouraged further discussion.
The colonial governor's imperious decrees provoked protests across the province.
Her imperious mother-in-law expected to be consulted on every family decision.
tc: Unlike his gentle predecessor, the new headmaster was ______, issuing orders and expecting instant obedience.
The contrast with 'gentle' and 'expecting instant obedience' show the blank means domineering.
se: Staff resented the director's ______ manner, which left no room for discussion.
overbearing
Both 'imperious' and 'overbearing' describe a bossy, arrogant manner.

m: not seeming reasonable or likely; hard to believe
x: His excuse that the dog had chewed up his phone charger sounded implausible.
The auditors found it implausible that a single clerk had approved such large payments.
The theory is elegant but implausible, since it contradicts most of the available data.
Investigators dismissed the company's claim that the leak was caused by sabotage as implausible.
It seemed implausible that she would forgive him so quickly, yet she did.
tc: The detective found the suspect's alibi ______, since it required him to have been in two cities at once.
Being 'in two cities at once' is impossible, so the alibi is hard to believe.
se: The novel's plot is so ______ that even devoted fans struggled to believe it.
improbable
Both 'implausible' and 'improbable' mean unlikely to be true.

m: to ask someone persistently and annoyingly for something; to pester
x: Street vendors importuned tourists at every corner of the old market.
She grew tired of salespeople importuning her with calls about new credit cards.
Students importuned the professor for hints about the final exam until she finally left the room.
The charity was criticized for importuning elderly donors with repeated letters asking for money.
He importuned his father for weeks before finally getting permission to study abroad.
tc: The child continued to ______ his mother for sweets, asking again and again until she finally gave in.
'Asking again and again' defines the blank as persistent begging.
se: Fundraisers were told not to ______ donors who had already declined to give.
pester
Both 'importune' and 'pester' mean to keep asking annoyingly.

m: clear-thinking and sharply analytical; going straight to the heart of a matter
x: My roommate asked an incisive question that exposed the flaw in my plan.
Her incisive analysis of the budget saved the department from a costly mistake.
The examiner praised the essay's incisive critique of modern economic theory.
The journalist is known for incisive reporting that cuts through official spin.
He has an incisive mind, but he can sometimes be too blunt with the people he loves.
tc: Rather than offering vague generalities, the critic made ______ comments that went straight to the heart of the novel's weaknesses.
The contrast with 'vague generalities' and 'went straight to the heart' show the blank means sharply analytical.
se: Her ______ questions quickly revealed the gaps in the witness's story.
sharp
Both 'incisive' and 'sharp' describe questions that cut to the key issue.

m: impossible to deny or dispute
x: The security camera footage was incontrovertible proof that our neighbor had taken the parcel.
The auditors presented incontrovertible evidence that the figures had been manipulated.
It is an incontrovertible fact that smoking increases the risk of lung cancer.
Most scientists now regard the link between human activity and global warming as incontrovertible.
Her love for her children was incontrovertible, even when she was strict with them.
tc: Once the DNA results came back, the evidence was ______, and even the defense stopped arguing.
'Even the defense stopped arguing' shows the evidence could not be disputed.
se: The prosecutor claimed to have ______ proof of the defendant's guilt.
irrefutable
Both 'incontrovertible' and 'irrefutable' mean the proof cannot be denied.

m: unable to be corrected or reformed, describing a person or a habit
x: My uncle is an incorrigible flirt, even at the age of seventy.
Our incorrigible office prankster has hidden the manager's stapler in the freezer again.
The teacher eventually gave up on the incorrigible student who skipped class every Friday.
Critics say the prison system treats young offenders as incorrigible instead of helping them reform.
She is an incorrigible optimist who believes every setback is secretly an opportunity.
tc: Despite years of punishment and counseling, the thief remained ______, returning to crime as soon as he was released.
Returning to crime 'despite years of punishment and counseling' shows he could not be reformed.
se: Everyone in the family knew he was ______ and would never stop gambling.
hopeless
Both 'incorrigible' and 'hopeless' mean he was beyond reform.

m: extremely poor; lacking money for basic needs
x: The clinic offers free care to indigent patients who cannot afford medicine.
Our law firm takes on several cases each year for indigent clients at no charge.
The study tracked the health of indigent families in rural areas over ten years.
The court must appoint a lawyer for indigent defendants who cannot pay for one.
My grandmother never forgot the indigent childhood she endured after the war.
tc: The charity serves ______ families who lack the money for even basic food and shelter.
'Lack the money for even basic food and shelter' defines the blank as extremely poor.
se: The new law guarantees free legal representation to ______ defendants.
needy
Both 'indigent' and 'needy' describe defendants too poor to pay.

m: impossible to defeat, subdue or discourage
x: Despite losing her job and her home, my aunt kept her indomitable sense of humor.
The team's indomitable spirit helped them meet the deadline despite three server crashes.
Her indomitable will carried her through years of night classes while working full time.
After the cyclone, the villagers rebuilt their homes with indomitable courage.
His indomitable mother raised four children alone and put all of them through university.
tc: Though repeatedly defeated and imprisoned, the rebel leader's will remained ______, and he never considered surrender.
'Never considered surrender' despite defeats shows the blank means unconquerable.
se: The marathon runner showed ______ determination, finishing the race despite a broken toe.
unyielding
Both 'indomitable' and 'unyielding' describe determination that cannot be broken.

m: lacking skill or ability; clumsy or incompetent
x: I'm hopelessly inept at fixing anything electrical, so I always call a technician.
The project failed because of inept management and constant changes in direction.
His inept handling of the lab equipment broke two expensive microscopes in a week.
Critics blamed inept planning for the long queues at polling stations.
He made an inept attempt to comfort her, which only made her cry harder.
tc: Unlike his ______ predecessor, who mishandled every crisis, the new minister proved highly competent.
'Mishandled every crisis' and the contrast with 'highly competent' show the blank means incompetent.
se: The agency was widely criticized for its ______ response to the emergency.
incompetent
Both 'inept' and 'incompetent' mean the response showed a lack of skill.

m: impossible to explain or account for
x: For some inexplicable reason, my phone keeps turning itself off at midnight.
The sudden drop in sales was inexplicable until we discovered a bug on the website.
Researchers are puzzled by the inexplicable rise in insect deaths across the region.
His decision to resign just before the election remains inexplicable to many supporters.
She felt an inexplicable sadness every time she heard that old song.
tc: Scientists could offer no account of the strange lights in the sky; the phenomenon remained ______.
'Could offer no account' shows the blank means unable to be explained.
se: For some ______ reason, the office printer only jams on Tuesdays.
unaccountable
Both 'inexplicable' and 'unaccountable' mean the reason cannot be explained.

m: to try to win someone's favor, especially by flattery or eagerness to please (used with oneself)
x: He tried to ingratiate himself with his new neighbors by bringing them homemade sweets.
The intern ingratiated herself with the manager by laughing loudly at all his jokes.
Some students try to ingratiate themselves with lecturers by sitting in the front row and nodding constantly.
The candidate tried to ingratiate himself with farmers by promising cheaper fertilizer.
She refused to ingratiate herself with her boyfriend's family by pretending to love cricket.
tc: Eager to win the boss's favor, he praised every idea she had in an attempt to ______ himself with her.
'Eager to win the boss's favor' and praising every idea show the blank means to gain favor by flattery.
se: Hoping for a promotion, the new recruit tried to ______ himself by flattering the senior partners at every opportunity.
endear
Both 'ingratiate himself' and 'endear himself' mean making himself liked to win favor.

m: spreading gradually and subtly, but with harmful effects
x: Mold is insidious; by the time you smell it, it may already have spread through the walls.
Office gossip can have an insidious effect on team morale.
The study examined the insidious influence of advertising on children's eating habits.
High blood pressure is an insidious condition that often shows no symptoms for years.
Her jealousy was insidious, slowly poisoning a friendship that had lasted since childhood.
tc: The disease is especially ______ because it causes no obvious symptoms until the damage is already severe.
Hidden symptoms while serious damage develops show the blank means harmful in a gradual, hidden way.
se: Experts warned of the ______ spread of misinformation, which damages public trust slowly and almost invisibly.
stealthy
Both 'insidious' and 'stealthy' describe a harmful spread that is hard to notice.

m: rude and openly disrespectful
x: The insolent teenager rolled his eyes and walked away while his father was still talking.
He was fired after sending an insolent reply to the director's email.
The headmaster would not tolerate insolent remarks from students during assembly.
Protesters were furious at the official's insolent claim that they had been paid to attend.
She could not forgive his insolent tone when she had only asked where he had been.
tc: Instead of answering the judge respectfully, the witness was ______, mocking the court with every reply.
