The contrast with 'respectfully' and 'mocking the court' show the blank means disrespectful.
se: The student's ______ remarks to the teacher earned him a week of detention.
impertinent
Both 'insolent' and 'impertinent' mean rudely disrespectful.

m: belonging naturally to something; part of its basic nature
x: A good friendship has intrinsic value, regardless of what you gain from it.
Flexible hours are intrinsic to the company's culture, not just a perk.
Educators debate whether students learn better through intrinsic motivation or external rewards.
Gold has little intrinsic usefulness, yet societies have prized it for thousands of years.
Her kindness seemed intrinsic to her character, not something she put on for others.
tc: The painting's value is ______ rather than external; it comes from the work itself, not from its famous owner.
'Rather than external' and 'comes from the work itself' show the blank means inherent.
se: Risk is ______ to any business venture; it can never be avoided entirely.
inherent
Both 'intrinsic' and 'inherent' mean risk is a built-in part of business.

m: impossible to change, reverse or undo; final
x: Once you click send, the email is irrevocable, so read it twice before you do.
Signing the contract was an irrevocable step that committed the firm for ten years.
The scholarship committee's decision is irrevocable, so appeals will not be considered.
Scientists warn that some damage to coral reefs may already be irrevocable.
Their quarrel caused an irrevocable break in a friendship that had lasted thirty years.
tc: Think carefully before you sign, because the agreement is ______ and cannot be canceled later.
'Cannot be canceled later' defines the blank as impossible to reverse.
se: The judge warned that the ruling was ______ and could not be appealed.
final
Both 'irrevocable' and 'final' mean the ruling cannot be changed.

m: traveling from place to place, especially to find or do work
x: An itinerant knife sharpener comes through our neighborhood every Friday, calling out his trade.
As an itinerant consultant, she spends more nights in hotels than in her own apartment.
Many itinerant scholars in medieval Europe moved from one university to another.
The government is trying to count the itinerant workers who follow the harvest from region to region.
His itinerant childhood, moving from town to town, made it hard for him to keep friends.
tc: Unlike the settled farmers of the valley, the ______ traders never stayed in one village for more than a few days.
The contrast with 'settled' and 'never stayed in one village' show the blank means traveling.
se: In his youth he was ______, playing music in a different town each night.
nomadic
Both 'itinerant' and 'nomadic' mean constantly moving from place to place.

m: having or showing good judgment; wise and sensible
x: With judicious use of leftovers, she fed the family for a week on a tiny budget.
The manager made a judicious decision to delay the launch until the bugs were fixed.
Judicious editing turned his rambling draft into a sharp, persuasive essay.
The central bank's judicious handling of interest rates helped the country avoid a recession.
A judicious friend knows when to give advice and when simply to listen.
tc: Rather than spending recklessly, the new treasurer made ______ cuts that saved money without hurting essential services.
The contrast with 'spending recklessly' and the careful result show the blank means wise.
se: With ______ planning, the small charity managed to stretch its budget through the whole year.
prudent
Both 'judicious' and 'prudent' mean showing careful good sense.

m: lacking energy; slow and relaxed, often in a pleasant way
x: We spent a languid Sunday afternoon reading on the veranda while the rain fell.
After lunch, the office fell into a languid silence broken only by the hum of the air conditioner.
The heat made the students languid, and few of them followed the lecture.
The economy's languid recovery has left many young graduates without jobs.
She gave him a languid smile and stretched out on the sofa beside him.
tc: Unlike her energetic younger sister, she moved through the day at a slow, ______ pace.
The contrast with 'energetic' and the word 'slow' show the blank means lacking energy.
se: The summer heat left the whole village feeling ______ and unwilling to work.
lethargic
Both 'languid' and 'lethargic' mean drained of energy.

m: existing but not yet developed, active or visible; hidden
x: Moving abroad for university brought out his latent talent for cooking.
The training program aims to uncover latent leadership skills in junior staff.
Some viruses remain latent in the body for years before causing any symptoms.
The scandal brought latent tensions within the coalition government into the open.
His latent resentment toward his brother surfaced during the argument over their father's will.
tc: The virus can remain ______ for decades, causing no symptoms until the immune system weakens.
'Causing no symptoms' for decades shows the blank means present but inactive.
se: The coach believed every child had ______ ability that only needed the right encouragement.
untapped
Both 'latent' and 'untapped' describe ability that exists but has not yet been developed.

m: to praise highly, especially in public
x: Our neighbors lauded the young man who pulled a child out of the flooded canal.
The chairman lauded the team's efforts at the annual staff meeting.
The journal lauded her paper as the most important contribution to the field in a decade.
Critics lauded the new film for its honest portrayal of life in the city's slums.
He never lauds his wife in public, but he is clearly very proud of her.
tc: Although critics once mocked the architect's designs, they now ______ her as a visionary.
'Although ... once mocked' sets up a contrast, so the blank means to praise.
se: Speakers at the ceremony rose one after another to ______ the retiring teacher's dedication.
praise
Both 'laud' and 'praise' mean to speak highly of the teacher's dedication.

m: very rich, elaborate or generous, often to the point of excess
x: My cousin's wedding was a lavish affair, with three days of feasts and over a thousand guests.
The company cut back on lavish parties after a disappointing year.
The review was lavish in its praise of the young author's first novel.
Officials were criticized for lavish spending on luxury cars and foreign trips.
He showered her with lavish gifts, but what she really wanted was his time.
tc: Instead of the modest celebration they had planned, his parents threw a party so ______ that it included a live band, fireworks and a five-course dinner.
The contrast with 'modest' and the list of extravagances show the blank means luxurious.
se: The minister faced criticism for the ______ banquet held while the country was in recession.
extravagant
Both 'lavish' and 'extravagant' describe a banquet that was excessively costly.

m: not strict, careful or firm enough
x: My parents were lax about bedtimes, so we often stayed up late watching cricket.
Lax security at the warehouse allowed thieves to steal goods for months.
Some teachers are lax about deadlines, which only encourages students to procrastinate.
Investigators blamed lax building regulations for the collapse of the garment factory.
He admitted he had been lax about keeping in touch with his old friends.
tc: Because enforcement had been so ______, few drivers bothered to obey the new speed limit.
Drivers ignoring the limit 'because' of enforcement shows the blank means not strict.
se: Regulators were accused of being ______ in their oversight of the banks.
remiss
Both 'lax' and 'remiss' mean failing to be careful or strict enough.

m: able to cause death; extremely harmful or destructive
x: Mixing those two cleaning products can create a lethal gas, so always store them apart.
Faulty wiring in the old office building posed a lethal fire risk.
The laboratory handles lethal viruses only under the strictest safety conditions.
Doctors warn that a lethal dose of the painkiller is surprisingly small.
Her sharp tongue could be lethal when she was really angry.
tc: Even a tiny amount of the toxin can be ______, so researchers handle it with extreme care.
'Toxin' and 'extreme care' show the blank means deadly.
se: The snake's venom is ______ to humans if the bite is left untreated.
deadly
Both 'lethal' and 'deadly' mean capable of causing death.

m: having or showing a wish to do harm to others
x: The old caretaker gave us such a malevolent stare that we left the garden without another word.
Office gossip turned malevolent when someone began spreading rumors meant to get a colleague fired.
In the novel, the narrator slowly realizes that the kindly uncle has a malevolent purpose.
Investigators found no malevolent intent behind the data leak, only a careless mistake by an engineer.
She couldn't believe her closest friend had been capable of such malevolent jealousy.
tc: Far from being the harmless prank the boys claimed it was, the act was clearly ______, designed to hurt someone who had never wronged them.
'Far from ... harmless' and 'designed to hurt' show that the blank must mean wishing harm.
se: The villagers believed the abandoned house was haunted by spirits that were ______ and meant them harm.
malicious
Both 'malevolent' and 'malicious' describe a desire to cause harm, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: to pretend to be ill in order to avoid work or duty
x: Whenever there was a maths test, my younger brother would malinger, complaining of a mysterious stomachache.
The manager suspected that some staff were malingering, since sick days always spiked on Mondays.
Army doctors were trained to tell genuinely wounded soldiers from those who were merely malingering.
A new report suggests that very few workers actually malinger; most sick leave is genuine.
He felt guilty for malingering at home while his friends helped clean up after the flood.
tc: Although the doctor could find nothing wrong with him, the soldier continued to ______, reporting a fever whenever a long march was announced.
Claiming illness with no medical cause, conveniently timed to avoid marches, signals faking sickness to escape duty.
se: Too proud to ______, the old farmer worked through his fever while younger men stayed home with minor colds.
shirk
Both 'malinger' and 'shirk' mean avoiding one's work, which the farmer refuses to do.

m: lacking in quantity or quality; barely enough
x: After paying rent and bills, there was only a meager amount left for groceries each month.
Despite meager resources, the small startup built an app that thousands of people now use daily.
As a research student, she lived on a meager stipend and shared a room with two others.
Farmers in the district complained that the meager rainfall had ruined most of the rice crop.
He was hurt by the meager praise his father offered after he passed the university admission test.
tc: The aid agency had hoped for generous donations, but the response was ______, barely enough to feed the village for a week.
'Hoped for generous' sets up a contrast, and 'barely enough' restates the meaning of scanty.
se: Workers struggled to support their families on wages that were ______ even by local standards.
paltry
Both 'meager' and 'paltry' mean too small to be adequate, giving the same sense.

m: of only average or ordinary quality; not very good
x: We waited forty minutes for a table and then got a mediocre meal at a high price.
His work was mediocre at best, so nobody was surprised when he was passed over for promotion.
The professor warned us that copying from textbooks would produce mediocre essays and mediocre grades.
Critics argued that the film's mediocre script wasted a remarkably talented cast.
She refused to settle for a mediocre relationship just because she was afraid of being alone.
tc: The reviews had promised a remarkable dining experience, but the food turned out to be ______, neither bad nor memorable.
The contrast with 'remarkable' and the restatement 'neither bad nor memorable' point to merely average.
se: Despite its huge budget, the sequel was ______, offering little that audiences had not seen before.
undistinguished
Both 'mediocre' and 'undistinguished' mean ordinary and unimpressive, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: motivated mainly by a desire for money, even at the expense of ethics
x: It felt mercenary to charge my own cousin a fee for helping with his visa forms.
Employees grew cynical about the firm's mercenary culture, where every decision came down to quarterly profit.
Some academics criticize universities for taking a mercenary approach to international students' fees.
The landlord's mercenary decision to triple rents after the flood angered the whole neighborhood.
She began to suspect that his interest in her was purely mercenary when he kept asking about her inheritance.
tc: Unlike her predecessor, who ran the clinic as a charity, the new director was openly ______, cutting free services to raise profits.
'Unlike ... a charity' and 'cutting free services to raise profits' signal a focus on money.
se: Voters were disgusted by the councillor's ______ habit of supporting whichever developer offered him the largest payment.
venal
Both 'mercenary' and 'venal' describe someone whose choices are driven by money, so the sentence means the same.

m: in terminal decline; losing vitality and close to ending
x: The once-busy market street looked moribund, with half its shops shuttered and empty.
The new CEO was hired to revive a moribund company that hadn't launched a successful product in years.
Linguists are racing to record moribund languages before their last speakers pass away.
Economists warned that the moribund textile sector needed urgent investment to save thousands of jobs.
By the end, their marriage was moribund, kept alive only by habit and concern for the children.
tc: Once the heart of the town's economy, the jute mill was now ______, with most of its machines silent and its workforce reduced to a handful.
'Once the heart' contrasts with silent machines and a tiny workforce, pointing to something in decline.
se: Only a fresh wave of investment could revive the ______ shipbuilding industry.
stagnant
Both 'moribund' and 'stagnant' describe an industry lacking life and growth that needs reviving.

m: showing a lack of experience or judgment; too ready to trust or believe
x: It was naive of me to think the bus would actually arrive on time during rush hour.
New interns are often naive about office politics and say exactly what they think in meetings.
Reviewers called the paper's assumptions naive, since they ignored how people actually behave under stress.
Critics say it is naive to expect a single law to end corruption overnight.
She was naive enough to believe he would change after the wedding.
tc: Experienced traders laughed at the newcomer's ______ belief that the market could only go up.
'Newcomer' and the unrealistic belief mocked by experienced traders signal inexperience.
se: He was ______ enough to believe the stranger who promised to double his money in a week.
gullible
Both 'naive' and 'gullible' mean too easily deceived, giving the same meaning.

m: unclear, vague, or poorly defined
x: My plans for the weekend are still nebulous; I might visit my aunt or just stay home.
The client gave us a nebulous brief and then complained when the design wasn't what he wanted.
Her supervisor told her the thesis topic was too nebulous and needed a sharper research question.
Voters grew frustrated with the candidate's nebulous promises of 'change' that came with no actual policies.
Her feelings for him remained nebulous, somewhere between friendship and something she couldn't name.
tc: The professor asked the student to replace his ______ thesis statement with one that made a specific, arguable claim.
The statement must be replaced by a 'specific' one, so the blank means vague.
se: Investors were unwilling to fund a startup whose business plan was so ______.
vague
Both 'nebulous' and 'vague' mean unclear and poorly defined, so the sentence means the same.

m: appearing casually calm and unconcerned
x: He tried to look nonchalant as he walked past the girl he liked, but he tripped on the stairs.
Despite the looming deadline, Rafiq was surprisingly nonchalant and even took a long lunch.
Her nonchalant answers during the viva impressed the examiners, who had expected her to be nervous.
Residents have become nonchalant about the regular power cuts, simply lighting candles and carrying on.
His nonchalant shrug when I said I was leaving hurt more than an argument would have.
tc: Although his heart was pounding, he waved in a manner so ______ that everyone assumed winning the award meant nothing to him.
'Although his heart was pounding' sets up a contrast with an outward show of calm unconcern.
se: She remained ______ when the flight was cancelled, calmly booking another one on her phone.
unconcerned
Both 'nonchalant' and 'unconcerned' describe calm indifference to a problem.

m: new and original; unlike anything seen before
x: Using a rice cooker to bake a cake was a novel idea, and it worked surprisingly well.
The team proposed a novel approach to scheduling that cut overtime by almost a third.
Her dissertation offers a novel interpretation of Tagore's early poems and their politics.
Scientists have identified a novel virus in bats that has not been described before.
Falling in love at fifty was a novel experience for him, and it made him feel young again.
tc: The engineer's design was genuinely ______; no one had ever thought of cooling a building with recycled rainwater in that way.
'No one had ever thought of' restates the idea of something new and original.
se: Reviewers praised the researchers for their ______ method, which no earlier study had attempted.
innovative
Both 'novel' and 'innovative' mean new and original, which matches 'no earlier study had attempted'.

m: not well known, or not clearly expressed and therefore hard to understand
x: We finally found the cafe tucked away down an obscure lane behind the old mosque.
The lawyer pointed out an obscure clause in the contract that nobody else had noticed.
His thesis cites several obscure journals that even the university library could not locate.
Before her discovery, she was an obscure researcher working in a tiny lab outside the capital.
For some obscure reason, he stopped answering my calls after the party.
tc: Although the composer is celebrated today, he died ______, his music unknown beyond a small circle of friends.
'Although ... celebrated today' contrasts with 'unknown beyond a small circle', so the blank means little known.
se: The quiz question was so ______ that none of the contestants had ever heard of the poet it mentioned.
arcane
Both 'obscure' and 'arcane' describe knowledge so little known that almost nobody has it.

m: no longer used or produced; out of date
x: My grandfather still keeps his obsolete Nokia phone in a drawer, just in case.
Much of the office software was obsolete, so the IT team spent the summer upgrading every computer.
Some textbooks in the library are so obsolete that they still describe Pluto as a planet.
Experts fear automation could make many routine jobs obsolete within a decade.
After the divorce, she felt that her old idea of marriage had become obsolete.
tc: Once essential in every office, the fax machine has been rendered ______ by email and cloud storage.
'Once essential' contrasts with being replaced by newer technology, so the blank means out of date.
se: The factory's machinery was so ______ that spare parts could no longer be found.
antiquated
Both 'obsolete' and 'antiquated' mean too old to be supported or used, so the meaning is the same.

m: not able to be seen through; hard to understand or explain
x: The bathroom window is made of opaque glass, so nobody can see in from the street.
Staff complained that the promotion process was opaque and seemed to depend on who you knew.
Many students find the philosopher's prose opaque until a teacher explains his key terms.
Activists criticized the government's opaque handling of the contract, which was never put to public tender.
His motives remained opaque to her, even after years of living together.
tc: Critics complained that the bank's lending decisions were ______, since it never explained why some applications were rejected.
'Never explained why' shows the decisions were hard to understand or see into.
se: The legal document was written in language so ______ that even the lawyers disagreed about what it meant.
impenetrable
Both 'opaque' and 'impenetrable' describe language too difficult to understand.

m: showing great wealth and luxury, often in a showy way
x: The wedding was held in an opulent hotel ballroom with crystal chandeliers and gold-trimmed chairs.
Clients were impressed by the firm's opulent offices, though some wondered who was paying for them.
Historians have studied the opulent lifestyle of the Mughal emperors through surviving court paintings.
The mayor's opulent new mansion raised questions about how he could afford it on a public salary.
She grew up in opulent surroundings but felt lonely in a house full of servants.
tc: Unlike the austere monastery where he had spent his youth, the merchant's home was ______, filled with silk carpets and gilded furniture.
'Unlike the austere monastery' and 'silk carpets and gilded furniture' point to rich luxury.
se: Guests were dazzled by the ______ decor of the palace, with its marble floors and velvet curtains.
sumptuous
Both 'opulent' and 'sumptuous' mean splendid and expensive-looking, giving the same meaning.

m: elaborately or excessively decorated
x: The ornate wooden door of my grandmother's house was carved by hand over a century ago.
Our boss dislikes ornate slides and asks us to keep presentations plain and simple.
Modern editors often trim the ornate prose of Victorian novels for younger readers.
Restorers spent two years repairing the ornate ceiling of the old city hall.
She wrote him an ornate love letter, full of flowery phrases he found a little embarrassing.
tc: The architect rejected the client's request for ______ columns, preferring clean lines and no decoration at all.
'Preferring clean lines and no decoration' contrasts with the client's wish, so the blank means heavily decorated.
se: The palace gates were so ______ that every inch was covered with carved flowers and vines.
elaborate
Both 'ornate' and 'elaborate' describe detailed, heavy decoration.

m: following traditional or generally accepted beliefs and practices
x: My parents have fairly orthodox views about marriage and expect me to settle down soon.
The manager rejected the orthodox approach and let the team set its own working hours.
Her findings challenge the orthodox view that the river changed course only once.
Orthodox economists warned that printing more money would simply drive inflation higher.
Coming from an orthodox family, he hesitated before telling them about his girlfriend.
tc: Rejecting the ______ methods, the coach had his bowlers train with tennis balls and blindfolds, to the horror of the selectors.
The selectors' horror at the strange training shows the coach rejected traditional methods.
se: Most doctors still prefer ______ treatments to the experimental therapies advertised online.
conventional
Both 'orthodox' and 'conventional' mean standard and accepted, in contrast to 'experimental'.

m: to exclude someone from a group or from society
x: Kids at school began to ostracize him after he reported the bullying to a teacher.
She was quietly ostracized at work after she questioned the director's expense claims.
Scholars who challenged the dominant theory were often ostracized by their own departments.
In some villages, families who marry outside their caste are still ostracized by their neighbors.
He feared his friends would ostracize him if he admitted he didn't drink.
tc: Instead of welcoming the whistle-blower as a hero, his colleagues chose to ______ him, refusing to speak to him or sit with him at lunch.
'Instead of welcoming' and 'refusing to speak to him' show he was shut out of the group.
se: The club voted to ______ any member caught cheating, banning them from all future events.
exclude
Both 'ostracize' and 'exclude' mean to shut someone out of the group, matching 'banning them'.

m: pale and unhealthy-looking; also lacking color, energy or interest
x: After a week of fever, his face was pallid and his eyes looked sunken.
Months of working night shifts under fluorescent lights had left her skin pallid.
The critic dismissed the novel as a pallid imitation of the author's earlier masterpiece.
Doctors noticed that many children in the slum were pallid and underweight, a sign of anemia.
Her pallid smile told me she was still upset about the argument.
tc: After months in the dim hospital ward, the once ruddy farmer looked ______ and frail.
'Once ruddy' sets up a contrast, so he now looks pale and unhealthy.
se: Her face turned ______ when the doctor said he needed to run more tests.
ashen
Both 'pallid' and 'ashen' describe a face drained of color by shock or fear.

m: a typical model or pattern; a widely accepted set of ideas and methods
x: For my mother, a government job was the paradigm of security, so she was shocked when I joined a startup.
Remote work has replaced the old paradigm of everyone sitting in the same office from nine to five.
Thomas Kuhn argued that science advances through occasional shifts from one paradigm to another.
The discovery of germs created a new paradigm in medicine and transformed public health.
Their marriage was hardly a paradigm of harmony, but they always supported each other in a crisis.
tc: Einstein's theory did not merely refine Newton's physics; it replaced the entire ______, forcing scientists to rethink space and time.
'Did not merely refine ... replaced the entire' points to a whole accepted framework of ideas.
se: The school's teaching method became the ______ that other institutions across the country tried to copy.
model
Both 'paradigm' and 'model' mean an example others follow, matching 'tried to copy'.

m: a statement or situation that seems self-contradictory but may still be true
x: It's a paradox that the more apps I install to save time, the less free time I seem to have.
Managers face the paradox of needing to cut costs while also being told to invest in growth.
Students in the logic class spent an hour debating the famous liar paradox.
Researchers describe it as a paradox that countries rich in oil often grow more slowly than those without it.
The paradox of their friendship was that they argued constantly yet couldn't bear to be apart.
tc: It seems the ultimate ______: the healthiest nation in the region is also the one that spends the least on medicine.
The colon introduces two facts that seem to contradict each other, which defines the blank.
se: Here is the ______ of modern life: we are more connected than ever, yet many of us feel isolated.
contradiction
Both 'paradox' and 'contradiction' describe the clash between being connected and feeling isolated.

m: a person or group rejected and avoided by others; an outcast
x: After he cheated in the final, he became a pariah in the neighborhood cricket club.
Once the fraud was exposed, the former star manager found himself a pariah in the industry.
Scientists who questioned the theory were treated as pariahs at international conferences.
The regime became an international pariah after it was found to be developing chemical weapons.
Having refused to attend her cousin's wedding, she felt like a pariah at every family gathering.
tc: Once celebrated as the town's hero, he became its ______ after the scandal, shunned by everyone who had once praised him.
'Once celebrated' contrasts with being 'shunned by everyone', so the blank means outcast.
se: After testifying against his own friends, he was treated as the village ______ and left to eat alone.
outcast
Both 'pariah' and 'outcast' mean someone rejected by the community.

m: an imitation that exaggerates a style for comic effect; also a poor, absurd imitation
x: My little sister did a hilarious parody of our father reading the newspaper.
At the office party, the interns performed a parody of our weekly management meeting.
The students wrote a parody of a Shakespeare sonnet about exam stress.
Critics described the rigged election as a parody of democracy, with only one candidate allowed to campaign.
He laughed at her parody of his accent, but secretly it stung a little.
tc: With the verdict decided before a single witness spoke, observers described the trial as a mere ______ of justice.
A verdict decided in advance means the trial only imitated justice in an absurd way.
se: The comedian's ______ of a television chef, complete with burnt food and fake French, had the audience in tears of laughter.
spoof
Both 'parody' and 'spoof' mean a comic, exaggerated imitation.

m: to treat someone as if they were less intelligent or important than you
x: Please don't patronize me; I know perfectly well how to use a washing machine.
New graduates often feel that senior colleagues patronize them in meetings.
The textbook patronizes its readers by explaining every simple term three times.
Voters resent politicians who patronize them with slogans instead of real answers.
She felt patronized when her husband explained her own job to their guests.
tc: Although she was the most experienced engineer on the team, the new manager continued to ______ her, explaining basic concepts as if she were a trainee.
'Although ... most experienced' contrasts with being treated 'as if she were a trainee', which is condescension.
se: Good teachers guide their students without ever trying to ______ them.
belittle
Both 'patronize' and 'belittle' mean making someone feel inferior, so the sentence means the same.

m: expressing contempt or disapproval
x: In our house, 'lazy' was the most pejorative word you could use about anyone.
HR reminded staff that pejorative nicknames for colleagues would not be tolerated.
Linguists note that many words gain pejorative meanings over time, such as 'silly', which once meant blessed.
The newspaper was criticized for using pejorative terms to describe refugees arriving by boat.
He didn't mean 'stubborn' in a pejorative sense; he actually admired her determination.
tc: Although 'ambitious' is usually a compliment, in his letter the word was clearly ______, implying ruthless greed.
'Although ... usually a compliment' and 'implying ruthless greed' show the word was used disapprovingly.
se: Commentators objected to the ______ labels the minister used to describe protesters.
derogatory
Both 'pejorative' and 'derogatory' mean expressing contempt, so the meaning is the same.

m: quick to notice and understand things others might miss; insightful
x: My grandmother is very perceptive; she can tell I'm worried before I say a word.
A perceptive manager notices burnout early and adjusts workloads before people quit.
The examiner praised her perceptive analysis of the poem's hidden themes.
Perceptive observers had predicted the housing crash years before it actually happened.
He was perceptive enough to realize that her silence meant she was hurt, not angry.
tc: Unlike his ______ sister, who sensed trouble the moment they walked in, Karim noticed nothing wrong until the shouting began.
The sister 'sensed trouble the moment they walked in', in contrast to Karim, so she was quick to notice.
se: Her ______ comments in the seminar showed she had grasped the author's deeper intentions.
insightful
Both 'perceptive' and 'insightful' mean showing deep understanding.

m: insisting on immediate obedience in a rude, commanding way that allows no discussion
x: My landlord sent a peremptory text demanding the rent by tonight, with no greeting at all.
The director's peremptory tone in emails made junior staff afraid to ask questions.
The professor dismissed the student's question with a peremptory wave of the hand.
The judge issued a peremptory order for the factory to close until safety checks were completed.
She resented his peremptory way of deciding where they would eat without asking her.
tc: Rather than politely asking, the officer barked commands so ______ that no one dared to question them.
'Rather than politely asking' and 'no one dared to question' point to commanding, no-discussion orders.
se: The manager's ______ refusal to hear any objections offended the whole team.
imperious
Both 'peremptory' and 'imperious' describe an arrogant, commanding manner that allows no debate.

m: causing great harm, especially gradually or in a way that is not easily noticed
x: Mold can have a pernicious effect on your health if a damp apartment is never properly aired.
Office gossip can be pernicious, slowly eroding trust between departments.
The study examines the pernicious influence of rote learning on students' creativity.
Health officials warned about the pernicious spread of fake medical advice on social media.
His constant criticism had a pernicious effect on her confidence that lasted for years.
tc: Because its damage builds up slowly and unnoticed over many years, air pollution is perhaps the most ______ threat the city faces.
'Damage builds up slowly and unnoticed' defines a subtly harmful threat.
se: Experts warned that the ______ belief that girls are bad at mathematics still discourages many talented students.
damaging
Both 'pernicious' and 'damaging' mean causing harm, as the belief discourages students.

m: to make someone anxious, worried, or unsettled
x: Nothing seems to perturb my father, not even a flat tire in the middle of a storm.
The sudden resignation of the finance director perturbed investors, and the share price fell.
Reviewers' harsh comments did not perturb the young researcher, who calmly revised her paper.
Scientists are perturbed by data showing that the glacier is melting faster than predicted.
It perturbed her that he had not called since the night of their argument.
tc: Even the alarming rumors of layoffs did not ______ the veteran engineer, who had calmly survived many such scares before.
Having 'calmly survived many such scares' explains why the rumors failed to worry him.
se: The doctor's long silence as she studied the scan began to ______ the patient.
unsettle
Both 'perturb' and 'unsettle' mean to make someone anxious.

m: childishly sulky or bad-tempered when one does not get one's way
x: When we turned off the TV, my nephew gave a petulant whine and stomped off to his room.
The client's petulant emails, complaining about every tiny change, exhausted the whole design team.
The professor ignored the student's petulant demand for a higher mark.
Commentators described the losing candidate's speech as petulant rather than gracious.
She grew tired of his petulant sulking whenever she spent an evening with her friends.
tc: Instead of accepting defeat gracefully, the star player kicked the ball away and refused to shake hands, behaving as ______ as a toddler denied a toy.
'Instead of ... gracefully' and the comparison to a toddler denied a toy point to childish sulkiness.
se: He became ______ whenever his parents refused to buy him the latest phone.
sulky
Both 'petulant' and 'sulky' describe childish bad temper at not getting one's way.

m: helping others, especially by generously giving money to good causes
x: My uncle is quietly philanthropic, paying school fees for several children in his home village.
The company runs a philanthropic foundation that funds clean water projects in coastal areas.
Many universities depend on philanthropic gifts from alumni to fund scholarships.
The tycoon's philanthropic pledges were welcomed, though some critics questioned his motives.
She found her philanthropic work at the shelter more fulfilling than her well-paid corporate job.
tc: Far from being a selfish tycoon, the factory owner was deeply ______, giving away half his fortune to build hospitals.
'Far from being selfish' and 'giving away half his fortune' define generosity to others.
se: The couple's ______ donations have funded libraries in dozens of rural schools.
charitable
Both 'philanthropic' and 'charitable' describe giving money to help others.

m: calm and peaceful; not easily upset or excited
x: After the noise of Dhaka, the placid lake in the hills felt like another world.
Our placid team leader never raises her voice, even when a deadline is missed.
The placid surface of the pond allowed the students to measure ripple patterns accurately.
Scientists warn that the volcano's placid appearance hides a great deal of activity underground.
He was a placid child who rarely cried, which made his sudden tantrums all the more surprising.
tc: Although his brother was hot-tempered and restless, Arif was ______, rarely bothered by anything.
'Although ... hot-tempered and restless' sets up a contrast, and 'rarely bothered' restates calmness.
se: The horse was so ______ that even small children could ride it safely.
calm
Both 'placid' and 'calm' describe a gentle, unexcitable temperament.

m: seeming reasonable or likely to be true
x: Traffic on the airport road is a plausible excuse for being late, but not for being three hours late.
The consultant offered a plausible explanation for the drop in sales, though she lacked hard data.
Students must present a plausible hypothesis before they are allowed to begin their experiments.
Investigators say it is plausible that the fire was started by faulty wiring.
His story sounded plausible at first, but she soon noticed that the details kept changing.
tc: The detective rejected the suspect's alibi; it was not even remotely ______, since the train he claimed to have taken did not run that day.
The alibi is rejected because the train did not run, so it was not believable.
se: The scientist's theory is ______, but it still needs to be tested before it can be accepted.
credible
Both 'plausible' and 'credible' mean reasonable enough to believe.

m: causing a strong feeling of sadness or regret
x: Finding my late grandfather's reading glasses in a drawer was a poignant reminder of his evenings with us.
The retiring teacher gave a poignant farewell speech that left several colleagues in tears.
Literature students discussed the poignant final chapter, in which the mother never sees her son again.
The museum displays poignant letters written by soldiers who never returned from the war.
Their reunion after twenty years apart was both joyful and poignant.
tc: The photograph of the empty classroom, taken the day after the school closed for good, was deeply ______, bringing tears to many former students.
'Bringing tears' and the sad loss of the school point to something that stirs sorrow.
se: The film's final scene, in which the old man rereads his late wife's letters, is profoundly ______.
moving
Both 'poignant' and 'moving' mean stirring deep, sad emotion.

m: slow and clumsy because of great weight; or dull, heavy and laborious in style
x: The ponderous old wardrobe took four of us to carry up the narrow staircase.
His ponderous presentation, read word for word from the slides, sent half the room to sleep.
Many students struggle with the ponderous style of nineteenth-century legal textbooks.
Critics say the ministry's ponderous approval process delays new medicines by years.
She loved him, but his ponderous jokes, explained at length, made her friends roll their eyes.
tc: Readers hoping for a lively thriller were disappointed by the novel's ______ style, with its long, heavy sentences and endless digressions.
The contrast with 'lively' and the 'long, heavy sentences' indicate a dull, laborious style.
se: The speech was so ______ that even the speaker's supporters began checking their phones.
tedious
Both 'ponderous' and 'tedious' describe something dull and boring to sit through.

m: having developed certain abilities or maturity unusually early
x: Our precocious six-year-old neighbor already beats her father at chess.
The firm hired a precocious graduate who had built her own software company at nineteen.
He was a precocious student who started university mathematics while still in secondary school.
The study followed precocious readers to see whether early talent predicted later success.
Her precocious maturity made her the person her friends turned to when they needed advice.
tc: Most children are still learning to count at that age, but Nadia was so ______ that she could already solve simple equations.
The contrast with other children 'still learning to count' shows she developed unusually early.
se: She was a remarkably ______ child, reading adult novels by the age of seven.
advanced
Both 'precocious' and 'advanced' describe a child ahead of her age.

m: a strong preference or special liking for something
x: My father has a predilection for spicy food and adds green chilies to almost everything.
The new manager's predilection for long meetings quickly made her unpopular.
Her predilection for Victorian novels shaped the topic of her master's dissertation.
Voters in the region have shown a predilection for independent candidates over party loyalists.
He confessed a predilection for old black-and-white films, which surprised friends who loved action movies.
tc: Given the chef's well-known ______ for bold flavors, nobody was surprised that the menu featured fiery curries.
'Nobody was surprised' that the menu was fiery implies the chef has a known liking for bold flavors.
se: Her ______ for bright colors was obvious from the orange walls of her apartment.
penchant
Both 'predilection' and 'penchant' mean a strong liking, so the sentence means the same.

m: to prevent something from happening; to make it impossible
x: A minor knee injury will not preclude you from taking the morning walk you enjoy.
The terms of my contract preclude me from working for a competitor for a year.
Missing the first exam does not preclude students from passing the course overall.
Officials said the heavy monsoon rain would preclude any rescue flights until morning.
His busy travel schedule seemed to preclude any serious relationship.
tc: The lack of evidence did not prove his innocence, but it did ______ a conviction, since the court required proof beyond reasonable doubt.
Without the required proof a conviction becomes impossible, so the blank means rule out.
se: Her lack of a visa will ______ her from attending the conference in person.
prevent
Both 'preclude' and 'prevent' mean to stop something from happening.

m: a strong feeling that something, usually unpleasant, is about to happen
x: I had a premonition that I'd left the stove on, so I turned the car around.
She had a vague premonition that the merger would fail, and she was proved right.
Psychologists studying premonitions have found that people mostly remember the ones that came true.
Several villagers reported a premonition of disaster in the days before the cyclone struck.
He couldn't shake the premonition that their relationship was about to end.
tc: Moments before the bridge collapsed, the driver was gripped by a strange dread, the ______ that something terrible was about to happen.
'Dread' that 'something terrible was about to happen' defines a feeling about the future.
se: Before the flight, she had an uneasy ______ that something would go wrong.
foreboding
Both 'premonition' and 'foreboding' mean a feeling that something bad will happen.

m: a young person with exceptional talent or abilities
x: The ten-year-old chess prodigy from our neighborhood beat three adults in the same afternoon.
The startup hired a coding prodigy who had finished university at seventeen.
Mozart is often cited as the classic example of a musical prodigy.
Selectors are watching a teenage cricket prodigy who scored a double century in the school league.
Being labeled a prodigy as a child put enormous pressure on her as an adult.
tc: By the age of eight, she was performing piano concertos with professional orchestras, and critics hailed her as the greatest ______ of her generation.
Performing with professional orchestras at eight shows exceptional talent at a young age.
se: Few people knew that the famous physicist had been considered the ______ of his village school, solving university problems at twelve.
genius
Both 'prodigy' and 'genius' describe someone of exceptional ability, here at a young age.

m: producing a great deal of work, fruit, or offspring
x: Our mango tree is so prolific that we give bags of fruit to the neighbors every summer.
She is the most prolific salesperson in the company, closing twice as many deals as anyone else.
The professor was a prolific writer, publishing more than two hundred papers in her career.
Rats are prolific breeders, which is why infestations spread so quickly in crowded cities.
He was a prolific letter-writer and sent his fiancee a long letter every day they were apart.
tc: Unlike his rival, who released one album a decade, the songwriter was astonishingly ______, producing several new records every year.
The contrast with 'one album a decade' and 'several new records every year' indicate high output.
se: Over a long career, the novelist was remarkably ______, publishing more than sixty books.
productive
Both 'prolific' and 'productive' mean producing a large amount of work.

m: acting with care and good judgment, especially by thinking ahead
x: It's prudent to carry an umbrella in Dhaka during the monsoon, even when the sky looks clear.
The board decided it would be prudent to delay the launch until the bugs were fixed.
A prudent student starts revising weeks before the exam rather than the night before.
Economists praised the central bank's prudent decision to raise interest rates gradually.
She made the prudent choice not to quit her job until the new offer was in writing.
tc: While his brother spent every taka the moment he earned it, Rafi was ______, saving part of each paycheck for emergencies.
'While his brother spent every taka' contrasts with saving for emergencies, which shows careful foresight.
se: Given the uncertain market, it would be ______ to keep some cash in reserve.
wise
Both 'prudent' and 'wise' mean showing good judgment about the future.

m: a state of uncertainty about what to do in a difficult situation
x: I'm in a quandary about whether to attend my friend's wedding or my cousin's on the same day.
The manager faced a quandary: fire a loyal but slow employee or keep missing deadlines.
Researchers are in a quandary over whether to publish findings that could be misused.
The flood left local officials in a quandary about where to house thousands of displaced families.
She was in a real quandary, torn between her parents' wishes and her own dreams of studying abroad.
tc: Offered two equally attractive jobs in different cities, she was in a genuine ______, unable to decide which to accept.
'Unable to decide' between two equal options defines a state of uncertainty.
se: Torn between loyalty to his friend and his duty to report the theft, he was in a real ______.
dilemma
Both 'quandary' and 'dilemma' mean a difficult choice between options.

m: to put an end to something, often by force; or to calm a fear or worry
x: A cup of tea and a chat did a lot to quell my nerves before the interview.
The CEO held a town-hall meeting to quell rumors about layoffs.
The lecturer's clear explanation quelled students' fears about the difficult final exam.
Police were called in to quell the unrest after the disputed election results.
Nothing he said could quell her suspicion that he was hiding something.
tc: The government's attempt to ______ the protests backfired; the harsh crackdown only drew more people onto the streets.
'Harsh crackdown' and 'backfired' show the aim was to suppress the protests.
se: The airline issued a statement to ______ passengers' fears about the safety of its aircraft.
allay
Both 'quell' and 'allay' mean to calm or reduce fears.

m: to criticize someone sharply for their behavior
x: My mother rebuked me for answering my phone during dinner with the guests.
The manager rebuked the team publicly for missing the client's deadline.
The editor rebuked the reporter for publishing a story without checking her sources.
The court rebuked the police for holding the suspect without charge for a week.
She immediately regretted rebuking him so harshly when she saw how hurt he looked.
tc: Instead of praising the intern for her initiative, the supervisor chose to ______ her for acting without permission.
'Instead of praising' signals the opposite, sharp criticism.
se: The coach did not hesitate to ______ any player who arrived late to practice.
reprimand
Both 'rebuke' and 'reprimand' mean to criticize someone formally or sharply.

m: to make conflicting ideas or facts consistent, or to restore friendly relations between people
x: I find it hard to reconcile my love of sweets with my plan to lose weight.
The accountant spent the afternoon reconciling the bank statements with the company's records.
Philosophers have long tried to reconcile free will with a scientific view of the brain.
The new policy attempts to reconcile economic growth with protection of the wetlands.
After years of silence, the two brothers finally reconciled at their father's funeral.
tc: The biographer struggled to ______ the man's public generosity with the cruelty he showed his own family in private.
Generosity and cruelty seem contradictory, so the biographer struggles to make them fit together.
se: The committee tried to ______ the two conflicting reports into a single account everyone could accept.
harmonize
Both 'reconcile' and 'harmonize' mean to make conflicting things consistent.

m: no longer needed or useful; more than is necessary
x: Once we bought a dishwasher, the old drying rack became redundant and went into storage.
The restructuring made several middle-management roles redundant, and twenty people lost their jobs.
My supervisor crossed out half my introduction, saying the sentences were redundant.
Critics argue the new agency is redundant, since two existing departments already do the same work.
He felt redundant at home after retiring, as if his family no longer needed him.
tc: Since the first paragraph already defines the term clearly, the second definition is ______ and should be deleted.
The term is 'already' defined, so a second definition is unnecessary.
se: Because the new app does everything the old one did, the old app is now completely ______.
unnecessary
Both 'redundant' and 'unnecessary' mean no longer needed.

m: continuing without stopping or weakening; harsh and persistent
x: The relentless honking outside my window made it impossible to sleep.
Her relentless focus on quality made her the most respected engineer in the department.
Medical students face a relentless schedule of lectures, ward rounds and exams.
The coastal town was battered by relentless rain for three days straight.
Despite his relentless efforts to win her back, she had already made up her mind.
tc: The heat wave was ______, offering not a single cool day in more than a month.
'Not a single cool day in more than a month' describes something that never let up.
se: The reporter's ______ questioning finally forced the official to admit the truth.
persistent
Both 'relentless' and 'persistent' mean continuing without giving up.

m: deep regret or guilt for something wrong one has done
x: I felt instant remorse after shouting at my little brother over something so trivial.
The employee showed genuine remorse for the error and stayed late to fix it.
The novel's hero is consumed by remorse after betraying his closest friend.
The judge noted that the defendant had shown no remorse for the attack.
She was filled with remorse for never visiting her grandmother during her final illness.
tc: Although he insisted he was sorry, his cheerful grin suggested that he felt no real ______ for the damage he had caused.
'Although he insisted he was sorry' contrasts with the grin, so he lacked genuine regret.
se: Overcome with ______, the boy returned the money he had taken from his mother's purse.
guilt
Both 'remorse' and 'guilt' describe the painful feeling of having done wrong.

m: to formally give up a claim, right, or possession, or to reject a belief or habit
x: After a health scare, my uncle decided to renounce sugar completely.
To take the government post, she had to renounce her shares in her family's firm.
The philosopher renounced his earlier theories in a remarkable final lecture.
He renounced his foreign citizenship in order to run for parliament.
The prince renounced his claim to the throne to marry the woman he loved.
tc: Far from defending his earlier views, the author now chose to ______ them entirely, calling them the mistakes of youth.
'Far from defending' and 'the mistakes of youth' show he formally rejected his views.
se: The rebel group agreed to ______ violence as a condition of the peace talks.
forswear
Both 'renounce' and 'forswear' mean to formally give something up.

m: deserving strong criticism; morally wrong
x: Cutting in front of an elderly woman in the line at the bank was a reprehensible thing to do.
The company's reprehensible treatment of factory workers led to a nationwide boycott.
Plagiarism is considered reprehensible in academia and can lead to expulsion.
The report described the delay in sending flood relief as morally reprehensible.
He knew that lying to his best friend was reprehensible, but he was too ashamed to confess.
tc: Whatever the provocation, attacking unarmed civilians is ______, and no cause can ever justify it.
'No cause can ever justify it' signals an act deserving condemnation.
se: Most people found the official's decision to ignore the warnings utterly ______.
deplorable
Both 'reprehensible' and 'deplorable' mean deserving strong condemnation.

m: able to recover quickly from difficulties, shocks, or setbacks
x: Children are often more resilient than their parents expect, settling into a new school within a few weeks.
Our supply chain proved resilient during the port strike because we had already lined up alternative suppliers.
Researchers are breeding rice varieties that are resilient to both flooding and drought.
Small shopkeepers in Dhaka have proved remarkably resilient, reopening within days of every monsoon flood.
After her divorce, she was resilient enough to rebuild her life and even start her own business.
tc: Although the town was devastated by the earthquake, its ______ residents had rebuilt most of the market within a year.
The contrast between 'devastated' and the quick rebuilding shows the residents bounce back from hardship.
se: Farmers in the region are ______, recovering quickly from floods that would ruin people elsewhere.
hardy
Both 'resilient' and 'hardy' describe people tough enough to recover from hardship, giving the same meaning.

m: deep respect mixed with awe for someone or something
x: My grandmother still speaks of her old village with a kind of reverence, as if it were sacred ground.
New hires treated the founder with such reverence that nobody dared to question his decisions in meetings.
Scholars handled the medieval manuscript with reverence, wearing gloves and turning each page slowly.
Many Bangladeshis hold the language martyrs of 1952 in deep reverence, laying flowers at the Shaheed Minar every February.
Even after decades of marriage, he spoke about his wife with a quiet reverence that moved everyone at dinner.
tc: Far from treating the ancient temple with ______, the tourists climbed its walls and scratched their names into the stone.
'Far from' signals the opposite of the tourists' disrespectful behavior, so the blank means deep respect.
se: The young musicians listened to the old master's advice with ______, hanging on his every word.
veneration
Both 'reverence' and 'veneration' mean awed respect, and both fit the image of hanging on his every word.

m: language meant to persuade or impress, often seen as insincere or lacking real substance
x: Strip away the rhetoric, and the company's new policy simply means longer hours for the same pay.
Her campaign speeches were full of fiery rhetoric but offered few concrete plans for the economy.
In our first-year seminar, we studied how ancient orators used rhetoric to sway large crowds.
Despite all the rhetoric about climate action, global emissions rose again last year.
He won her back not with grand rhetoric but with small, consistent acts of kindness.
tc: Voters wanted concrete policies, not more of the empty ______ that had filled every speech of the campaign.
'Empty' and the contrast with 'concrete policies' point to persuasive but hollow language.
se: The senator's speech was all ______, full of grand phrases but short on actual proposals.
bombast
Both 'rhetoric' and 'bombast' mean impressive-sounding language without substance, matching 'short on actual proposals'.

m: the quality of being extremely thorough, exact, and careful; also severe strictness
x: She plans even her weekend trips with surprising rigor, comparing every train time and hotel price.
The audit team praised the rigor of our documentation, which made their review much faster.
Reviewers rejected the paper because its statistical analysis lacked rigor.
Scientists called for greater rigor in drug trials after several published results could not be replicated.
Her father's rigor about curfews felt suffocating when she was a teenager, though she appreciates it now.
tc: Unlike his sloppy earlier studies, this research was conducted with great ______, every measurement checked twice.
The contrast with 'sloppy' and the detail 'checked twice' point to thoroughness and precision.
se: The committee was impressed by the ______ of her analysis, which left no assumption untested.
thoroughness
Both 'rigor' and 'thoroughness' describe careful, complete work, matching 'left no assumption untested'.

m: to think deeply and at length about something, often going over it repeatedly
x: I lay awake until three in the morning, ruminating on a silly comment I had made at dinner.
Before accepting the promotion, he took a week to ruminate over whether he really wanted to manage people.
Philosophers have ruminated on the nature of consciousness for thousands of years.
Psychologists say that people who constantly ruminate about their failures are more prone to depression.
After the breakup, she spent months ruminating on what she could have done differently.
tc: Instead of deciding quickly, she preferred to ______ on the offer for several days, turning it over endlessly in her mind.
'Turning it over endlessly in her mind' restates the idea of thinking about something at length.
se: He would sit by the window for hours and ______ over the mistakes of his youth.
brood
Both 'ruminate over' and 'brood over' mean to dwell on something at length, giving the same meaning.

m: most noticeable or important; standing out from the rest
x: The salient point of the lease is that we can't keep pets, so the dog is going to be a problem.
In your summary for the board, highlight only the salient figures and skip the routine details.
A good literature review identifies the salient themes rather than summarizing every single paper.
The report's most salient finding was that air pollution now shortens life expectancy in the capital by several years.
What was most salient to her about their first date was how carefully he listened.
tc: The lawyer ignored the trivial details and focused the jury's attention on the few ______ facts of the case.
The contrast with 'trivial details' shows the blank means the most important facts.
se: The most ______ feature of the design is its enormous glass roof, which you notice immediately.
striking
Both 'salient' and 'striking' mean standing out and immediately noticeable.

m: extremely careful to be accurate, honest, and correct in every detail
x: He is scrupulous about returning borrowed books, often with a thank-you note tucked inside.
Our accountant is scrupulous with expense claims and will query even a single missing taxi receipt.
The historian was scrupulous in citing her sources, so every quotation could be checked.
Inspectors demanded scrupulous hygiene after the outbreak was traced to a hospital kitchen.
She was scrupulous about keeping her friend's secret, even when telling it would have been easier.
tc: Unlike his careless predecessor, the new treasurer kept ______ records, accounting for every last cent.
The contrast with 'careless' and 'every last cent' point to extreme carefulness.
se: She is ______ in her research, double-checking every date and quotation.
meticulous
Both 'scrupulous' and 'meticulous' mean extremely careful about details, matching the double-checking.

m: to examine something closely and critically
x: Always scrutinize the fine print before you sign up for a new phone contract.
Interviewers will scrutinize your CV for gaps, so be ready to explain them.
Peer reviewers scrutinized every table in the manuscript before recommending it for publication.
Journalists are scrutinizing the government's spending on the new metro line.
Her future in-laws seemed to scrutinize every word she said at that first family dinner.
tc: Rather than merely glancing at the contract, the lawyer began to ______ each clause for hidden risks.
'Rather than merely glancing' signals the opposite: close, critical examination.
se: Auditors will ______ the company's accounts for any sign of fraud.
examine
Both 'scrutinize' and 'examine' mean to look at closely, and both give the same meaning here.

m: involving a lot of sitting and very little physical activity
x: After a sedentary weekend of watching television, I felt stiff and sluggish on Monday morning.
Office workers with sedentary jobs should stand up and stretch at least once an hour.
The study linked sedentary behavior among teenagers to poor sleep and lower grades.
Doctors warn that sedentary lifestyles are driving a sharp rise in diabetes across South Asia.
Since retiring, my father has become rather sedentary, so we take him for a walk every evening.
tc: Unlike her active childhood spent playing outdoors, her adult life as a programmer has been largely ______.
The contrast with 'active childhood' shows the blank means inactive and seated.
se: Doctors warn that ______ habits, such as sitting at a desk all day, increase the risk of heart disease.
inactive
Both 'sedentary' and 'inactive' describe habits with little movement, as the example of sitting all day shows.

m: the occurrence of happy or useful discoveries or events purely by chance
x: By pure serendipity, I found my favorite cafe when I took a wrong turn in the rain.
Our best hire came through serendipity: she happened to sit next to our manager on a flight.
The discovery of penicillin is a classic example of serendipity in science.
Some urban planners design streets to encourage serendipity, so that neighbors bump into each other more often.
They call their meeting serendipity, since both of them had missed the same train to Chittagong.
tc: The discovery was the result not of careful planning but of sheer ______, since the chemist had been looking for something else entirely.
The contrast with 'careful planning' and finding something unsought point to a lucky accident.
se: It was pure ______ that we met again, years later, in a bookshop in another country.
chance
Both 'pure serendipity' and 'pure chance' describe an unplanned, lucky meeting.

m: too eager to obey or please others, lacking self-respect
x: The waiter's servile manner, bowing at every request, made the guests feel uncomfortable.
Employees who are servile toward the boss are rarely the ones with the best ideas.
Historians note that court poets often wrote servile praise of the kings who paid them.
Critics accused the newspaper of servile coverage that never questioned the government.
She refused to be servile in her marriage and insisted that big decisions be made together.
tc: Far from being independent, the committee was ______, approving every proposal the chairman put forward without debate.
'Far from being independent' and approving everything without debate point to excessive submissiveness.
se: His ______ flattery of the director embarrassed everyone else in the room.
obsequious
Both 'servile' and 'obsequious' describe embarrassingly eager attempts to please.

m: having sharp practical judgment and the ability to see what is really going on
x: My mother is a shrewd bargainer and never pays the first price a shopkeeper quotes.
Hiring a lawyer before the merger talks was a shrewd move that saved the company millions.
A shrewd observer of human nature, the novelist captured small-town gossip perfectly.
Analysts described the decision to delay the election as politically shrewd.
She made a shrewd guess about why he had suddenly become so attentive.
tc: Her brother was easily fooled by salesmen, but she was far more ______ and spotted every trick at once.
The contrast with 'easily fooled' and 'spotted every trick' point to sharp practical judgment.
se: It was ______ of him to buy land near the planned highway before prices soared.
astute
Both 'shrewd' and 'astute' mean showing clever practical judgment, giving the same meaning.

m: to waste money, time, or opportunities in a careless and foolish way
x: Don't squander your entire salary in the first weekend of the month.
The company squandered its early lead in the market by ignoring customer complaints.
Many students squander their first semester and then panic before the final exams.
Auditors found that the agency had squandered millions on consultants who produced nothing useful.
He squandered her trust with one careless lie, and it took years to rebuild.
tc: Instead of investing his inheritance wisely, he managed to ______ it all on fast cars and lavish parties within two years.
'Instead of investing wisely' signals the opposite: wasteful spending.
se: Don't ______ this chance; opportunities like this rarely come twice.
waste
Both 'squander' and 'waste' mean to fail to use something valuable, giving the same meaning.

m: serious, respectable, and conventional, often to the point of being dull
x: My parents' staid Sunday routine of lunch, a nap, and the evening news has not changed in twenty years.
The bank tried to shed its staid image by hiring young designers and launching a playful app.
Compared with his daring early novels, the author's later work seems rather staid.
The usually staid parliament erupted into shouting when the new budget was announced.
Friends were surprised that she, so lively and spontaneous, married such a staid accountant.
tc: The once ______ newspaper surprised its older readers by adding a gossip column and splashy color photos.
Readers are surprised by the lively changes, so the paper must previously have been dull and conventional.
se: The museum's ______ atmosphere, all hushed rooms and dark wood, put off younger visitors.
stuffy
Both 'staid' and 'stuffy' describe something formal and old-fashioned that puts off younger people.

m: firm and unwavering in loyalty, belief, or purpose
x: Through every one of my exam failures, my best friend remained steadfast in her belief that I would pass.
The manager's steadfast support for the project kept it alive through two rounds of budget cuts.
Her steadfast dedication to the research paid off when a top journal accepted her paper after five years.
Despite international pressure, the country remained steadfast in its refusal to sign the treaty.
He was a steadfast companion to his wife throughout her long illness.
tc: While his other allies abandoned him at the first sign of trouble, his sister remained ______, defending him at every turn.
The contrast with allies who 'abandoned him' shows the sister was firmly loyal.
se: Throughout the scandal, the senator's wife remained ______ in her support of him.
unwavering
Both 'steadfast' and 'unwavering' mean firm and unchanging in support.

m: enduring pain or hardship calmly, without complaining or showing one's feelings
x: My grandfather was stoic about his bad knee and never mentioned it, even on long walks.
She remained stoic when her project was cancelled, though she later admitted she was devastated.
Students were struck by the stoic tone of the soldiers' letters in the archive.
Flood victims waited with stoic patience for relief boats that took days to arrive.
His stoic silence at the funeral hid how deeply he missed his brother.
tc: Though the injury must have been agonizing, the runner remained ______, finishing the race without a single grimace.
'Though... agonizing' and 'without a single grimace' show he endured pain without showing it.
se: She was ______ throughout the long hospital stay, never once complaining about the pain.
uncomplaining
Both 'stoic' and 'uncomplaining' describe enduring pain without protest, as 'never once complaining' confirms.

m: loud and harsh; expressing views in an unpleasantly forceful way
x: The strident ring of my neighbor's alarm clock wakes me up every morning at five.
His strident emails demanding immediate answers annoyed the whole team.
Some reviewers felt the book's strident tone undermined its otherwise careful arguments.
Protesters made strident demands for the minister's resignation outside parliament.
Their arguments became so strident that the children would hide upstairs until the shouting stopped.
tc: Rather than shouting slogans like her more ______ colleagues, the activist made her case calmly and quietly.
'Rather than' sets the blank against 'calmly and quietly', so it must mean loud and harsh.
se: The debate was dominated by ______ voices shouting each other down.
shrill
Both 'strident' and 'shrill' describe loud, harsh voices, giving the same meaning.

m: to bring a person or group under complete control, especially by force
x: The new landlord tried to subjugate his tenants with endless rules about noise and visitors.
Workers complained that the new rules seemed designed to subjugate them rather than improve productivity.
Colonial powers used education policy to subjugate local cultures as well as territories.
The army attempted to subjugate the rebellious province but met fierce resistance.
She refused to let her own ambitions be subjugated to her husband's career.
tc: The empire tried to ______ the neighboring tribes, but they fought fiercely to keep their independence.
The tribes fighting 'to keep their independence' shows the empire was trying to conquer them.
se: The invaders sought to ______ the local population by force.
subdue
Both 'subjugate' and 'subdue' mean to bring people under control by force.

m: so slight or delicate that it is hard to notice or describe
x: There is a subtle difference between being frank and being rude.
Her manager dropped a subtle hint that the presentation was running too long.
Students often miss the subtle irony in the novel's opening chapter.
Climate scientists have detected subtle shifts in monsoon patterns over the past half century.
He noticed a subtle change in her voice and knew immediately that something was wrong.
tc: The changes to the logo were so ______ that most customers did not notice them at all.
'Most customers did not notice them' shows the changes were very slight.
se: There was a ______ hint of sarcasm in his reply that only his close friends caught.
faint
Both 'subtle' and 'faint' describe something barely noticeable, as 'only his close friends caught' shows.

m: expressed clearly in very few words
x: Please keep your wedding speech succinct, because the guests will be hungry.
Our director prefers succinct emails that get to the point in three sentences or fewer.
The professor asked for a succinct abstract of no more than 150 words.
The court's ruling was succinct, just two pages that settled a decade-long dispute.
When I asked whether he still loved me, his succinct reply was simply 'Always.'
tc: Whereas his first draft rambled on for ten pages, the final report was ______, making its case in a single paragraph.
'Whereas' contrasts the rambling draft with a report that is brief and clear.
se: Her ______ summary captured the whole argument in just a few sentences.
concise
Both 'succinct' and 'concise' mean brief and clear, matching 'in just a few sentences'.

m: unnecessary, especially because there is already more than enough
x: With two remote controls already on the table, a third one seemed completely superfluous.
My editor cut every superfluous word from the report, shortening it by a third.
Reviewers suggested removing the superfluous appendix, which only repeated the data in chapter two.
Critics argue that the new agency is superfluous because three existing departments already do the same work.
Between such close friends, apologies felt superfluous; they simply understood each other.
tc: The editor removed every ______ sentence, keeping only what was essential to the argument.
The contrast with 'essential' shows the blank means unnecessary.
se: The extra security guard was ______, since the building already had cameras on every floor.
unnecessary
Both 'superfluous' and 'unnecessary' mean not needed, as the existing cameras explain.

m: done secretly because it would not be approved of
x: He took a surreptitious glance at his phone during the wedding ceremony.
Several employees were caught making surreptitious copies of client files before they resigned.
The student's surreptitious use of notes during the exam was spotted by an alert invigilator.
Investigators uncovered surreptitious payments to officials in exchange for building permits.
Their surreptitious meetings in the park went on for months before their families found out.
tc: Knowing his mother disapproved of sweets, the boy made ______ trips to the kitchen whenever she was asleep.
His mother's disapproval and the timing 'whenever she was asleep' show the trips were secret.
se: She cast a ______ look at the clock, hoping nobody would notice she was bored.
furtive
Both 'surreptitious' and 'furtive' describe a secret look meant to go unnoticed.

m: a person who flatters powerful people to gain favor or advantage
x: My cousin turns into a sycophant whenever our rich uncle visits, laughing loudly at all his jokes.
The new director surrounded herself with sycophants who praised every idea she had.
The philosopher warned that a ruler surrounded by sycophants will never hear the truth.
Critics described the state television hosts as sycophants who never asked a difficult question.
She stopped trusting his compliments once she saw him play the sycophant with every powerful person they met.
tc: Every powerful executive seems to attract at least one ______ who praises each decision in hopes of a promotion.
Praising every decision 'in hopes of a promotion' defines a self-serving flatterer.
se: Everyone in the office saw him as the boss's ______, always ready with a compliment.
toady
Both 'sycophant' and 'toady' mean someone who flatters a superior for advantage.

m: habitually quiet and saying very little
x: My taciturn neighbor nods each morning but has never said more than a few words to me.
The taciturn engineer rarely spoke in meetings, yet his rare comments were always worth hearing.
Biographers struggle with taciturn subjects who left behind few letters or diaries.
Police found the taciturn suspect unwilling to answer even the most basic questions.
Her father was taciturn by nature, so his brief 'well done' meant the world to her.
tc: Unlike his chatty brother, who could talk for hours, Rafiq was ______ and answered most questions with a single word.
The contrast with 'chatty' and 'a single word' show the blank means quiet and uncommunicative.
se: The ______ farmer said little during dinner, nodding occasionally as the guests talked.
reticent
Both 'taciturn' and 'reticent' describe someone who says little, as 'said little' confirms.

m: boring because it is too long, slow, or repetitive
x: Filling in the same form at three different counters is tedious, but the passport office insists on it.
Data entry is tedious work, so we finally automated it with a simple script.
Checking every reference by hand was tedious, but it caught several errors in my thesis.
The trial has become a tedious affair, with lawyers reading out documents for days on end.
He found the long family dinners tedious, though he went every week to please his mother.
tc: The lecture was so ______ that half the students were asleep within twenty minutes.
Students falling asleep is the result, so the lecture must have been dull and tiresome.
se: Sorting thousands of receipts by date is ______ work that nobody ever volunteers for.
monotonous
Both 'tedious' and 'monotonous' describe dull, repetitive work that nobody wants to do.

m: persistent and determined; refusing to give up
x: My little sister is tenacious; she practiced the same guitar chord for weeks until she got it right.
A tenacious salesperson, she followed up with the client every week until he signed.
Only a tenacious researcher would spend ten years tracking down a single missing manuscript.
Tenacious reporting by a local newspaper exposed the fraud at the city hospital.
Her tenacious love for him survived two years of long-distance calls across different time zones.
tc: Though dozens of investors rejected her idea, the ______ founder kept pitching until she finally secured funding.
'Though... rejected' and 'kept pitching until' show she refused to give up.
se: The detective was ______, following every lead for years until the case was solved.
dogged
Both 'tenacious' and 'dogged' mean stubbornly persistent, as following leads for years shows.

m: using very few words, often in a way that seems abrupt or unfriendly
x: When I asked my brother how the exam went, he gave a terse 'fine' and shut his door.
Her manager's terse reply, 'See me tomorrow,' kept her awake all night.
Some students mistake a terse writing style for clarity, but readers still need explanations.
The ministry issued a terse statement denying the reports and declined to comment further.
Their texts had grown terse over the past month, a sign that something between them had changed.
tc: Normally chatty and warm, she gave only the most ______ answers that evening, which told us she was still angry.
The contrast with 'normally chatty and warm' shows her answers were brief and abrupt.
se: His ______ email, just two words long, made it clear he was annoyed.
curt
Both 'terse' and 'curt' mean rudely brief, matching 'just two words long' and 'annoyed'.

m: lasting only for a short time; not permanent
x: The pain from the injection is transient and usually fades within an hour.
Many startups enjoy only transient success before larger competitors catch up with them.
Students soon learn that fashions in literary theory are often transient, replaced every decade or so.
Economists described the price spike as transient, caused by a temporary shortage of fuel.
He had several transient romances at university, but nothing lasted until he met Nadia.
tc: Contrary to the permanent damage the critics had feared, the side effects proved ______, disappearing within a few days.
The contrast with 'permanent' and 'disappearing within a few days' show the effects were short-lived.
se: Fame on social media is often ______, gone as quickly as it arrived.
fleeting
Both 'transient' and 'fleeting' mean lasting only briefly, as 'gone as quickly as it arrived' shows.

m: overused and therefore dull and lacking originality
x: Telling someone to 'stay positive' after a loss can sound trite, however well meant.
The marketing team rejected the slogan as trite and asked for something fresher.
Her essay was well organized, but its conclusion relied on trite phrases about following your dreams.
