Critics dismissed the film's message about family values as trite and predictable.
He worried that saying 'I love you' would sound trite, so he wrote her a long letter instead.
tc: The judges wanted fresh, original stories, so they rejected any entry built around ______ plots they had seen many times before.
The contrast with 'fresh, original' and 'seen many times before' point to overused, unoriginal plots.
se: The speech was full of ______ remarks about hard work that the audience had heard a hundred times.
hackneyed
Both 'trite' and 'hackneyed' mean worn out by overuse, as 'heard a hundred times' confirms.

m: full of conflict, disorder, or sudden change; not calm or stable
x: The flight was so turbulent that the crew suspended the meal service.
After a turbulent year of layoffs and mergers, staff were relieved to have some stability.
Historians describe the decade after independence as one of the most turbulent periods in the nation's history.
Investors fled as markets became turbulent following the surprise election result.
Their turbulent relationship lurched from passionate reconciliations to bitter fights.
tc: After decades of ______ politics marked by coups and riots, the country finally enjoyed a period of calm.
'Coups and riots' and the contrast with 'finally... calm' show the politics were chaotic.
se: The company went through a ______ period, with three different chief executives in a single year.
tumultuous
Both 'turbulent' and 'tumultuous' describe a chaotic, unstable time.

m: never done, known, or experienced before
x: This summer's heat was unprecedented; even the oldest people in the village could not remember anything like it.
The firm saw unprecedented demand for its product, forcing it to add a night shift.
The university received an unprecedented number of applications this year, nearly double the usual figure.
Scientists warn that the current rate of glacier loss is unprecedented in recorded history.
Her decision to move abroad alone was unprecedented in a family where daughters rarely left home.
tc: Never before had the city seen floods of this size; the damage was truly ______.
'Never before had the city seen' restates the meaning of the blank.
se: The pandemic caused ______ disruption to schools, unlike anything seen in living memory.
unparalleled
Both 'unprecedented' and 'unparalleled' mean without any earlier equal, as 'unlike anything seen' confirms.

m: to take a position of power or authority illegally or by force
x: My younger brother usurped my seat at the head of the table the moment I left for university.
The deputy manager tried to usurp his boss's role by calling meetings without her.
Historians still debate whether the king usurped the throne or inherited it legitimately.
Critics argue that the courts are usurping powers that properly belong to parliament.
She felt that her mother-in-law was trying to usurp her place in her own household.
tc: The general plotted to ______ the throne while the rightful heir was still a child.
'Rightful heir' shows the general's claim was illegitimate, so he planned to seize power wrongfully.
se: The council accused the mayor of trying to ______ powers that belonged to the elected assembly.
seize
Both 'usurp' and 'seize' mean to take powers that belong to someone else.

m: showing very strong, forceful feeling, especially in opposition
x: My father is a vehement opponent of fast food and refuses to set foot in a burger restaurant.
Despite vehement objections from staff, management closed the branch office.
The theory provoked vehement debate among biologists for more than a decade.
Residents staged vehement protests against the plan to build a factory beside the river.
Her vehement denial only convinced him that she was hiding something.
tc: Far from being mildly concerned, the residents were ______ in their opposition, staging protests every week.
'Far from being mildly concerned' and weekly protests show their feeling was intense.
se: The proposal met with ______ opposition from the farmers whose land would be flooded.
passionate
Both 'vehement' and 'passionate' describe opposition driven by strong feeling.

m: experienced indirectly by imagining or watching what happens to someone else
x: I get vicarious pleasure from watching travel videos of places I will probably never visit.
The manager took vicarious pride in the success of the interns she had trained.
Psychologists study vicarious learning, in which children pick up behaviors by watching others.
Fans of reality television enjoy a vicarious thrill from other people's dramas.
Through her daughter's admission to medical school, she lived a vicarious version of the dream she had abandoned.
tc: Unable to travel herself, the old woman took ______ delight in her grandson's letters from abroad, enjoying his adventures as if they were her own.
'Unable to travel herself' and 'as if they were her own' show she experienced the trips through someone else.
se: Watching his son play professional cricket gave him ______ satisfaction, a taste of the career he had never had.
indirect
Both 'vicarious' and 'indirect' describe satisfaction felt through another person's experience.

m: to clear someone of blame or suspicion, or to prove that someone was right
x: The afternoon downpour vindicated my decision to carry an umbrella despite everyone's teasing.
Strong quarterly results vindicated the manager's controversial decision to cut the product line.
New fossil evidence vindicated the scientist, whose theory had been mocked for decades.
The court's ruling vindicated the journalist, clearing her of all charges of defamation.
He felt vindicated when his sister finally admitted that he had been right about her boyfriend.
tc: For years the engineer's warnings were ignored, but the bridge's collapse would ______ him completely.
The ignored warnings coming true shows that events proved him right.
se: The DNA evidence will ______ the man who spent ten years in prison for a crime he did not commit.
exonerate
Both 'vindicate' and 'exonerate' mean to clear someone of blame, giving the same meaning.

m: having or showing a strong desire for revenge
x: My vindictive neighbor reported my car to the council after I complained about his dog.
A vindictive manager can make life miserable for any employee who once disagreed with him.
The novel's villain is a vindictive aunt who spends decades plotting against her sister's children.
Critics called the new law vindictive, saying it punished protesters rather than addressing their complaints.
Even after the divorce, she refused to be vindictive and spoke kindly of him to their children.
tc: Rather than forgiving his rival, the ______ politician spent years trying to ruin his career.
'Rather than forgiving' and the years spent seeking ruin point to a desire for revenge.
se: She sent the ______ message purely to hurt him, as revenge for the breakup.
spiteful
Both 'vindictive' and 'spiteful' describe a deliberate wish to hurt someone in revenge.

m: extremely harmful or infectious, as a disease; also, bitterly hostile
x: A virulent stomach bug swept through our apartment building last week, leaving half the residents in bed.
The memo provoked virulent criticism from staff, who flooded the director's inbox with angry replies.
Researchers are studying why some strains of the virus are far more virulent than others.
Health officials warned that a virulent form of dengue was spreading through Dhaka during the monsoon.
Their quarrel over the inheritance turned into a virulent feud that split the family for years.
tc: Unlike the mild seasonal flu, this new strain is highly ______, killing many of those it infects.
The contrast with 'mild' and 'killing many' show the strain is extremely harmful.
se: The essay was a ______ attack on the government, full of bitter and hostile language.
vicious
Both 'virulent' and 'vicious' describe a bitterly hostile attack, as 'bitter and hostile' confirms.

m: lively, cheerful, and full of energy, especially in personality
x: Our vivacious host kept the party going with games and stories until midnight.
The new receptionist is so vivacious that clients often stay to chat after their appointments.
Students loved the vivacious lecturer, whose classes felt more like conversations than lectures.
The festival drew a vivacious crowd that danced through the streets until dawn.
He fell for her vivacious laugh before he even knew her name.
tc: Her sister was shy and quiet, but she herself was ______, chatting with everyone and laughing loudly at every joke.
The contrast with 'shy and quiet' and her chatting and laughing show she was lively.
se: The ______ young teacher filled the classroom with energy and laughter.
lively
Both 'vivacious' and 'lively' mean full of energy, matching 'energy and laughter'.

m: wanting or consuming great amounts of something; extremely eager
x: After football practice, my teenage son has a voracious appetite and empties the fridge.
The new trainee has a voracious appetite for learning and asks a dozen questions every hour.
A voracious reader since childhood, she finished the entire reading list before term began.
The city's voracious demand for water is draining groundwater faster than the rain can replace it.
Their voracious curiosity about each other kept them talking until sunrise on their first date.
tc: The boy's appetite for books was ______; he read three novels a week and still asked for more.
Reading three novels a week and still wanting more shows an appetite that cannot be satisfied.
se: The caterpillars are ______ eaters, stripping the leaves from a whole tree in a few days.
ravenous
Both 'voracious' and 'ravenous' describe eating huge amounts hungrily.

m: to gradually become weaker, smaller, or less important
x: My enthusiasm for the gym started to wane after the first month.
Interest in the project waned once the initial funding ran out.
By the third hour of the lecture, the students' attention had clearly waned.
Support for the ruling party has waned in recent polls as food prices continue to rise.
Their friendship waned after she moved abroad, though they still exchange birthday messages.
tc: At first the crowd was enthusiastic, but as the speech dragged on, its excitement began to ______.
'At first... but' signals a contrast with the initial enthusiasm, so the excitement decreased.
se: As the evening wore on, the guests' energy began to ______ and they drifted home.
fade
Both 'wane' and 'fade' mean to grow gradually weaker, giving the same meaning.

m: to lower oneself or another in dignity, respect, or status; to humiliate
x: I refuse to abase myself by begging my landlord for a few more days.
He would not abase himself before the board just to keep his job.
In the novel, the proud hero must abase himself before the woman he once insulted.
Critics said the delegation had abased the nation by agreeing to every demand of the foreign power.
She loved him, but she would never abase herself to win back his affection.
tc: Too proud to ______ himself, he refused to apologize even though it cost him the contract.
'Too proud' signals that he would not lower his dignity.
se: She would rather lose the job than ______ herself before such an arrogant manager.
humble
Both 'abase herself' and 'humble herself' mean to lower one's own dignity before someone.

m: to give up a throne, power, or responsibility, often formally or irresponsibly
x: When the dishes piled up, my roommate simply abdicated all responsibility and went to bed.

'Though he argued stubbornly' and 'eventually forced' show he finally had to admit he was wrong.
se: Even the most loyal fans had to ______ that the team had played badly.
admit
Both 'concede' and 'admit' mean to acknowledge an unwelcome truth, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to agree or be of the same opinion
x: My wife thinks we should move closer to her office, and I concur.
The board concurred with the auditors' recommendation to cut costs.
Most historians concur that the treaty sowed the seeds of the next war.
Several independent studies concur in finding that the vaccine is safe for children.
I could not concur with my friend's harsh verdict on her former partner.
tc: While the junior judges ______ with the ruling, the senior judge wrote a sharp dissent.
'While' contrasts with 'a sharp dissent', so the blank must mean to agree.
se: The second doctor examined the scan and was happy to ______ with the original diagnosis.
agree
Both 'concur' and 'agree' mean to share the same opinion, so the sentence means the same.

m: to behave as though one is superior to others; to lower oneself to do something
x: My cousin always condescends to me because I didn't attend a famous university.
Good managers explain their decisions clearly without condescending to junior staff.
The lecturer condescended to first-year students, answering their questions with obvious impatience.
Many rural voters felt that city politicians condescended to them throughout the campaign.
Please don't condescend to me; I understand perfectly well why you're upset.
tc: Instead of treating the new interns as equals, the senior partner would ______ to them as if they were children.
'Instead of treating them as equals' and 'as if they were children' show the blank means to act superior.
se: The famous author did not even ______ to reply to my carefully written letter.
deign
Both 'condescend' and 'deign' mean to lower oneself to do something, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: making a particular situation or outcome likely or easier to achieve
x: A cluttered, noisy bedroom is hardly conducive to a good night's sleep.
Open-plan offices with constant chatter are not always conducive to focused, careful work.
The library's quiet reading rooms are conducive to long hours of study.
Economists argue that stable interest rates are conducive to long-term investment.
Candlelight and soft music are said to be conducive to romance.
tc: Dhaka's honking traffic and endless construction noise are hardly ______ to calm reflection.
'Hardly' with noisy surroundings shows they do not help calm reflection, so the blank means favourable to.
se: The warm, humid climate is ______ to the growth of mould.
favourable
Both 'conducive to' and 'favourable to' mean helping something happen, so the sentence means the same.

m: a coming together of people, things or events; the place where two rivers meet
x: The old trading town grew up at the confluence of two great rivers.
The startup's success came from a confluence of good timing, cheap funding and talented engineers.
The seminar explored the confluence of economics and psychology in modern behavioural research.
A confluence of drought, war and rising prices pushed millions into hunger last year.
Their friendship was born from a happy confluence of shared hobbies and similar senses of humour.
tc: The crisis did not have one single cause; rather, it arose from the ______ of several unrelated pressures at once.
'Not one single cause' but several pressures 'at once' points to a coming together of factors.
se: The festival celebrates the ______ of Eastern and Western musical traditions.
convergence
Both 'confluence' and 'convergence' mean a meeting or merging of different things, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: an opinion or conclusion based on incomplete information; a guess
x: Whether the restaurant will reopen after the floods is still a matter of conjecture.
Our sales forecast is pure conjecture until we see the first month's figures.
The professor warned that my essay relied on conjecture rather than solid evidence.
Media conjecture about the merger sent the company's shares soaring on Monday.
Her friends' conjecture about why she had moved away was mostly wrong and quite unkind.
tc: With no documents surviving from that period, any claim about the king's motives is mere ______ rather than established fact.
No surviving documents and the contrast with 'established fact' show the blank means a guess.
se: Until the investigators release their report, the cause of the crash remains a matter of ______.
speculation
Both 'conjecture' and 'speculation' mean guessing without firm evidence, so the sentence means the same.

m: to make or declare something sacred; to dedicate solemnly to a purpose
x: The villagers gathered to watch the priest consecrate the newly built temple by the river.
The founder consecrated his whole career to building a company that treated its workers fairly.
The archaeologist believes the hilltop was consecrated as a burial site thousands of years ago.
The bishop consecrated the new cathedral before a crowd of several thousand worshippers.
On their anniversary, they returned to the chapel where their marriage had been consecrated twenty years before.
tc: Whereas the invading soldiers had desecrated the temple, the returning priests sought to ______ it once again.
'Whereas' contrasts with 'desecrated', so the blank must mean to make sacred.
se: The priest will ______ the ground before the first burial takes place.
sanctify
Both 'consecrate' and 'sanctify' mean to make holy, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: general agreement among the members of a group
x: After an hour of arguing, our family finally reached a consensus on where to spend Eid.
The team could not reach consensus on the budget, so the decision went to the director.
There is broad consensus among economists that the policy will push up prices.
The scientific consensus on climate change has grown stronger with each new report.
My friends and I rarely reach a consensus about films, which makes movie nights lively.
tc: Far from being divided, the committee members showed rare ______, voting unanimously for the proposal.
'Far from being divided' and 'voting unanimously' show the blank means general agreement.
se: The negotiators worked late into the night but failed to reach ______ on the key issues.
agreement
Both 'consensus' and 'agreement' mean shared acceptance by a group, so the meaning is the same.

m: a feeling of anxiety or dismay, usually at something sudden or unexpected
x: To the consternation of the passengers, the flight was cancelled moments before boarding.
The surprise announcement of layoffs caused consternation throughout the office.
Rumours of a harder exam format caused consternation among the final-year students.
The sudden rise in fuel prices has caused consternation among farmers and transport workers.
I could see the consternation on my father's face when I told him I was quitting engineering.
tc: Expecting a routine update, the shareholders reacted with ______ when the chairman suddenly announced the company was nearly bankrupt.
An unexpected announcement of near-bankruptcy would cause alarmed dismay, which is what the blank needs.
se: The referee's controversial decision caused ______ among the home team's supporters.
dismay
Both 'consternation' and 'dismay' mean shocked distress, so the sentence means the same.

m: to restrict or limit what someone or something can do
x: Our small apartment constrains how many guests we can invite for dinner.
Tight budgets will constrain what the department can spend on training this year.
The study was constrained by the small number of patients willing to take part.
Heavy debts constrain the government's ability to invest in schools and hospitals.
He felt constrained by his parents' expectations and longed to choose his own path.
tc: Rather than freeing the artists to experiment, the strict new rules only served to ______ their creativity.
'Rather than freeing' signals the opposite, so the blank must mean to restrict.
se: Lack of funding continues to ______ the hospital's plans for expansion.
limit
Both 'constrain' and 'limit' mean to restrict, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: showing that one considers someone or something worthless or beneath respect
x: She gave the cheap souvenir a contemptuous glance and handed it back to the seller.
His contemptuous emails to junior colleagues eventually led to a formal complaint.
The reviewer was openly contemptuous of the study's methods, calling them sloppy and naive.
Many citizens have grown contemptuous of politicians who break their promises so easily.
I was hurt by the contemptuous way he laughed at my dream of becoming a writer.
tc: Instead of showing the elderly guard any respect, the young officer treated him with ______ indifference, as if he were worthless.
'Instead of showing respect' and 'as if he were worthless' show the blank means scornful.
se: The critic was openly ______ of the director's latest film, dismissing it as worthless.
scornful
Both 'contemptuous of' and 'scornful of' express a low opinion of something, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to bring about or create something through clever, often secret, planning
x: Somehow she contrived to cook a three-course meal in our tiny student kitchen.
The manager contrived a reason to dismiss the employee who had complained about him.
The students contrived an ingenious device to measure rainfall using old plastic bottles.
Investigators believe the officials contrived the shortage to push up grain prices.
He contrived to sit next to her at every family gathering that summer.
tc: Rather than leaving their meeting to chance, she managed to ______ an encounter at the café he visited every morning.
'Rather than leaving it to chance' shows she deliberately arranged the meeting, so the blank means to plan cleverly.
se: The prisoners spent months trying to ______ a way to escape without being noticed.
devise
Both 'contrive' and 'devise' mean to work out a clever plan, so the sentence means the same.

m: to argue against or deny the truth of a statement or claim
x: Nobody at the dinner table dared to controvert my grandmother's version of the family history.
The finance team produced figures that controverted the sales department's optimistic claims.
No later study has controverted her original findings on childhood memory.
The defence lawyer called witnesses to controvert the prosecution's account of the evening.
He did not try to controvert her accusations, which only convinced her they were true.
tc: The evidence was so overwhelming that not even the most skilled defence lawyer could ______ it.
Evidence that is 'overwhelming' cannot be argued against, so the blank means to dispute.
se: The scientist published new data to ______ her rival's claims about the drug's safety.
dispute
Both 'controvert' and 'dispute' mean to argue that a claim is untrue, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: following what is traditionally done or believed; not original or unusual
x: My parents expected me to choose a conventional career such as medicine or engineering.
The firm abandoned conventional office hours and let staff work whenever it suited them.
The researchers challenged the conventional wisdom that bilingual children learn to speak later.
Conventional farming relies heavily on chemical fertilisers, while organic methods avoid them.
They had a fairly conventional wedding, but the speeches were anything but ordinary.
tc: Unlike his ______ colleagues, who followed the textbook to the letter, the young surgeon was always willing to try radical new techniques.
'Unlike' contrasts with 'radical new techniques', and 'followed the textbook' confirms the blank means traditional.
se: The architect rejected ______ designs in favour of something bold and experimental.
traditional
Both 'conventional' and 'traditional' describe the usual, established way of doing things, so the meaning is the same.

m: warm, polite and friendly
x: Our new neighbours gave us a cordial welcome and brought round a plate of sweets.
Relations between the two departments have been cordial since the merger.
The visiting professor received a cordial invitation to speak at the annual conference.
Despite deep disagreements, the two leaders held cordial talks on trade and security.
Although they divorced years ago, they remain on cordial terms for their children's sake.
tc: Expecting a frosty reception from his former rival, he was surprised to be greeted with ______ handshakes and warm smiles.
'Surprised' after expecting a 'frosty reception', plus 'warm smiles', shows the blank means friendly.
se: Despite their political differences, the two families have always maintained ______ relations.
friendly
Both 'cordial' and 'friendly' describe warm, pleasant relations, so the sentence means the same.

m: an abundant supply of good things
x: The market in Old Dhaka is a cornucopia of spices, fabrics and street food.
The new job offered a cornucopia of benefits, from free lunches to generous parental leave.
The university archive is a cornucopia of rare manuscripts waiting to be studied.
Coral reefs support a cornucopia of marine life that scientists are still cataloguing.
Her grandmother's attic was a cornucopia of childhood memories, from old dolls to faded letters.
tc: Far from being sparse, the harvest festival displayed the region's full ______ of fruit, grain and vegetables.
'Far from being sparse' signals the opposite, so the blank must mean an abundant supply.
se: Visitors were amazed by the sheer ______ of dishes laid out at the wedding feast.
abundance
Both 'cornucopia' and 'abundance' mean a plentiful supply, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: not openly shown or acknowledged; secret
x: She cast covert glances at her phone throughout the long family dinner.
Managers suspected a covert campaign among staff to resist the new attendance rules.
The researchers used covert observation to study how shoppers behave when no one is watching.
The newspaper revealed a covert operation to spy on opposition activists.
There was a covert hostility between the two brothers that their parents never noticed.
tc: Whereas the first protest was loud and overt, the second campaign was entirely ______, carried out through anonymous leaflets at night.
'Whereas' contrasts with 'overt', and anonymous night-time leaflets confirm the blank means secret.
se: Agents carried out ______ surveillance of the suspects for several months.
secret
Both 'covert' and 'secret' mean hidden from those being watched, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to want something very strongly, especially something that belongs to someone else
x: My little brother has always coveted my cricket bat, signed by the whole school team.
Many junior lawyers covet a corner office and the prestige that comes with it.
Places at the country's top medical colleges are among the most coveted in higher education.
Rival nations have long coveted the region's rich oil reserves.
He knew it was wrong to covet his best friend's girlfriend, but he couldn't help it.
tc: Though she claimed to be content with her small car, she could not help but ______ her neighbour's gleaming new sports car.
'Though she claimed to be content' signals a contrast, so the blank means to desire what another person owns.
se: Every young actor in the city seemed to ______ the lead role in the new production.
crave
Both 'covet' and 'crave' mean to want something intensely, so the sentence means the same.

m: to crouch down or shrink back in fear
x: Our dog cowers under the bed whenever there is thunder during the monsoon.
Staff used to cower in their offices whenever the director was in a bad mood.
No student should have to cower before a teacher who shouts at every mistake.
Residents cowered in their basements as shells fell on the city overnight.
She refused to cower before her abusive partner any longer and finally left him.
tc: Instead of standing up to the bully, the frightened boy would ______ in the corner whenever he approached.
'Instead of standing up to' and 'frightened' show the blank means to shrink back in fear.
se: The abandoned puppy would ______ whenever anyone raised a voice near it.
cringe
Both 'cower' and 'cringe' mean to shrink back in fear, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: large or heavy and hard to handle; slow and complicated to use

The approval process is so cumbersome that even small purchases take weeks.
Students complained that the online registration system was cumbersome and confusing.
Critics say the country's cumbersome tax code encourages evasion and discourages small businesses.
Old resentments can feel as cumbersome as heavy luggage you never quite put down.

Needing two people to carry it, and the contrast with a 'light laptop', shows the blank means bulky and hard to handle.
se: Engineers replaced the ______ machinery with smaller, more efficient units.
unwieldy
Both 'cumbersome' and 'unwieldy' describe something too large or awkward to manage easily, so the meaning is the same.

She curtailed her late nights out after realising how much they were hurting her health.

'Instead of extending' signals the opposite, so the blank means to cut short.
se: The government plans to ______ spending on non-essential projects next year.
reduce
Both 'curtail' and 'reduce' mean to cut back, so the sentence means the same.

m: believing that people act only out of self-interest; distrustful of others' sincerity

Her painful divorce left her cynical about love, though she hid it well.

'Unlike her idealistic colleagues' and assuming hidden motives show the blank means distrustful of people's sincerity.
se: Years of broken promises have made residents ______ about the council's plans.
sceptical
Both 'cynical' and 'sceptical' describe doubting that promises are sincere, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to take part in an activity casually or superficially, without serious commitment

The tech giant has dabbled in electric cars but never fully committed to them.
He dabbled in online dating for a while before meeting his wife at a friend's wedding.

'Rather than devoting himself seriously' and 'without mastering any' show the blank means to try something casually.
se: As a student, she liked to ______ with radical politics, but she never joined a party.
flirt
Both 'dabble with' and 'flirt with' mean to show casual, uncommitted interest, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to make someone feel intimidated, discouraged or nervous about a task

Her father's stern silence used to daunt him, but now he simply ignored it.

'Yet' contrasts with the hiker relishing the challenge, so the blank must mean to intimidate.
se: Setbacks that would ______ most entrepreneurs only made her more determined.
discourage
Both 'daunt' and 'discourage' mean to sap someone's confidence, so the sentence means the same.

m: a sudden, complete and humiliating failure; a fiasco

'Meant to be a triumph, but instead' signals the opposite, and 'embarrassing' points to a humiliating failure.

fiasco
Both 'debacle' and 'fiasco' mean a humiliating failure, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to lower the quality, value or moral character of something

'Rather than enhancing' signals the opposite, so the blank means to lower in quality.
se: Critics argued that the tacky advertising campaign would ______ the reputation of the famous brand.
cheapen
Both 'debase' and 'cheapen' mean to reduce the value or dignity of something, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

Years of underfunding have debilitated research in the physics department.
Dengue outbreaks during the monsoon debilitate thousands of people in Dhaka each year.
Years of loneliness had debilitated him more than his illness ever had.

'Far from strengthening' signals the opposite, so the blank must mean to weaken.

Both 'debilitate' and 'weaken' mean to reduce someone's strength, so the sentence means the same.

The contrast with starving peasants and days-long feasts shows the blank means excessive self-indulgence.
se: The novel paints a vivid picture of the ______ of the aristocracy in its final years.
self-indulgence
Both 'decadence' and 'self-indulgence' describe excessive pursuit of pleasure, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to work out the meaning of something hard to read, understand or decode

It took the team an hour to decipher what the client actually wanted from his vague email.
Linguists spent decades trying to decipher the ancient script carved on the temple walls.
Codebreakers deciphered enemy messages that changed the course of the war.
She struggled to decipher his mood from the short, one-word replies he sent her.
tc: The message was written in a secret code that only the general's most trusted aides could ______.
A message in 'secret code' that only a few can understand points to a word meaning to decode.
se: Experts are still trying to ______ the symbols carved into the ancient stone.
decode
Both 'decipher' and 'decode' mean to work out the meaning of obscure writing, so the sentence means the same.

m: polite, restrained and in keeping with good taste and proper behaviour

Even during heated negotiations, she kept her emails polite and decorous.
The graduation ceremony was a decorous affair, with gowns, speeches and polite applause.
Parliamentary debates were once far more decorous than today's shouting matches.
Their courtship was decorous and old-fashioned, conducted mostly through letters and family visits.
tc: At the solemn memorial service, guests were expected to behave in a quiet, ______ manner rather than laugh and shout.
A 'solemn' setting and the contrast with laughing and shouting show the blank means proper and dignified.
se: Guests at the embassy dinner were expected to be ______ and well mannered.
proper
Both 'decorous' and 'proper' mean behaving with good taste and correctness, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to damage someone's good reputation by saying or writing false things about them
x: A jealous neighbour tried to defame our family by spreading rumours about my father's business.
The employee was sued for defaming his former boss in a series of online posts.
The professor claimed that the anonymous review had defamed her and damaged her career.
The newspaper apologised after a court ruled that it had defamed a local businessman.
She was devastated when her ex-husband tried to defame her in front of their friends.

se: The politician threatened to sue anyone who tried to ______ him with false accusations.
slander
Both 'defame' and 'slander' mean to harm someone's reputation with lies, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to accept another person's opinion or decision out of respect for their authority or knowledge
x: When it comes to choosing restaurants, I always defer to my wife's excellent taste.

On matters of medieval history, I defer to my colleague, who has studied it for decades.
Courts generally defer to scientific experts when assessing complex environmental evidence.
In many traditional families, children are expected to defer to their elders on marriage decisions.
tc: Rather than insisting on his own opinion, the new manager wisely chose to ______ to his experienced team on technical matters.
'Rather than insisting on his own opinion' shows the blank means to give way to others' judgement.
se: On questions of law, the committee will ______ to the advice of its legal counsel.
yield
Both 'defer to' and 'yield to' mean to accept someone else's authority, so the sentence means the same.

m: final and authoritative; settling a question conclusively or serving as the most reliable version
x: We still haven't had a definitive answer from the landlord about whether the rent will go up.

Her three-volume study is widely regarded as the definitive history of the Bengal famine.
Scientists say there is still no definitive evidence that the drug slows memory loss in older patients.
After months of mixed signals, I wanted a definitive yes or no about where our relationship was going.
tc: Earlier studies had offered only suggestive hints, but the new trial provided ______ proof that the vaccine works.
The contrast with 'only suggestive hints' shows the blank must mean proof that settles the matter once and for all.
se: The committee's ______ ruling on the dispute, due next month, cannot be appealed.
final
Both 'definitive' and 'final' describe a ruling that settles the matter, and 'cannot be appealed' confirms that sense.

m: to make someone, often oneself, believe something that is not true
x: Don't delude yourself into thinking you can clean the whole flat in an hour.
The manager deluded himself that the project was on schedule, even as deadline after deadline slipped by.
Students who only skim the summaries often delude themselves into believing they have mastered the material.
Thousands of investors were deluded by glossy brochures promising returns that no honest fund could deliver.
She had deluded herself for years that he would change once they were married.
tc: Despite clear evidence that his business was failing, he continued to ______ himself with dreams of quick success.
'Despite clear evidence' signals that he was fooling himself, believing something untrue.
se: Clever advertising can ______ consumers into believing that a product is healthier than it really is.
mislead
Both 'delude' and 'mislead' mean causing people to believe something false, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to declare publicly that someone or something is wrong or evil
x: Neighbours gathered outside the pharmacy to denounce the owner for selling expired medicine.
Several employees signed an open letter denouncing the company's decision to cut sick pay.
In his essay, the philosopher denounces the idea that wealth is a sign of moral worth.
Human rights groups were quick to denounce the arrests as an attack on free speech.
He felt deeply betrayed when his closest friend denounced him in front of the entire family.
tc: Rather than quietly ignoring the scandal, the editor chose to ______ it openly in a front-page column.
'Rather than quietly ignoring' points to the opposite action: open, public condemnation.
se: Religious leaders from every faith came together to ______ the attack on the mosque.
condemn
Both 'denounce' and 'condemn' mean to declare publicly that the attack was wrong.

m: to use up or greatly reduce the supply of something

Months of constant overtime have depleted the team's energy, and mistakes are starting to creep in.
Planting the same crop year after year can deplete the soil of nitrogen.
Decades of overfishing have severely depleted cod stocks in the North Atlantic.
Caring for her sick father for months had left her emotionally depleted.
tc: Unless the government finds new sources of income, years of heavy spending will ______ the nation's foreign currency reserves.
Heavy spending with no new income means the reserves will be used up, which is what the blank must express.
se: Long hikes in the summer heat can quickly ______ the body's reserves of salt and water.
exhaust
Both 'deplete' and 'exhaust' mean to use up a supply, so the sentence means the same with either.

m: to feel or express strong disapproval of something
x: My grandmother deplores the habit of checking phones at the dinner table.
Staff deplored the way the layoffs were announced by email late on a Friday evening.
Many teachers deplore the growing reliance on coaching centres rather than on classroom learning.
The UN statement deplored the bombing of hospitals and called for an immediate ceasefire.
Although she deplored his temper, she found it hard to stay angry with him for long.
tc: Far from welcoming the new policy, critics continue to ______ it as a serious threat to academic freedom.
'Far from welcoming' signals the opposite reaction, strong disapproval.
se: All decent people must ______ the use of children as soldiers.
condemn
Both 'deplore' and 'condemn' express strong moral disapproval of the practice.

m: empty, bleak and without people; also, of a person, utterly lonely and miserable
x: After the shops close at night, the market street becomes strangely desolate.
The company moved its staff to a desolate industrial park miles from the nearest café.
Field researchers spent two winters studying penguins in a desolate corner of the Antarctic peninsula.
Years of drought have left once-fertile farmland desolate and abandoned.
She felt utterly desolate in the weeks after her mother's death.
tc: Once a crowded fishing port, the village is now ______, its houses empty and its boats left to rot.
The contrast with 'once a crowded fishing port' and the restatement 'houses empty' show the blank means deserted and bleak.
se: The hikers crossed miles of ______ plain where nothing grew and no one lived.
barren
Both 'desolate' and 'barren' describe empty, lifeless land, as the rest of the sentence confirms.

m: in low spirits because of a loss of hope or courage
x: He grew despondent after his fourth job application in a month was rejected.
The despondent mood in the office lifted when the client finally renewed its contract.
Many students become despondent after a poor mock test, but one bad score proves very little.
Despondent voters stayed at home on election day, convinced that nothing would change.
She sounded so despondent on the phone that I drove over to see her straight away.
tc: Although the fans had been cheerful before the match, they left the stadium ______ after their team's crushing defeat.
'Although' contrasts with 'cheerful', and 'crushing defeat' explains why they lost hope.
se: After weeks of failed attempts to find a flat, Rahim felt increasingly ______.
dejected
Both 'despondent' and 'dejected' describe low spirits caused by repeated failure.

m: to discourage someone from doing something, usually by making them fear the consequences
x: A loud dog in the yard is often enough to deter burglars.
High legal fees deter many small businesses from taking their disputes to court.
Strict penalties for plagiarism are meant to deter students from copying each other's work.
There is little evidence that the death penalty deters violent crime more effectively than long prison sentences.
Nothing her parents said could deter her from marrying the man she loved.
tc: The city installed bright lights and cameras in the car park, hoping to ______ thieves who had been breaking into vehicles.
Lights and cameras are meant to scare off thieves, so the blank means to discourage.
se: The heavy rain did not ______ thousands of fans from queuing outside the stadium.
discourage
Both 'deter' and 'discourage' fit 'from queuing' and mean the rain failed to put the fans off.

m: harm or damage done to someone or something
x: He works such long hours that it is clearly to the detriment of his health.
Cutting the training budget saved money in the short term, but to the detriment of staff morale.
She studied economics alongside medicine without any detriment to her grades.
Critics argue that the dam will be built to the detriment of thousands of farmers downstream.
Constant arguments over money proved a serious detriment to their marriage.
tc: The factory increased its profits, but only to the ______ of the river, which became too polluted for fishing.
'Only' and 'too polluted for fishing' show the profits came at the cost of harm to the river.
se: The new rules will work to the ______ of small shopkeepers, who cannot afford the higher fees.
disadvantage
'Work to the detriment of' and 'work to the disadvantage of' both mean the rules will harm the shopkeepers.

m: completely lacking something; always followed by 'of'
x: The hotel room was spotlessly clean but devoid of any personal touch.
His report was long but almost entirely devoid of useful recommendations.
Her lecture, though technically accurate, was devoid of any real enthusiasm.
Satellite images show a landscape devoid of vegetation after years of drought.
His apology sounded rehearsed and completely devoid of genuine feeling, which only made her angrier.
tc: The critic praised the film's visuals but found the dialogue ______ of wit, calling it flat and lifeless.
'Flat and lifeless' restates the idea that the dialogue has no wit at all.
se: The desert road was ______ of any sign of human life for nearly fifty kilometres.
empty
Both 'devoid of' and 'empty of' mean completely without any sign of life.

m: deeply religious, or sincerely committed to a belief or cause
x: My uncle is a devout man who never misses his morning prayers, even when travelling.
Our accountant, a devout vegetarian, brought his own lunch to the team barbecue.
The study compared the health habits of devout and non-practising members of the community.
The town's devout residents packed the cathedral for the midnight Christmas service.
She remained a devout believer in the power of kindness, even after many disappointments.
tc: Unlike her brother, who rarely went to temple, Priya was ______, praying every morning and fasting on holy days.
'Unlike her brother' sets up a contrast, and daily prayer and fasting describe deep religious commitment.
se: Her grandparents were ______ people who read scripture every night before bed.
pious
Both 'devout' and 'pious' describe deeply religious people, matching the nightly scripture reading.

m: skill and quickness in using the hands, or cleverness in handling situations
x: My mother peels a mango with a dexterity I have never managed to match.
She handled the hostile questions with remarkable dexterity, never once losing her composure.
Surgeons in training practise on models to improve their manual dexterity.
Some robots now show enough dexterity to fold laundry and sort small parts.
He admired the dexterity with which she smoothed over every family argument.
tc: Watchmaking demands extraordinary ______, since a single clumsy movement can ruin hours of delicate work.
The contrast with 'a single clumsy movement' shows the blank means skill with the hands.
se: The pianist played the difficult passage with astonishing ______.
skill
Both 'dexterity' and 'skill' describe the pianist's quick, expert handling of a hard passage.

m: (of fabric or similar material) light, delicate and almost transparent
x: She wore a diaphanous scarf that fluttered gently in the evening breeze.
For the photo shoot, the stylist hung diaphanous curtains to soften the window light.
Under the microscope, the insect's diaphanous wings revealed a fine network of veins.
Early-morning fog hung over the river like a diaphanous veil, softening the outline of the boats.
He still remembered the diaphanous white dress she wore on the night they first met.
tc: The curtains were so ______ that we could see the shapes of people moving in the street outside.
Being able to see through the curtains shows they were thin and almost transparent.
se: The dancers wore ______ silk costumes that seemed to float as they moved.
sheer
Both 'diaphanous' and 'sheer' describe very thin, light fabric, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: in a state of disrepair or ruin because of age or neglect
x: We spent the weekend clearing out my grandparents' dilapidated garden shed.
The startup's first office was a dilapidated warehouse with a leaking roof.
Students complained that the dilapidated library had not been renovated in thirty years.
Thousands of families in the old city still live in dilapidated buildings that could collapse in an earthquake.
Seeing his childhood home so dilapidated filled him with a quiet sadness.
tc: Once the grandest mansion in town, the house is now ______, with broken windows and a sagging roof.
The contrast with 'once the grandest' and the details of broken windows and a sagging roof show it has fallen into ruin.
se: The charity plans to repair ______ schools in remote villages before the monsoon.
run-down
Both 'dilapidated' and 'run-down' describe buildings in poor repair, which is why they need fixing.

m: extremely or unusually small
x: Despite her diminutive size, my aunt can carry a full sack of rice up three flights of stairs.
Our diminutive new manager has a voice that fills any meeting room.
The museum's prize exhibit is a diminutive manuscript no larger than a playing card.
Scientists have discovered a diminutive species of frog that could sit comfortably on a fingernail.
He looked at his diminutive daughter asleep in her cot and felt a rush of tenderness.
tc: Although the jockey was ______, barely reaching the shoulders of the other riders, he controlled the huge horse with ease.
'Barely reaching the shoulders of the other riders' restates that he was very small.
se: The ______ village church can seat only about twenty people.
tiny
Both 'diminutive' and 'tiny' mean very small, which fits a church seating only twenty.

m: disagreement or conflict between people
x: Arguments over who should host the Eid dinner have caused discord in our family for years.
Unequal bonuses created discord within the sales team, and two of its best people resigned.
The research group fell into discord over who deserved credit for the discovery.
The bitter election campaign left deep discord between rural and urban voters.
Their marriage survived years of discord before they finally learned to talk openly.
tc: Instead of the harmony the founders had hoped for, the commune was soon torn by ______ over money and leadership.
'Instead of the harmony' signals the opposite, so the blank means conflict.
se: The new shift system has caused considerable ______ among the staff.
friction
Both 'discord' and 'friction' mean disagreement and tension between people.

m: careful in what one says or does, especially to keep something private or avoid embarrassment
x: Please be discreet about the surprise party, because she mustn't find out.
HR made discreet inquiries before confronting the manager about the complaints.
During my thesis defence, my supervisor gave me a discreet nod whenever I answered well.
Diplomats held discreet talks in Geneva, away from the glare of the press.
He was always discreet about his friends' problems, which is why everyone trusted him.
tc: Because the investigation involved senior officials, the detectives had to be ______, revealing nothing to reporters or colleagues.
'Revealing nothing to reporters or colleagues' restates the idea of keeping things quiet and private.
se: If you are planning to change jobs, be ______ until you have a written offer in hand.
circumspect
Both 'discreet' and 'circumspect' advise careful, quiet behaviour so that nothing leaks out too early.

m: the feeling that someone or something is unworthy of respect or attention
x: She looked at the instant noodles with open disdain and ordered a proper meal instead.
His disdain for paperwork meant that his expense claims were always months late.
Some academics treat popular science writing with disdain, though it inspires many future researchers.
The minister's disdain for public opinion eventually cost him his seat.
She couldn't hide her disdain when her cousin started boasting about his new car again.
tc: Far from admiring the new building, most architects regarded it with ______, calling it a soulless glass box.
'Far from admiring' and 'soulless glass box' show the architects felt contempt for it.
se: The waiter glanced at our cheap shoes with barely concealed ______.
contempt
Both 'disdain' and 'contempt' describe looking down on something as unworthy.

m: gloomy and depressing, or very poor in quality
x: It was a dismal afternoon, grey and wet, so we stayed in and watched films.
The quarterly results were dismal, with sales down for the third straight period.
Despite months of preparation, his first practice exam score was dismal.
The country's dismal record on road safety has prompted calls for stricter licensing.
After the breakup, she spent a dismal week barely leaving her room.
tc: Critics expected the sequel to be a hit, but its box-office takings were ______, barely covering the cost of advertising.
'But' contrasts with 'expected to be a hit', and 'barely covering the cost' shows the takings were very poor.
se: The rain and fog made the first day of our holiday rather ______.
dreary
Both 'dismal' and 'dreary' describe a gloomy, depressing day caused by bad weather.

m: not influenced by strong emotion; calm, impartial and rational
x: When friends argue, my sister is usually the one who offers a calm, dispassionate view.
We need a dispassionate review of the project's failures, not a search for someone to blame.
Good scientists try to be dispassionate observers, letting the data speak for itself.
The judge delivered a dispassionate summary of the evidence before the jury retired.
It was hard to be dispassionate about the house where he had grown up and where his father had died.
tc: Although the debate quickly turned heated, the moderator remained ______, never letting her own feelings show.
'Although' contrasts with 'heated', and 'never letting her own feelings show' restates calm impartiality.
se: We hired an outside consultant because we needed an assessment that was ______ and free of office politics.
objective
Both 'dispassionate' and 'objective' describe a judgment not swayed by personal feelings or bias.

m: to make a doubt, fear or false belief disappear
x: A quick phone call from my brother dispelled my fears that he had missed his flight.
The director's town-hall meeting did little to dispel rumours of layoffs.
The first lecture of the course aims to dispel some common myths about evolution.
Health officials are working to dispel misinformation about the vaccine in rural areas.
Her warm smile and easy laughter quickly dispelled any awkwardness between them at their first meeting.
tc: The minister's vague reassurances did nothing to ______ public doubts; if anything, they made people more suspicious.
'Made people more suspicious' shows the reassurances failed to remove the doubts.
se: The test results should ______ any lingering concerns about the bridge's safety.
allay
Both 'dispel' and 'allay' mean to put concerns to rest, so the sentence means the same.

m: to scatter or spread over a wide area, or to break up and go in different directions
x: Once the speeches ended, the wedding guests began to disperse into the garden.
After the meeting, the team dispersed to their desks without saying much.
Dandelion seeds are dispersed by the wind over remarkably great distances.
Police used water cannon and tear gas to disperse protesters gathered outside parliament.
After graduation, our close group of friends dispersed across three continents.
tc: The crowd that had gathered to watch the fire began to ______ once the flames were finally put out.
With the fire out, the crowd that had 'gathered' does the opposite, breaking up and leaving.
se: The morning sun soon helped to ______ the thick fog over the river.
dissipate
Both 'disperse' and 'dissipate' describe fog thinning out and disappearing.

m: too large or too small in comparison with something else
x: Our youngest dog gets a disproportionate share of the attention at home.
A disproportionate amount of my working day goes on answering emails.
Researchers found that a disproportionate number of dropouts came from low-income families.
Flooding has a disproportionate impact on the poorest communities, who cannot afford to move.
His furious reaction to her harmless joke seemed completely disproportionate to everyone at the table.
tc: The punishment was clearly ______ to the offence: a five-year sentence for stealing a loaf of bread.
The colon introduces an example of a sentence far too large for the crime, which defines the blank.
se: Critics argued that the army's ______ response to a minor border incident risked starting a war.
excessive
Both 'disproportionate' and 'excessive' describe a response far greater than a 'minor' incident deserved.

m: fond of arguing; inclined to start or prolong disputes
x: My disputatious uncle can turn a simple conversation about the weather into a heated debate.
Meetings dragged on because one disputatious member questioned every single decision.
The seminar attracted disputatious graduate students who loved nothing more than a good argument.
The disputatious tone of the parliamentary debate left little room for compromise.
She found it exhausting to live with such a disputatious partner.
tc: Unlike his mild-mannered brother, Karim was so ______ that he could not let any remark pass without challenging it.
The contrast with 'mild-mannered' and the habit of challenging every remark show he loves to argue.
se: The committee was so ______ that it rarely reached a decision on anything.
argumentative
Both 'disputatious' and 'argumentative' describe a group that keeps arguing instead of deciding.

m: the state of having a bad reputation or of losing people's respect
x: One viral video of a cockroach in the kitchen can bring a small restaurant into disrepute overnight.
Staff were warned that posting offensive comments online could bring the company into disrepute.
A series of faked studies has brought the once-respected journal into disrepute among researchers.
Match-fixing scandals have brought cricket into disrepute in several South Asian countries.
He felt that his son's behaviour had brought the family name into disrepute.
tc: Once a respected method, phrenology fell into ______ when scientists showed that skull shape reveals nothing about character.
'Once a respected method' contrasts with what happened after it was disproved: it lost its good name.
se: After the cheating scandal, the once-celebrated scientist quickly fell into ______.
disgrace
'Fell into disrepute' and 'fell into disgrace' both mean the scientist lost respect and reputation.

m: disagreement with an official or widely held opinion
x: When we voted on where to go for dinner, there was only one voice of dissent.
The proposal passed without dissent, though several managers privately had doubts.
Good universities encourage intellectual dissent among students rather than punishing those who challenge accepted ideas.
The government has been accused of using new laws to silence political dissent.
Any hint of dissent from his children made their father furious.
tc: In a country where any criticism of the ruling party is punished, open ______ is rare.
Because criticism is punished, open disagreement with those in power would be rare.
se: The plan was approved unanimously; there was not a single word of ______.
objection
'Unanimously' shows nobody disagreed, and both 'dissent' and 'objection' express that idea.

m: to disappear gradually or make something disappear; also, to waste money or energy foolishly
x: By mid-morning the fog had dissipated and the ferry was able to leave.
The initial excitement about the merger quickly dissipated once job cuts were announced.
Heat is dissipated through the metal fins on the back of the processor.
He dissipated his entire inheritance on gambling and fast cars within five years.
Her anger dissipated the moment she saw how upset he was.
tc: The tension in the room began to ______ as soon as the host cracked a joke and everyone laughed.
Laughter after a joke suggests the tension was fading away.
se: Once the storm passes, the clouds will ______ and the sky will clear.
disperse
Both 'dissipate' and 'disperse' describe clouds breaking up and disappearing.

m: to persuade someone not to do something
x: I tried to dissuade my brother from buying a motorbike, but he wouldn't listen.
Her manager dissuaded her from resigning until a better offer came along.
My adviser dissuaded me from taking on two research projects in my first year.
Public health campaigns aim to dissuade young people from taking up smoking.
Nothing could dissuade him from flying home to be with his sick mother.
tc: Although his friends tried to ______ him from quitting his job, he handed in his resignation the next morning.
'Although' contrasts their effort with his resignation, so they must have tried to talk him out of it.
se: Bad reviews did not ______ us from trying the new restaurant.
deter
Both 'dissuade' and 'deter' fit 'from trying' and mean the reviews failed to put us off.

m: to separate and go in different directions; to differ
x: About a kilometre past the bridge, the road diverges and you take the left fork.
Our views on marketing diverge sharply, so meetings with him are never short.
The two theories diverge on the question of what caused the extinction.
Economic forecasts for next year diverge widely, depending on assumptions about oil prices.
The sisters' lives began to diverge after one moved to Canada and the other stayed in Dhaka.
tc: Although the twins agreed on most things, their opinions tended to ______ sharply when the talk turned to politics.
'Although they agreed on most things' sets up a contrast, so on politics their opinions must differ.
se: At this point the two historians' accounts begin to ______, and readers must decide which to believe.
differ
Both 'diverge' and 'differ' mean the accounts stop agreeing, which is why readers must choose.

m: to reveal information that is private or secret
x: My sister refused to divulge where she had bought the dress.
Employees are not allowed to divulge client details to anyone outside the firm.
Researchers must not divulge the identities of people who take part in their surveys.
The journalist went to prison rather than divulge the name of her source.
He finally divulged that he had been unhappy in the marriage for years.
tc: The spokesperson would neither confirm nor deny the report and refused to ______ any details about the negotiations.
'Neither confirm nor deny' shows secrecy, so the spokesperson refused to reveal anything.
se: The bank promised never to ______ customers' personal information to third parties.
disclose
Both 'divulge' and 'disclose' mean to reveal private information to others.

m: quiet and easy to control; ready to accept instructions without objection
x: Our neighbour's huge dog looks fierce, but it is actually very docile.
Some managers prefer docile employees who never question decisions, but they rarely get fresh ideas.
The teacher missed last year's lively class; this group was polite but strangely docile.
Critics accuse the state-owned media of keeping the public docile and uninformed.
She was tired of playing the docile wife and decided to speak her mind.
tc: Unlike its wild relatives, which bite anyone who approaches, the domesticated breed is ______ and easy to handle.
The contrast with wild animals that bite, plus 'easy to handle', shows the blank means gentle and manageable.
se: The once-rebellious pupil had become surprisingly ______ under his new teacher.
obedient
The contrast with 'once-rebellious' shows the pupil now follows instructions, which both 'docile' and 'obedient' express.

m: stern, severe and gloomy in manner or appearance
x: The dour shopkeeper never smiled, even when we bought half his stock.
Our new finance director is a dour man who rarely speaks in meetings.
The professor's dour expression gave nothing away as she handed back our exams.
The finance minister's dour warnings about inflation did little to dampen the festive mood in the markets.
Behind his dour exterior, my grandfather had a wonderful sense of humour.
tc: Although his letters were warm and funny, in person he was ______, rarely smiling or joking.
'Although' contrasts with 'warm and funny', and 'rarely smiling' describes a stern, gloomy manner.
se: The ______ guard at the gate checked every pass without a word or a smile.
stern
Both 'dour' and 'stern' describe a severe, unsmiling manner.

m: hard, boring and tiring work
x: Washing dishes for a family of eight every night is pure drudgery.
Automation has removed much of the drudgery from data entry in our office.
Copying out references by hand was the worst drudgery of my first year as a research assistant.
For many women in rural areas, fetching water remains a daily drudgery.
He escaped the drudgery of his office job by planning weekend trips with his wife.
tc: The new software spared the clerks hours of ______, such as typing the same figures into three different forms.
Typing the same figures again and again is given as an example of boring, tiring work.
se: She found the endless ______ of housework exhausting and unrewarding.
toil
Both 'drudgery' and 'toil' describe hard, wearisome work, so the meaning stays the same.

m: doubtful or uncertain; also, probably dishonest or not to be relied upon
x: I was dubious about the cheap hotel, and the photos online turned out to be fake.
The supplier has a dubious record of missing deadlines and inflating invoices.
Reviewers questioned the paper's dubious statistical methods and asked the authors to share their raw data.
The company made its fortune through dubious land deals on the edge of the city.
His mother was dubious about the match but kept her doubts to herself.
tc: Several experts have challenged the study's findings, calling its methods ______ and its conclusions unsupported.
Experts 'challenged' the study and called its conclusions 'unsupported', so its methods must be questionable.
se: Investors should be wary of companies with ______ accounting practices.
questionable
Both 'dubious' and 'questionable' describe practices that may be dishonest, which is why investors should be wary.

m: threats or pressure used to force someone to do something
x: My little brother apologised only under duress, after our mother confiscated his phone.
The contract was ruled invalid because he had signed it under duress.
The student said she had withdrawn her complaint against the professor only under duress.
Human rights groups say the confessions were obtained under duress.
She insisted that she had stayed in the marriage out of love, not under duress.
tc: Since the prisoner had been threatened and beaten, the judge ruled that his statement had been made under ______ and could not be used.
Being 'threatened and beaten' is a clear case of being forced by pressure.
se: Any agreement signed under ______ is not legally binding.
coercion
'Under duress' and 'under coercion' both mean signed because of threats or force.

m: to gradually decrease or fade away, like the tide going out
x: By late evening, the traffic on the main road had finally begun to ebb.
Enthusiasm for the project ebbed once the budget was cut in half.
My concentration tends to ebb after two hours of study, so I take a short walk.
Public support for the war steadily ebbed as casualties mounted and the economy weakened.
As the weeks passed and he kept apologising, her anger slowly ebbed away.
tc: His initial excitement about the job began to ______ as he realised how much of it involved filling in forms.
'Initial excitement' set against dull form-filling shows his enthusiasm fading.
se: The pain will slowly ______ as the medicine takes effect.
subside
Both 'ebb' and 'subside' mean to decrease gradually, which is what the medicine does to the pain.

m: unconventional and slightly strange in behaviour or appearance
x: Our eccentric neighbour walks his cat on a lead every evening.
The founder's eccentric habit of holding meetings while walking soon spread through the company.
An eccentric professor, he lectured in a straw hat and quoted poetry in his physics classes.
The newspaper profiled an eccentric millionaire who left his entire fortune to his cats.
She loved him for his eccentric sense of humour, even when it baffled her friends.
tc: In a town where everyone dressed conservatively, the artist's purple suits and feathered hats made him seem ______.
His outfits stand out against a conservative town, so the blank means unconventional and odd.
se: My grandfather had some ______ habits, such as reading the newspaper from back to front.
quirky
Both 'eccentric' and 'quirky' describe harmless, unusual habits like the one in the example.

m: famous and highly respected within a particular field
x: My cousin's wedding was attended by an eminent heart surgeon from the city hospital.
The firm hired an eminent lawyer to defend it against the lawsuit.
Several eminent scholars contributed chapters to the new history of Bengal.
A panel of eminent scientists warned that the river's fish stocks could collapse within a decade.
She was nervous about meeting her fiancé's father, an eminent judge with a fearsome reputation.
tc: Though he began his career as an obscure village teacher, he later became one of the most ______ historians of his generation.
'Though' contrasts with 'obscure', so the blank means famous and respected.
se: The conference will open with speeches by two ______ economists from Oxford.
distinguished
Both 'eminent' and 'distinguished' describe highly respected experts in their field.

m: based on observation or experiment rather than on theory or pure logic
x: My mother takes an empirical approach to cooking: she never measures anything, she just tastes and adjusts.
Before redesigning the website, we need empirical data on how customers actually use it.
Her thesis tests the theory against empirical evidence gathered from twenty countries.
There is little empirical support for the claim that violent video games cause violent behaviour.
He trusted his feelings, while she wanted empirical proof before she believed anything.
tc: The philosopher's argument was purely theoretical, but her critics demanded ______ evidence gathered from real experiments.
The contrast with 'purely theoretical' and the phrase 'from real experiments' define the blank as based on observation.
se: The claim is popular, but there is little ______ evidence to support it.
experimental
Both 'empirical' and 'experimental' describe evidence from testing in the real world rather than from theory.

m: filled with love, fascination or strong admiration for someone or something
x: My daughter is so enamored of her new kitten that she wants it to sleep in her bed.
Investors were so enamored with the startup's charismatic founder that they ignored its mounting losses.
Few students are enamored of statistics at first, but many grow to love the subject.
Voters seem far less enamored of the ruling party than they were five years ago.
He was completely enamored of her from the moment they met at his cousin's wedding.
tc: Although critics found the novel dull, ordinary readers were ______ of it, buying millions of copies.
'Although' contrasts with the critics' view, and buying millions of copies shows readers loved the book.
se: The young poet was clearly ______ with the editor's daughter.
smitten
Both 'enamored with' and 'smitten with' mean strongly attracted to or in love with someone.

m: to gradually intrude on someone else's territory, rights or time
x: Our neighbour's new wall encroaches on our garden by almost a metre.
Work emails increasingly encroach on evenings and weekends, leaving many staff feeling permanently on call.
Exam preparation began to encroach on the time she usually spent practising the sitar.
Illegal settlements are encroaching on the river's banks and narrowing its flow.
He felt that his mother-in-law was encroaching on decisions that belonged to him and his wife.
tc: As the city expanded, housing estates began to ______ on farmland that had been cultivated for centuries.
A growing city spreading onto old farmland describes gradual intrusion.
se: The new security law threatens to ______ on citizens' right to privacy.
infringe
Both 'encroach on' and 'infringe on' mean to intrude upon a right.

m: to improve the quality, value or extent of something
x: A squeeze of lime enhances the flavour of almost any curry.
Learning Excel properly could enhance your chances of promotion.
Well-run group discussions can greatly enhance students' understanding of difficult texts.
The new satellite will enhance scientists' ability to track cyclones in the Bay of Bengal.
Spending a few months apart actually enhanced their appreciation of each other.
tc: Far from damaging her reputation, the controversy actually helped to ______ it, making her the most talked-about writer of the year.
'Far from damaging' signals the opposite effect, so the blank means to improve.
se: Good lighting can greatly ______ the appeal of a small apartment.
heighten
Both 'enhance' and 'heighten' mean to increase or improve the apartment's appeal.

m: a feeling of listless dissatisfaction caused by boredom or lack of interest
x: By the third week of the holidays, a deep ennui had settled over the whole household.
The long, pointless meetings filled her with a creeping ennui.
Graduate students often describe a kind of ennui in the middle years of a doctorate.
The novel captures the ennui of a wealthy class with nothing meaningful to do.
He tried to shake off his ennui by taking up painting and calling old friends.
tc: Having nothing to do all summer, the teenager sank into ______, spending whole afternoons staring at the ceiling.
Having nothing to do and staring at the ceiling describe listless boredom.
se: The rich characters in the play suffer from a profound ______ that no amount of money can cure.
boredom
Both 'ennui' and 'boredom' describe the dull dissatisfaction that wealth cannot fix.

m: to happen afterwards, especially as a result of something
x: When the power went out during the wedding, chaos ensued as guests searched for candles.
A long argument ensued over who had forgotten to book the meeting room.
After the professor questioned the data, a lively debate ensued among the students.
If the river breaches its banks, widespread flooding is likely to ensue.
They quarrelled about money, and a week of icy silence ensued.
tc: If the old dam fails during the monsoon, a disaster of enormous scale is certain to ______.
The 'if' clause sets up a cause, so the blank must mean to follow as a result.
se: If the two sides cannot agree, a long legal battle is likely to ______.
follow
Both 'ensue' and 'follow' mean to happen afterwards as a consequence of the failure to agree.

m: to establish something so firmly that it is very difficult to change or remove
x: Giving in to every tantrum only entrenches the behaviour you are trying to stop.
The new manager tried to change the culture, but old practices were deeply entrenched.
Some scholars argue that standardised testing entrenches existing inequalities rather than reducing them.
Opponents warn that the amendment would entrench the ruling party's power for decades.
Years of mistrust had entrenched the brothers in their positions, and neither would apologise.
tc: Reformers want to act quickly, before corrupt officials have time to ______ themselves even further in the system.
The urgency to act 'before' and 'even further' suggest officials digging themselves firmly into place.
se: Critics fear the new rules will ______ the privileges of a small elite.
cement
Both 'entrench' and 'cement' mean to fix the privileges so firmly that they become hard to remove.

m: to name things one by one, as in a list
x: Before I left for university, my mother enumerated everything I needed to pack, from socks to medicine.
The memo enumerates the steps staff must follow before submitting an expense claim.
In the introduction, the author enumerates the main questions the book will try to answer.
The inspection report enumerates more than forty safety violations found at the garment factory.
She calmly enumerated all the times he had broken his promises.
tc: Rather than give a vague summary, the inspector chose to ______ each defect, one by one, in a numbered list.
'One by one, in a numbered list' restates the idea of naming items individually.
se: The contract should ______ all the services the agency will provide.
list
Both 'enumerate' and 'list' mean to name each service one by one.

m: a perfect example of a particular quality or type
x: With its spotless rooms and friendly staff, the little guesthouse was the epitome of comfort.
In his tailored suit and polished shoes, the new partner was the epitome of professionalism.
Her thesis was the epitome of careful scholarship, with every claim supported by evidence.
For many architects, the old parliament building is the epitome of colonial grandeur.
My grandmother was the epitome of patience, never once raising her voice at us.
tc: Always calm, always polite and never late, the butler was the ______ of discretion and reliability.
The list of flawless qualities shows he was a perfect example of reliability.
se: With its white beaches and clear water, the island is the ______ of a tropical paradise.
embodiment
Both 'epitome' and 'embodiment' mean a perfect example of a tropical paradise.

m: fair and impartial, treating everyone equally
x: We worked out an equitable way to split the household chores among the four of us.
The union is pressing for a more equitable pay structure across departments.
The university introduced quotas to ensure equitable access for students from rural areas.
Economists still debate whether the new tax system is truly equitable.
After the divorce, they reached an equitable arrangement for sharing custody of the children.
tc: The old system gave most of the water to large farms; the new law aims for a more ______ distribution among all users.
The contrast with the old system that favoured large farms shows the new aim is fairness for all users.
se: Both brothers agreed that the judge's division of the family property was ______.
fair
Both 'equitable' and 'fair' describe a division that treats both brothers justly.

m: to destroy or remove something completely
x: We tried every spray on the market but could not eradicate the cockroaches from our kitchen.
The new director promised to eradicate the culture of favouritism in promotions.
Teachers hope the reading programme will help eradicate illiteracy in the district.
Smallpox was eradicated in 1980 after a long global vaccination campaign.
Years of kindness could not eradicate the hurt he had caused her.
tc: Health workers hope to ______ polio entirely, so that not a single new case is ever reported again.
'Entirely' and 'not a single new case' show the goal is complete destruction of the disease.
se: The government has launched a campaign to ______ corruption in the police force.
eliminate
Both 'eradicate' and 'eliminate' mean to get rid of corruption completely.

m: to adopt or support a cause, belief or way of life
x: My father espouses a simple philosophy: never borrow money you can't repay.
The company publicly espouses work-life balance but expects staff to answer emails at midnight.
In his early essays, the economist espoused free trade, but he later became more cautious.
The party espouses policies that favour small farmers over large corporations.
She was drawn to him partly because he espoused the same values she did.
tc: Although he had once rejected socialism, in later life he came to ______ it with great enthusiasm.
'Although he had once rejected' signals a reversal, so he came to support it.
se: Many young activists ______ the cause of climate justice.
champion
Both 'espouse' and 'champion' mean to adopt and support a cause.

m: to cause someone to become unfriendly, distant or no longer close; to alienate
x: His constant complaining about money gradually estranged him from his closest friends.
The new manager's rigid rules estranged several senior engineers, who soon began looking for other jobs.
Her obsession with abstract theory slowly estranged her from colleagues who preferred practical research.
Critics argue that the party's harsh rhetoric has estranged younger voters who once supported it.
She had been estranged from her father for ten years before a letter finally brought them back together.
tc: Rather than bringing the siblings closer, the bitter dispute over their inheritance served only to ______ them.
'Rather than bringing the siblings closer' signals the opposite, so the blank must mean drive apart.
se: Her habit of mocking colleagues in meetings began to ______ even her most loyal supporters.
alienate
Both 'estrange' and 'alienate' mean to turn people away from someone, giving the same meaning.

m: extremely delicate and light, seeming too perfect or otherworldly for this world
x: Early morning mist gave the tea gardens of Srimangal an ethereal beauty that most tourists never see.
