Her ethereal voice filled the concert hall, and nobody dared to cough until the song ended.
The designer's new collection features ethereal gowns of silk and chiffon that seem to float as models walk.
Astronomers released ethereal images of a distant nebula glowing in soft shades of blue and pink.
The professor described the poet's imagery as ethereal, full of moonlight, mist and fading dreams.
tc: Unlike the heavy, earthy tones of his earlier paintings, his recent work is pale, light and almost ______.
'Unlike the heavy, earthy tones' sets up a contrast, and 'pale, light' restates the delicate quality the blank needs.
se: The dancer moved with such grace that she seemed ______, as if she weighed nothing at all.
otherworldly
Both 'ethereal' and 'otherworldly' describe a delicate, unearthly quality and give the same meaning.

m: to bring a feeling, memory or image into someone's mind
x: The smell of rain on hot pavement always evokes memories of my childhood monsoons in Dhaka.
Our new advertising campaign aims to evoke a sense of trust rather than simply list product features.
In her thesis, she explores how Victorian novelists used weather to evoke a character's inner turmoil.
The minister's speech evoked strong reactions online, with thousands of people criticizing his remarks.
Hearing that old song evoked such sadness that she had to turn off the radio.
tc: The museum's careful reconstruction of a 1950s kitchen was designed to ______ nostalgia, and many older visitors left in tears.
Older visitors leaving in tears shows the exhibit was meant to call up feelings from the past.
se: The photographs of the abandoned village are meant to ______ a deep sense of loss in viewers.
elicit
Both 'evoke' and 'elicit' mean to draw out a feeling, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to irritate someone intensely, often through repeated annoyance
x: Nothing exasperates me more than a slow driver hogging the fast lane on the highway.
Her refusal to give a straight answer exasperated the interviewer, who repeated the question three times.
Students were exasperated by the admission portal, which crashed every time results were published.
Repeated delays to the bridge project have exasperated commuters who sit in traffic for hours each day.
He adores his younger brother, though the boy's endless questions sometimes exasperate him.
tc: The client kept changing his mind about the design, and his indecision began to ______ even the most easygoing members of the team.
Constant changes that bother 'even the most easygoing' people point to intense irritation.
se: The waiter's slowness and repeated mistakes began to ______ the hungry diners.
irritate
Both 'exasperate' and 'irritate' mean to annoy, and both fit the diners' growing frustration.

m: serving as an excellent model; so good that it deserves to be copied
x: The hotel's service was exemplary, and the staff remembered our names from the very first day.
She received a bonus for her exemplary handling of the crisis with our largest supplier.
The professor cited his lab notebook as an exemplary record of careful scientific practice.
Officials praised the volunteers for their exemplary conduct during the flood relief operation.
My grandfather lived an exemplary life, never telling a lie and always helping neighbors in need.
tc: Far from being disciplined, the young officer was singled out for praise because her conduct under pressure had been ______.
'Far from being disciplined' and 'singled out for praise' show the blank means worthy of imitation.
se: The judges awarded the hospital a national prize for its ______ standards of patient care.
commendable
Both 'exemplary' and 'commendable' mean deserving praise, so the sentence means the same.

m: including every possible part or detail; thorough and complete
x: After an exhaustive search of the house, we finally found the car keys inside the refrigerator.
The auditors conducted an exhaustive review of our accounts but found no irregularities.
Her literature review is exhaustive, covering nearly every study published on the topic since 1990.
Investigators released an exhaustive report on the factory fire, listing dozens of safety failures.
He gave me an exhaustive account of his breakup, sparing no detail of their final argument.
tc: The guidebook is far from ______; it covers only the major sights and leaves out most of the city's smaller museums.
'Covers only the major sights' shows the book is not complete, so the blank means thorough.
se: The committee spent six months preparing a truly ______ analysis of the proposal.
comprehensive
Both 'exhaustive' and 'comprehensive' mean covering everything, giving the same meaning.

m: to make a process or action happen faster
x: If you pay an extra fee, the passport office will expedite your application.
Our manager hired two temporary staff to expedite the processing of customer refunds.
The department introduced online submission to expedite the review of thesis proposals.
The government promised new rules to expedite relief payments to families affected by the cyclone.
Hoping to expedite their reunion, she booked the earliest flight home after hearing her mother was ill.
tc: Frustrated that the paperwork was moving so slowly, the lawyer asked the court clerk to ______ the filing.
'Moving so slowly' signals that the lawyer wants the filing sped up.
se: The company hired additional engineers to ______ the launch of its new app.
accelerate
Both 'expedite' and 'accelerate' mean to speed up, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: stated clearly and in detail, leaving no room for confusion
x: The recipe gives explicit instructions about how long to soak the rice before cooking.
My boss was explicit that nobody could take leave during the final week of the quarter.
The exam guidelines make explicit reference to the penalty for using a phone in the hall.
The new law makes explicit what was previously only implied: employers must pay for overtime.
She made her feelings explicit, telling him plainly that she no longer wanted to see him.
tc: The rule was never ______ in the handbook; employees simply understood it from watching how their managers behaved.
Learning the rule only by watching contrasts with it being clearly stated, so the blank means clearly spelled out.
se: The contract was ______ about the penalty for late delivery, so neither side could claim confusion.
unambiguous
Both 'explicit' and 'unambiguous' mean perfectly clear, which is why no one could claim confusion.

m: to explain or present an idea or theory in detail
x: Over dinner, my uncle loves to expound on his theories about why our local cricket team keeps losing.
At the strategy meeting, the director expounded her plan for entering three new markets.
In his lecture, the professor expounded the basic principles of thermodynamics with remarkable clarity.
The new party leader used the rally to expound her vision of a fairer tax system.
He would expound at length on the meaning of love, though he had never been in a relationship.
tc: Rather than merely mention her theory in passing, the scholar chose to ______ it in detail across an entire chapter.
The contrast with 'merely mention ... in passing' and the phrase 'in detail' show the blank means explain fully.
se: The visiting economist was invited to ______ her views on inflation before a panel of students.
elucidate
Both 'expound' and 'elucidate' mean to explain clearly and in detail, giving the same meaning.

m: to free someone or something from a difficult situation or a physical trap
x: It took me ten minutes to extricate my scarf from the zipper of my jacket.
The firm is trying to extricate itself from a costly contract with an unreliable supplier.
She struggled to extricate herself from a group project that had become hopelessly disorganized.
Rescue workers spent hours extricating passengers from the wreckage after the train derailed.
He found it hard to extricate himself from the relationship without hurting her feelings.
tc: Having signed the lease without reading it carefully, the tenant now found it almost impossible to ______ himself from the agreement.
Signing carelessly left him trapped, so the blank must mean to free himself.
se: Firefighters worked through the night to ______ the miners trapped beneath the rubble.
free
Both 'extricate' and 'free' mean to release the trapped miners, so the meaning is the same.

m: full of energy, excitement and cheerfulness
x: Exuberant fans poured into the streets of Dhaka after the national team's last-ball victory.
The new intern's exuberant personality brightened even the dullest Monday morning meetings.
Children at the science fair were exuberant as their homemade rockets shot into the sky.
After a year of exuberant growth, the economy is now showing signs of slowing down.
She gave him an exuberant hug the moment he walked through the door after six months away.
tc: The team's ______ celebrations after the final whistle stood in sharp contrast to the gloomy silence of the losing side.
The contrast with 'gloomy silence' shows the blank means joyfully energetic.
se: The children were ______ on the last day of school, laughing and shouting as they ran out the gates.
ebullient
Both 'exuberant' and 'ebullient' mean bubbling with cheerful energy, giving the same meaning.

m: a false outward appearance that hides someone's true feelings or a real situation
x: Behind her cheerful facade, she was worried sick about her mother's health.
The company's glossy reports were merely a facade concealing years of mounting debt.
His confident facade crumbled during the oral exam when the examiner asked a simple question he couldn't answer.
Critics say the election was a democratic facade designed to give the regime some legitimacy.
Every Sunday the family kept up a facade of happiness in front of relatives, though the parents rarely spoke at home.
tc: Although he seemed calm in public, the composure he displayed was merely the ______ behind which he hid deep anxiety.
'Seemed' and 'hid deep anxiety' show his calm was only a false outward appearance.
se: Behind the ______ of wealth, the family was struggling to pay its bills.
veneer
Both 'facade' and 'veneer' mean a thin, misleading outer appearance, so the meaning is the same.

m: filled with excessive, uncritical enthusiasm or zeal, especially for a cause or belief
x: My cousin is fanatical about cricket and once stayed up all night to watch a Test match in Australia.
Our new director is fanatical about punctuality and locks the meeting room door at exactly nine.
Some students become almost fanatical in their devotion to a single theory and refuse to consider alternatives.
The documentary examines how a small fanatical group recruited young people through social media.
His fanatical jealousy eventually drove away the woman he claimed to love.
tc: Unlike his moderate colleagues, who accepted occasional compromise, he was ______ in his commitment and would tolerate no deviation from the party line.
The contrast with 'moderate colleagues' and 'tolerate no deviation' show the blank means extremely zealous.
se: The band's ______ fans followed it from city to city, sleeping outside venues to get front-row spots.
rabid
Both 'fanatical' and 'rabid' describe fans with extreme, obsessive enthusiasm, giving the same meaning.

m: to understand something difficult or puzzling after careful thought
x: I can't fathom why anyone would pay that much for a cup of coffee.
Engineers are still trying to fathom why the new software crashes only on certain machines.
Students often struggle to fathom the strange logic of quantum mechanics in their first course.
Scientists have yet to fathom exactly how the ancient builders moved such enormous stones.
She could not fathom how her best friend had kept such a big secret from her for years.
tc: The instructions were so convoluted that even the experienced technician could not ______ what they meant.
'So convoluted' explains why even an expert could not understand them.
se: Her parents could not ______ why she would give up a secure job to become a painter.
comprehend
Both 'fathom' and 'comprehend' mean to understand, so the sentence means the same.

m: to flatter or praise someone excessively in order to win their favor
x: Waiters fawned over the famous guest while the rest of us waited half an hour for menus.
He fawns over the boss in every meeting, laughing loudly at even her weakest jokes.
Graduate students sometimes fawn over a well-known professor in the hope of a recommendation letter.
Critics accused the newspaper of fawning over the government instead of asking hard questions.
She was tired of suitors who fawned on her because of her family's wealth.
tc: Rather than offering honest criticism, the junior staff would ______ over the director, praising every idea she proposed.
'Rather than offering honest criticism' and 'praising every idea' point to excessive flattery.
se: Junior ministers would shamelessly ______ whenever the prime minister entered the room.
grovel
Both 'fawn' and 'grovel' mean to act with servile flattery toward someone powerful, giving the same meaning.

m: possible to do or achieve in practice
x: Cycling to work is feasible only if the office provides somewhere to shower.
The engineers concluded that building the bridge in eighteen months was simply not feasible.
My supervisor asked whether it was feasible to finish the experiments before the conference deadline.
Officials are studying whether a new rail link to the airport would be financially feasible.
Moving abroad together seemed feasible at first, until they calculated the cost of visas and rent.
tc: Although the plan sounded attractive on paper, the budget cuts meant it was no longer ______.
'Although ... attractive on paper' contrasts with the budget cuts, so the plan can no longer be carried out.
se: Without extra funding, it is not ______ to expand the clinic this year.
practicable
Both 'feasible' and 'practicable' mean able to be done in practice, giving the same meaning.

m: to pretend to feel, have or be something
x: He feigned a headache to avoid going to his cousin's wedding.
During the meeting, she feigned interest in the sales figures while secretly checking her phone.
Some students feign understanding in class rather than admit that they are completely lost.
The suspect feigned ignorance when police asked about the missing money.
She feigned indifference when her ex walked into the room, though her heart was pounding.
tc: Not wanting to spoil the party, she tried to ______ surprise, even though she had known about it for weeks.
She already knew about the party, so her surprise had to be pretended.
se: The child would ______ sleep whenever his parents came in to check on him.
fake
Both 'feign' and 'fake' mean to pretend, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: well chosen and perfectly suited to the situation; apt
x: Adding a squeeze of lime to the soup turned out to be a felicitous idea.
Her felicitous choice of words calmed the angry client within minutes.
The editor praised the essay for its felicitous phrasing and clear argument.
The merger of the two charities proved felicitous, combining one's funding with the other's local expertise.
Their meeting at a friend's wedding in Chittagong was a felicitous accident that led to thirty happy years together.
tc: The speaker's remarks were usually clumsy, but on this occasion her words were ______ and perfectly suited to the solemn mood.
The contrast with 'usually clumsy' and the restatement 'perfectly suited' show the blank means apt.
se: The translator's choice of words was so ______ that it captured the poet's playful tone exactly.
apt
Both 'felicitous' and 'apt' mean well suited, so the sentence means the same.

m: savagely fierce, violent or intense
x: A ferocious storm knocked out power across the city and uprooted dozens of trees.
The two companies are locked in a ferocious battle for market share.
Her thesis defense drew ferocious questioning from an examiner who disagreed with her methods.
Wildlife officials warned villagers that a ferocious tiger had been spotted near the edge of the Sundarbans.
Their arguments were ferocious, but they always made up before going to sleep.
tc: The normally gentle dog became ______ when a stranger tried to climb over the fence, snarling and baring its teeth.
The contrast with 'normally gentle' and the detail 'snarling and baring its teeth' show the blank means savagely fierce.
se: As election day approached, the campaign grew increasingly ______, with each candidate launching bitter personal attacks.
fierce
Both 'ferocious' and 'fierce' mean extremely intense and aggressive, giving the same meaning.

m: to restrict someone's freedom or progress, as if with chains
x: I don't want to be fettered by a long phone contract that I can't cancel.
Small businesses complain that they are fettered by endless paperwork and licensing fees.
Good researchers refuse to be fettered by the assumptions of their own field.
Critics argue that the new law will fetter the press and discourage investigative reporting.
She felt fettered by her family's expectations and longed to make her own choices.
tc: The artist believed that rules would only ______ her imagination, so she ignored every convention she had been taught.
Ignoring every convention shows she thought rules would restrict her creativity.
se: Excessive regulation can ______ innovation in young industries.
hamper
Both 'fetter' and 'hamper' mean to restrict or hold back, so the meaning is the same.

m: changing loyalties, opinions or affections often and unpredictably
x: Spring weather here is fickle: bright sunshine in the morning, a hailstorm by lunch.
Fashion retailers know that consumer tastes are fickle and can change in a single season.
His fickle approach to studying, with a new timetable every week, left him unprepared for the finals.
Politicians quickly learn how fickle public opinion can be after a single scandal.
She was tired of fickle friends who disappeared whenever she needed help.
tc: Unlike her ______ brother, who changed his career plans almost every month, she had wanted to be a doctor since childhood.
'Changed his career plans almost every month' contrasts with her lifelong goal, so the blank means changeable.
se: Football fans can be ______, cheering a player one week and booing him the next.
capricious
Both 'fickle' and 'capricious' mean changing suddenly and unpredictably, giving the same meaning.

m: faithfulness to a person, cause or duty; also exactness in copying an original
x: The dog's fidelity to its owner was touching: it waited at the gate every single evening.
Our auditors check the fidelity of the translated contracts to the original French documents.
Historians praised the film for its fidelity to the events of the 1971 Liberation War.
Recording engineers prize high fidelity, so that every instrument sounds exactly as it did in the studio.
After twenty years of marriage, they still valued fidelity and honesty above everything else.
tc: The knight was celebrated for his ______ to the king; even under torture he refused to betray his master.
Refusing to betray his master even under torture restates loyalty.
se: Voters rewarded the senator for her ______ to the promises she had made during the campaign.
faithfulness
Both 'fidelity' and 'faithfulness' mean keeping faith with commitments, so the meaning is the same.

m: skill and delicacy in handling a situation or performing a task
x: She arranged the flowers with such finesse that the cheap vase looked elegant.
Negotiating with that particular client requires finesse rather than threats, as our sales team learned the hard way.
The surgeon's finesse impressed the medical students watching the operation from the gallery.
Diplomats handled the border dispute with considerable finesse, avoiding any open conflict.
He lacks the finesse to break bad news gently, so his friends often end up hurt.
tc: Where his predecessor had relied on brute force, the new coach approached problems with patience and ______.
The contrast with 'brute force' shows the blank means delicate skill.
se: Handling an angry customer without losing the sale takes considerable ______.
tact
Both 'finesse' and 'tact' mean skillful, delicate handling of people, giving the same meaning.

m: soft and limp; lacking firmness, energy or force
x: After a week in the fridge, the lettuce had turned flaccid and pale.
The board rejected the marketing plan as flaccid and lacking any clear message.
Reviewers called the novel's ending flaccid after three hundred pages of rising tension.
Economists blamed the flaccid recovery on weak consumer spending and a lack of business investment.
Her flaccid handshake left him wondering whether she was nervous or simply uninterested.
tc: Critics complained that the director's once energetic style had become ______, with scenes that dragged on without purpose.
The contrast with 'once energetic' and the phrase 'dragged on' show the blank means lacking vigor.
se: Without water, the plant's leaves grew ______ and drooped over the edge of the pot.
limp
Both 'flaccid' and 'limp' mean soft and drooping, so the sentence means the same.

m: showy, bold and confident in a way that attracts attention
x: He showed up to the picnic in a flamboyant purple suit and a gold scarf.
Our flamboyant sales director ends every presentation with a dramatic bow.
The professor's flamboyant lecturing style made even dry statistics entertaining.
Investors grew wary of the startup's flamboyant founder after reports of lavish spending.
She was drawn to his flamboyant charm, though her friends found him exhausting.
tc: Unlike her ______ sister, who loved bright colors and dramatic entrances, she preferred plain clothes and quiet corners.
'Bright colors and dramatic entrances' contrast with plain clothes, so the blank means showy.
se: The singer was known for her ______ costumes, covered in sequins and feathers.
flashy
Both 'flamboyant' and 'flashy' mean eye-catchingly showy, giving the same meaning.

m: new and inexperienced; recently formed and still developing
x: Our fledgling vegetable garden produced just three tomatoes this summer.
She left a secure job to launch a fledgling design studio with two friends.
The fledgling research group published its first paper only last year.
Observers worry that the fledgling democracy may not survive another disputed election.
Their fledgling romance was tested when he accepted a job in another city.
tc: Unlike established firms with decades of experience, ______ companies often struggle to win the trust of large clients.
The contrast with 'established firms with decades of experience' shows the blank means new and inexperienced.
se: The ______ airline has only four planes and flies to just two cities.
nascent
Both 'fledgling' and 'nascent' mean just beginning to develop, so the meaning is the same.

m: lasting only a very short time
x: I caught a fleeting glimpse of the deer before it vanished into the trees.
Sales enjoyed a fleeting boost after the advertisement, then quickly returned to normal.
For a fleeting moment during the exam, my mind went completely blank.
Astronomers recorded a fleeting burst of radio waves from a distant galaxy.
Their friendship was fleeting, lasting only one summer by the sea at Cox's Bazar.
tc: Fame on social media is often ______: a video can be everywhere one day and forgotten the next.
The clause after the colon restates that the fame lasts only briefly.
se: Her sense of triumph was ______, vanishing the moment the next problem demanded her attention.
momentary
Both 'fleeting' and 'momentary' mean lasting only an instant, giving the same meaning.

m: not showing the seriousness or respect that a situation deserves
x: When I asked about the broken window, my son gave a flippant shrug and kept playing.
The manager's flippant reply to the customer's complaint quickly went viral.
The professor warned that flippant answers would earn no marks on the ethics exam.
The official apologized for his flippant remarks about the flood victims.
She found his flippant attitude toward their anniversary deeply hurtful.
tc: Given the gravity of the accident, the spokesman's ______ joke struck everyone as wildly inappropriate.
'Given the gravity' contrasts with a joke seen as inappropriate, so the blank means unserious.
se: His ______ response to a serious question made the interviewers doubt his maturity.
glib
Both 'flippant' and 'glib' describe a casual, unserious answer, giving the same meaning.

m: to grow or develop successfully and vigorously; to thrive
x: Our tomato plants flourished once we moved them to the sunny side of the balcony.
Small businesses tend to flourish when local governments cut red tape.
Bored and restless at school, she flourished at university, where professors finally challenged her to think.
Coral reefs flourish in warm, clear water but decline quickly when temperatures rise too high.
Their marriage flourished after they learned to talk openly about money.
tc: While many rival shops closed during the recession, hers continued to ______, opening two new branches.
The contrast with shops that 'closed' and the new branches show the blank means thrive.
se: Children tend to ______ when they feel safe, loved and encouraged.
thrive
Both 'flourish' and 'thrive' mean to grow and do well, so the meaning is the same.

m: to rise and fall irregularly in number, amount or level
x: Vegetable prices in Dhaka fluctuate wildly during the monsoon season.
My working hours fluctuate depending on how many orders come in each week.
In the experiment, the temperature was not allowed to fluctuate by more than half a degree.
Currency markets fluctuated sharply after the central bank's surprise announcement.
His moods fluctuate so much that his friends never know what to expect.
tc: Rather than holding steady, the patient's blood pressure continued to ______ throughout the night, rising and falling every hour.
'Rather than holding steady' and 'rising and falling' define the blank as changing irregularly.
se: Attendance at the club tends to ______ with the seasons, rising in winter and dropping in summer.
vary
Both 'fluctuate' and 'vary' mean to change up and down, giving the same meaning.

m: pitifully sad and lonely; also, having little hope of success
x: A forlorn puppy sat outside the shop, waiting for an owner who never came back.
After the layoffs, the half-empty office looked forlorn, with abandoned chairs and dead plants on every desk.
He made a forlorn attempt to finish his assignment in the final hour before the deadline.
Residents gazed at the forlorn remains of their village after the floodwaters receded.
She looked forlorn at the airport, waving goodbye as her son left to study abroad.
tc: Abandoned by his friends and left alone in the rain, the boy cut a sad and ______ figure at the bus stop.
Being abandoned and alone, together with 'sad', points to a lonely, pitiful appearance.
se: The old house, empty for years, stood ______ at the end of the lane.
desolate
Both 'forlorn' and 'desolate' convey a lonely, abandoned sadness, so the meaning is the same.

m: inspiring fear or respect because it is powerful, impressive or very difficult
x: Climbing the stairs to the top of the tower proved a formidable challenge for my elderly aunt.
Our main competitor has a formidable sales team and very deep pockets.
The professor's reputation for formidable exams kept many students away from her course.
The defending champions remain formidable opponents, especially on their home ground in front of a packed stadium.
Even as a child, she had a formidable will and never gave up an argument.
tc: The opposing team was far more ______ than expected, and our players, who had anticipated an easy win, were soundly defeated.
The players 'anticipated an easy win' but were defeated, so the opponents were powerful and hard to beat.
se: Rebuilding the city's entire drainage system in just one year poses ______ challenges.
daunting
Both 'formidable' and 'daunting' describe challenges that are intimidatingly difficult, giving the same meaning.

m: to abandon or give up someone or something
x: I refuse to forsake my morning cup of tea, even on the busiest days.
He forsook a well-paid banking career to run a small bakery in his hometown.
She forsook her plan to study medicine after discovering a passion for mathematics.
Critics accuse the party of forsaking the workers who first elected it.
She promised never to forsake her old friends, no matter how successful she became.
tc: Even when threatened with prison, the activist refused to ______ the cause to which she had devoted her life.
'Refused' and 'devoted her life' show she would not abandon her cause.
se: He would never ______ his elderly parents, however hard life became.
abandon
Both 'forsake' and 'abandon' mean to leave someone behind, so the meaning is the same.

m: courage and strength of mind in facing pain, danger or hardship
x: My neighbor faced months of chemotherapy with remarkable fortitude and good humor.
It took real fortitude to keep the business running after the fire destroyed the warehouse.
Finishing a PhD while working full time requires both patience and fortitude.
The villagers showed great fortitude in rebuilding their homes after the cyclone.
Her quiet fortitude during her husband's long illness inspired the whole family.
tc: Despite years of hardship and pain, she endured her illness with ______, never once complaining.
Enduring 'hardship and pain' while 'never once complaining' shows courageous strength of mind.
se: The soldiers displayed great ______ during the long and bitter winter campaign.
courage
Both 'fortitude' and 'courage' mean bravery in the face of hardship, giving the same meaning.

m: fast and energetic in a wild, frantic or uncontrolled way
x: The frenetic energy of Dhaka's markets leaves first-time visitors both thrilled and exhausted.
The office was frenetic in the days before the product launch.
Students engaged in frenetic last-minute revision the night before the final exam.
Reporters described frenetic scenes at the stock exchange as prices collapsed.
Their frenetic social life left them little time to talk to each other.
tc: After the ______ activity of the holiday rush, the shopkeepers welcomed the calm of January.
The contrast with 'the calm of January' shows the blank means frantic.
se: The kitchen was ______ during the dinner rush, with cooks shouting orders and plates flying.
hectic
Both 'frenetic' and 'hectic' describe wild, busy activity, so the meaning is the same.

m: lacking any serious purpose or value; silly or trivial
x: I try not to waste money on frivolous purchases like designer phone cases.
The judge dismissed the lawsuit as frivolous and ordered the plaintiff to pay costs.
Some professors regard pop-culture courses as frivolous, but students often find them valuable.
Lawmakers criticized the agency for spending public money on frivolous foreign trips.
He treated their engagement as something frivolous, which deeply hurt her.
tc: During the crisis, the board had no patience for ______ suggestions; it wanted only serious, practical proposals.
The contrast with 'serious, practical proposals' shows the blank means silly or unimportant.
se: My grandfather considered video games ______ and refused to let us play them on school nights.
silly
Both 'frivolous' and 'silly' mean lacking serious value, giving the same meaning.

m: to protest or criticize something angrily and loudly
x: My father fulminates against the price of fish every time he returns from the market.
At the board meeting, the chairman fulminated about the company's falling profits.
Old-fashioned scholars fulminated against the new theory, dismissing it as a passing fad.
Opposition leaders fulminated against the tax increase in a series of fiery speeches.
She fulminated for an hour about her ex's behavior before finally calming down.
tc: Instead of calmly discussing the proposal, the senator began to ______ against it, shouting that it would ruin the country.
'Instead of calmly discussing' and 'shouting' show the blank means to protest angrily.
se: Newspaper columnists continued to ______ against the government's decision for weeks.
rail
Both 'fulminate against' and 'rail against' mean to criticize bitterly, so the meaning is the same.

m: done secretly or quietly to avoid being noticed, often out of guilt
x: A furtive cat crept along the wall, keeping one eye on the barking dog next door.
I noticed a furtive exchange of looks between the two managers when the budget came up.
Students made furtive attempts to check their notes while the invigilator's back was turned.
Police filmed the suspect's furtive meetings with a known smuggler at the harbor.
Their furtive affair continued for months before his sister discovered it.
tc: Unlike the open, confident manner he showed in public, his movements at night were ______, as if he feared being seen.
The contrast with 'open' and the phrase 'feared being seen' show the blank means secretive.
se: The boy gave the shopkeeper several ______ looks before slipping the chocolate into his pocket.
surreptitious
Both 'furtive' and 'surreptitious' describe secret, guilty glances, giving the same meaning.

m: the habit of eating or consuming far more than one needs
x: After three plates of biryani at the wedding, I felt rather guilty about my gluttony.
The company's gluttony for acquisitions eventually left it buried in debt.
Medieval writers listed gluttony among the seven deadly sins, alongside pride, envy and greed.
Activists linked rising obesity rates to a culture of gluttony encouraged by cheap fast food.
She teased her husband about his gluttony whenever he finished the children's leftovers.
tc: Monks in the monastery practiced strict moderation at meals and regarded ______ as a serious moral failing.
The contrast with 'strict moderation at meals' shows the blank means excessive eating.
se: The feast was an exercise in pure ______, with guests eating until they could barely move.
excess
Both 'gluttony' and 'excess' describe overindulgence here, so the meaning is the same.

m: to provoke or push someone into doing something, often by annoying them
x: My brother goaded me into jumping into the cold lake by calling me a coward.
Her manager goaded the team into working through the weekend with constant reminders of the deadline.
The debate coach deliberately goaded students to sharpen their arguments under pressure.
Protesters tried to goad the police into overreacting in front of the cameras.
He knew exactly what to say to goad her into an argument.
tc: Although he had no interest in fighting, the bully's constant insults finally managed to ______ him into throwing a punch.
Constant insults pushing an unwilling person to act show the blank means provoke.
se: The crowd tried to ______ the young boxer into attacking recklessly.
provoke
Both 'goad' and 'provoke' mean to push someone into action by stirring them up, giving the same meaning.

m: impressive or ambitious in scale, often far more than is practical or justified
x: My uncle has grandiose plans to turn his tiny backyard into a luxury resort.
The consultant's grandiose proposal promised to double profits within a single year.
The student's thesis made grandiose claims that her small sample could not support.
Critics mocked the mayor's grandiose scheme to build a giant statue in the city center.
He spoke in grandiose terms about their future together but never saved a single taka.
tc: The architect's ______ design, with marble towers and golden domes, was rejected as far too extravagant for a small town library.
'Far too extravagant for a small town library' restates the overblown scale of the design.
se: Voters grew tired of the candidate's ______ promises, which had no realistic chance of being fulfilled.
overambitious
Both 'grandiose' and 'overambitious' describe promises too big to be realistic, so the meaning is the same.

m: a distinctive feature that is typical of a particular person or thing
x: Fresh coriander and green chilies are the hallmarks of my mother's cooking.
Attention to detail is the hallmark of a good accountant, and our new hire has plenty of it.
Clear, careful reasoning is the hallmark of her scholarship, which is why her papers are so widely cited.
Economists note that rising inequality is a hallmark of many rapidly growing economies.
Generosity has always been the hallmark of their friendship; neither of them keeps track of who paid last.
tc: Precise brushwork and muted colors, found in nearly all her paintings, are the ______ of her style.
'Found in nearly all her paintings' shows these features are typical and distinctive.
se: Simplicity has long been the ______ of the studio's furniture designs.
trademark
Both 'hallmark' and 'trademark' mean a distinctive, characteristic feature, giving the same meaning.

m: arrogantly proud and treating others as inferior
x: The haughty shop assistant ignored us because we weren't dressed expensively.
His haughty manner in meetings made colleagues reluctant to share their ideas.
The visiting scholar gave haughty replies to every question from the audience.
Voters rejected the party's haughty leadership, which seemed out of touch with ordinary families.
She found him handsome but haughty, and she turned down his invitation to dinner.
tc: Despite his humble origins, the newly rich merchant became ______, refusing to speak to anyone he considered beneath him.
The contrast with 'humble origins' and 'anyone he considered beneath him' show the blank means arrogant.
se: The duchess answered the servant in a voice so ______ that he felt utterly insignificant.
condescending
Both 'haughty' and 'condescending' describe a superior, belittling tone, so the meaning is the same.

m: a person who believes that pleasure is the most important goal in life
x: My roommate is a true hedonist who spends his weekends on long brunches and late nights.
The firm's founder was a hedonist who charged lavish parties to the company account.
In philosophy class, we debated whether a hedonist could also live a moral life.
The magazine profiled wealthy hedonists who fly around the world chasing parties and perfect beaches.
She worried that marrying a hedonist would mean a life of fun but little stability.
tc: Unlike his ascetic brother, who denied himself every comfort, Karim became the family's ______, spending every taka on fine food and luxury.
The contrast with 'ascetic' and the spending on 'fine food and luxury' show the blank means pleasure-seeker.
se: The novel's hero is the ultimate ______, caring only about luxury, food and parties.
sybarite
Both 'hedonist' and 'sybarite' mean a person devoted to pleasure and luxury, giving the same meaning.

m: shockingly evil or wicked
x: Leaving a dog locked in a hot car is a heinous act of cruelty.
The company was fined for the heinous practice of dumping toxic waste into the river.
Students studying the war were moved by testimonies describing heinous crimes against civilians.
The court sentenced the man to life in prison for what the judge called a heinous murder.
She could not forgive him for the heinous lie that had destroyed her reputation.
tc: The prosecutor argued that the crime was not merely wrong but truly ______, shocking even veteran investigators.
'Not merely wrong but' intensifies the idea, and 'shocking even veteran investigators' shows the blank means shockingly evil.
se: The dictator was condemned for ______ crimes against his own people.
monstrous
Both 'heinous' and 'monstrous' mean shockingly wicked, so the meaning is the same.

m: a belief or opinion that strongly contradicts accepted or official views
x: In our house, putting ketchup on biryani is considered heresy, and my grandmother never lets anyone forget it.
Suggesting a four-day workweek was once heresy at the firm, but now it is official policy.
Galileo's claims about the solar system were treated as heresy by the church authorities of his time.
In economics, questioning the benefits of free trade was long regarded as heresy.
To her traditional parents, marrying outside the community was nothing short of heresy.
tc: In a company that worshipped growth at any cost, her suggestion to slow down was regarded as nothing less than ______.
Her idea directly contradicts the company's sacred belief in growth, so it counts as a heretical opinion.
se: To the old professors, any criticism of the founding theory was ______.
blasphemy
Both 'heresy' and 'blasphemy' are used here for an outrageous attack on a cherished belief, giving the same meaning.

m: made up of parts or members of different kinds; diverse
x: Our neighborhood is heterogeneous, with students, retirees and young families living side by side.
Managing a heterogeneous team from five countries requires clear and patient communication.
The researchers drew a heterogeneous sample of patients to make their results more general.
Cities with heterogeneous populations often enjoy richer food and music scenes.
Her circle of friends is remarkably heterogeneous, ranging from artists and farmers to bankers.
tc: Far from being uniform, the soil samples were highly ______, containing clay, sand, gravel and organic matter.
'Far from being uniform' and the list of different materials show the blank means mixed.
se: The evening class was ______, including engineers, artists and retired teachers.
diverse
Both 'heterogeneous' and 'diverse' mean made up of different kinds of people, so the meaning is the same.

m: a pause or break in an activity or process
x: After a two-year hiatus, my book club finally met again last Thursday.
She returned to work after a hiatus to care for her newborn twins.
The journal resumed publication following a lengthy hiatus caused by funding problems.
Peace talks resumed after a three-month hiatus, raising hopes of a ceasefire.
The band's hiatus gave the members time to repair their strained friendships.
tc: Following the show's ______, which lasted nearly two years, fans were thrilled to see the cast reunite.
A gap that 'lasted nearly two years' followed by a reunion shows the blank means a break.
se: Construction resumed after the ______ caused by weeks of heavy rain.
interruption
Both 'hiatus' and 'interruption' mean a break in activity, giving the same meaning.

m: a system in which people or things are ranked one above another by status or authority
x: In our family, there is a clear hierarchy when it comes to choosing the TV channel.
The company flattened its hierarchy so that junior staff could speak directly to senior managers.
Biologists study the social hierarchy of chimpanzees to understand primate behavior.
Critics say the party's rigid hierarchy discourages new ideas from younger members.
She sensed an unspoken hierarchy among her friends, with the wealthiest always at the top.
tc: In the army, orders flow from the top down through a strict ______ of ranks, and no one may skip a level.
'From the top down' and 'no one may skip a level' describe a ranked system.
se: Within five years she had risen almost to the top of the corporate ______.
ladder
Both 'corporate hierarchy' and 'corporate ladder' mean the ranked levels of a company, so the meaning is the same.

m: to create difficulties that slow down or prevent progress
x: Heavy rain hindered our efforts to finish painting the house before the guests arrived.
A lack of reliable internet continues to hinder productivity at the branch office.
Poor sleep can seriously hinder students' ability to concentrate during exams.
Bureaucratic delays have hindered aid deliveries to flood-hit districts in northern Bangladesh.
His jealousy hindered their relationship from growing into something deeper.
tc: Rather than helping the investigation, the witness's contradictory statements only served to ______ it.
'Rather than helping' signals the opposite, so the blank means obstruct.
se: Strict regulations may ______ the growth of small businesses.
hamper
Both 'hinder' and 'hamper' mean to hold back progress, giving the same meaning.

m: something that makes progress, movement, or action more difficult
x: Without a car, living so far from the station turned out to be more of a hindrance than I had expected.
The outdated approval process has become a real hindrance to getting projects finished on time.
Weak academic English was the biggest hindrance to his research being published in international journals.
Critics argue that the new regulations are a hindrance to small businesses rather than a help.
She felt that her family's constant worrying was a hindrance, not a support, as she tried to start over.
c: more of a hindrance than a help
tc: Far from being an asset, the heavy equipment proved to be the main ______ to the climbers' rapid ascent.
'Far from being an asset' signals that the blank means something that slows progress.
se: Lack of funding was the greatest ______ to the expansion of rural clinics.
obstacle
Both 'hindrance' and 'obstacle' mean something that blocks progress, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to sharpen or refine a skill or ability through practice
x: She spent the summer honing her cooking skills by making dinner for the whole family every night.
The workshop is designed to help junior managers hone their negotiation and presentation skills.
Writing a weekly blog helped him hone his arguments before he submitted his thesis.
Young cricketers in Bangladesh often hone their batting on narrow streets and crowded school fields.
Over years of difficult conversations, the couple honed the ability to disagree without hurting each other.
tc: Rather than learning a dozen new techniques, the coach told her to ______ the few she already had until they were flawless.
The contrast with learning new techniques and the phrase 'until they were flawless' show the blank means to refine through practice.
se: Debating every week allowed the students to ______ their public speaking skills.
sharpen
To 'hone' or 'sharpen' a skill both mean to improve it through practice.

m: pretending to have beliefs or virtues that one does not actually hold or practise
x: It's sheer hypocrisy to lecture your kids about screen time while you scroll through your phone all evening.
Employees were angered by the hypocrisy of a management team that preached cost-cutting while flying business class.
The novel exposes the hypocrisy of a society that praises charity but despises the poor.
Voters are tired of the hypocrisy of politicians who campaign against corruption and then quietly accept bribes.
She could forgive his mistakes, but not the hypocrisy of demanding honesty from her while lying himself.
tc: The senator who demanded strict water rationing while filling his private pool every week was rightly accused of ______.
His behaviour contradicts what he demands of others, which is exactly what hypocrisy means.
se: Critics pointed out the ______ of a company that advertised its green values while dumping waste into the river.
duplicity
Both words describe the deceit of claiming one set of values while acting against them.

m: based on an imagined situation or idea rather than on known facts
x: Let's take a hypothetical example: what would you do if you lost your job tomorrow?
The manager refused to answer hypothetical questions about layoffs that had not been announced.
Physics students often work through hypothetical scenarios, such as a ball rolling forever on a frictionless surface.
Engineers stress that the risk of a major earthquake in Dhaka is real, not merely hypothetical.
He kept asking hypothetical questions about whether she would have married him ten years ago.
tc: The danger is no longer ______; last month's flood showed that the city's defences really can fail.
The second clause shows the danger is now real, so the blank must mean merely imagined.
se: The lawyer objected that the question was purely ______ and had nothing to do with the facts of the case.
speculative
Both words describe a question based on imagined possibilities rather than facts.

m: seeming real or true but actually false; based on an illusion
x: The discount turned out to be illusory, since the shop had raised the price the week before.
Any sense of job security at the start-up proved illusory when the funding suddenly dried up.
Researchers warned that the apparent link between the two variables might be illusory.
Economists argue that the recent growth is illusory, driven largely by borrowing rather than real productivity.
The calm between them was illusory; underneath, both were still angry about the argument.
tc: The progress the company boasted about was ______: once the accounting errors were corrected, profits had actually fallen.
Correcting the errors reveals that the progress only seemed real, so the blank means deceptively unreal.
se: Their hope of a quick settlement proved ______, as the talks dragged on for another two years.
false
A hope that proves 'illusory' or 'false' is one that turns out not to be true.

m: about to happen very soon
x: Dark clouds and a sudden cool wind told us that the monsoon rain was imminent.
With the deadline imminent, the entire team stayed late to finish the report.
Graduate students tend to panic when their thesis defence is imminent and their data is still incomplete.
Officials evacuated coastal villages after warning that the cyclone's landfall was imminent.
She sensed an imminent breakup in the way he had stopped calling her every evening.
tc: Residents were told to leave their homes at once because engineers believed the dam's collapse was ______.
Being told to 'leave at once' shows the collapse was expected very soon.
se: Investors fled the market, convinced that a crash was ______.
impending
Both words mean about to happen, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to weaken or damage something, making it work less well
x: Staring at bright screens late at night can impair the quality of your sleep.
Constant interruptions in an open-plan office seriously impair people's concentration.
The study found that even mild dehydration impairs students' performance on memory tests.
Doctors warn that alcohol impairs judgement long before a person feels drunk.
Years of mistrust had impaired their ability to talk openly with each other.
tc: Far from improving her concentration, the medication seemed to ______ it, leaving her foggy and slow.
'Far from improving' signals that the blank means the opposite: to weaken.
se: Lack of sleep can seriously ______ a driver's ability to react quickly.
weaken
To 'impair' or 'weaken' an ability both mean to make it less effective.

m: treating all sides fairly and equally; not biased
x: We asked our neighbour to settle the argument because he was the only impartial person around.
HR appointed an impartial investigator to look into the complaints against the department head.
A good peer reviewer offers impartial feedback, regardless of who wrote the paper.
Citizens expect an impartial election commission that does not favour the ruling party.
As the eldest sibling, she tried to stay impartial whenever her brothers quarrelled.
tc: A referee must be strictly ______, giving no advantage to the home team however loudly the crowd cheers.
'Giving no advantage' to either side defines the blank as fair and unbiased.
se: The judge was praised for remaining ______ throughout a trial that divided the nation.
unbiased
Both words mean not favouring either side, so the meaning stays the same.

m: to slow down or block the progress of something
x: Fallen trees and flooded roads impeded our drive home after last night's storm.
Endless rounds of approval tend to impede decision-making in large organisations like ours.
A lack of reliable data has impeded research into the disease for decades.
Rival factions accused each other of deliberately impeding the peace talks.
His pride impeded any real reconciliation with his estranged father.
tc: Instead of speeding up the rescue effort, the crowds of onlookers only served to ______ it.
'Instead of speeding up' signals that the blank must mean to slow down or obstruct.
se: Heavy snowfall continued to ______ efforts to reach the stranded villagers.
hamper
Both 'impede' and 'hamper' mean to slow or obstruct, giving the same meaning.

m: absolutely necessary or extremely important
x: It's imperative that you bring your original passport to the visa interview.
Clear communication becomes imperative when a team works across several time zones.
Accurate record-keeping is imperative in any laboratory where experiments must be repeated by others.
Experts say urgent investment in flood defences is imperative for low-lying coastal cities.
She felt it was imperative to tell her parents the truth before they heard it from someone else.
tc: Because even a tiny leak could endanger the crew, it was ______ that every seal be checked twice.
The danger posed by even a tiny leak shows the checks were absolutely necessary.
se: With the virus spreading quickly, it is ______ that people get vaccinated as soon as possible.
essential
'It is imperative that' and 'it is essential that' both express absolute necessity.

m: to show or suggest that someone is involved in a crime or wrongdoing
x: Muddy paw prints across the kitchen floor implicated the dog in the case of the missing sausages.
The leaked emails implicated two senior managers in the accounting fraud.
Several studies have implicated poor diet in the rise of type 2 diabetes.
The minister resigned after a police report implicated his aides in a land scandal.
She refused to say anything that might implicate her closest friend.
tc: Rather than clearing the suspect, the new DNA evidence served only to ______ him further in the robbery.
'Rather than clearing' signals the opposite: showing his involvement in the crime.
se: The witness's testimony was enough to ______ the accountant in the fraud.
incriminate
Both words mean to show that someone took part in wrongdoing.

m: very poor; or seriously weakened by lacking something important
x: She grew up in an impoverished village where few children finished primary school.
The new CEO inherited an impoverished company with almost no cash in the bank.
Critics say that rote learning leaves students with an impoverished understanding of science.
Aid agencies are struggling to reach impoverished families displaced by the floods.
After the divorce, he felt emotionally impoverished, as if all the warmth had gone out of his life.
tc: Once the wealthiest family in the district, the Chowdhurys were left ______ after a series of disastrous investments.
'Once the wealthiest' contrasted with 'disastrous investments' shows they became very poor.
se: The charity provides free school meals for children from ______ households.
needy
Both words describe households without enough money, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: done or said without planning or preparation
x: When the power went out, we held an impromptu singing session on the roof.
The CEO gave an impromptu speech after the team landed its biggest contract.
Our professor sprang an impromptu quiz to see who had actually done the reading.
Hundreds of fans gathered for an impromptu celebration outside the stadium after Bangladesh's victory.
His impromptu proposal at the dinner table took her completely by surprise.
tc: Nothing about the party had been planned; it was a completely ______ gathering that began when a few neighbours brought out snacks.
'Nothing about the party had been planned' defines the blank as unplanned.
se: The singer surprised the audience with a short, ______ performance of an old folk song.
spontaneous
Both words describe a performance done on the spur of the moment without preparation.

m: freedom from punishment or from the harmful consequences of an action
x: Drivers in the city seem to run red lights with impunity, knowing the police rarely stop them.
The manager's favourite employee broke the rules with impunity while everyone else was disciplined.
Historians have documented how colonial officials acted with impunity in remote provinces.
Human rights groups say a culture of impunity allows security forces to abuse detainees.
He had grown used to insulting his siblings with impunity, since their parents never scolded him.
tc: Because the hackers were based in a country with no extradition treaty, they could attack foreign banks with ______.
Having no extradition treaty means they face no punishment, which is what the blank means.
se: Corrupt officials enjoyed near-total ______ because the courts never prosecuted them.
immunity
Both words mean protection from punishment, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: in an early stage; just beginning to develop
x: I could feel an incipient headache after two hours stuck in Dhaka traffic.
The new manager spotted the incipient tension between the two departments and addressed it early.
The paper describes how incipient cracks in concrete can be detected with ultrasound.
Economists warned that the incipient recovery could easily be derailed by rising interest rates.
She noticed an incipient jealousy in her friend whenever she talked about her new job.
tc: The doctor caught the disease in its ______ stage, long before it could become serious.
'Long before it could become serious' shows the blank means just beginning.
se: Investors watched nervously for signs that the ______ recovery might stall.
nascent
Both words describe a recovery that has only just begun.

m: (of weather) cold, wet, stormy, or otherwise unpleasant
x: We had to cancel the family picnic because of inclement weather on Saturday.
Flights may be delayed during periods of inclement weather, so please check with your airline.
The geology field trip was postponed until spring, when conditions would be less inclement.
Schools across the region closed early as inclement weather swept in from the bay.
Despite the inclement weather, she walked an hour in the rain to see him off at the station.
c: in the event of inclement weather
tc: The match was called off because of ______ weather, with heavy rain and gale-force winds lashing the ground.
Heavy rain and gale-force winds describe stormy, unpleasant weather.
se: Hikers are advised to carry waterproof gear in case of ______ weather in the mountains.
foul
'Inclement weather' and 'foul weather' both mean bad, stormy weather.

m: unable to exist or work together because of basic differences
x: This charger is incompatible with my new phone, so I need to buy another one.
The new software proved incompatible with the company's ancient accounting system.
Some of the survey results seem incompatible with the theory we started with.
Critics argue that the minister's business interests are incompatible with his public duties.
They loved each other, but their goals in life were simply incompatible.
tc: The two theories are ______: if one is true, the other must be false.
If one being true makes the other false, the theories cannot coexist.
se: The findings of the new study are ______ with earlier research on the drug.
inconsistent
Both words mean the findings cannot be reconciled with the earlier research.

m: not important or significant
x: We wasted an hour arguing over inconsequential details like the colour of the invitations.
For most employees, the changes in the new leave policy are largely inconsequential.
The reviewer noted that the difference between the two samples was too small to be anything but inconsequential.
What seemed an inconsequential rule change ended up affecting millions of taxpayers.
He felt inconsequential at family gatherings, where no one ever asked his opinion.
tc: Although the error seemed ______ at the time, it eventually caused the entire bridge design to fail.
'Although' contrasts the error's apparent unimportance with its serious result.
se: Don't waste the meeting on ______ matters; focus on the budget.
trivial
Both words mean unimportant, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: unwilling or unable to believe something
x: My mother was incredulous when I told her I had cleaned my room without being asked.
Staff were incredulous when the company announced bonuses in the middle of a loss-making year.
The examiners looked incredulous as the student claimed his dog had eaten his laptop charger.
Scientists were initially incredulous at reports of bacteria thriving in boiling acid.
She gave him an incredulous look when he said he had forgotten their anniversary again.
tc: Hearing that the tiny café charged twenty dollars for a cup of tea, the tourists were ______ and asked the waiter to repeat the price.
Asking to hear the price again shows they could not believe it.
se: The audience was ______ when the magician claimed he had never practised the trick.
disbelieving
Both words describe people who cannot believe what they are told.

m: impossible to remove, erase, or forget
x: Voters in Bangladesh have a finger marked with indelible ink after casting their ballots.
Her first boss left an indelible mark on the way she manages people today.
That brilliant professor made an indelible impression on a whole generation of students.
The war left indelible scars on the country's collective memory.
The day their son was born remains an indelible memory for both of them.
tc: Unlike the pencil notes, which could easily be rubbed out, the signature was written in ______ ink.
The contrast with notes that 'could easily be rubbed out' shows the ink cannot be erased.
se: That summer at her grandparents' village left ______ memories that she still cherishes.
lasting
Both words describe memories that remain and cannot be lost.

m: to formally charge someone with a serious crime
x: Our neighbour's son was indicted for stealing cars, and the whole street was shocked.
The company's former finance director was indicted on charges of embezzling client funds.
The law professor explained exactly what evidence is needed to indict a suspect.
A grand jury indicted three officials for their role in the bridge collapse.
She refused to believe her brother could be indicted for something so cruel.
tc: After months of investigation, prosecutors finally gathered enough evidence to ______ the mayor for bribery.
Prosecutors gather evidence in order to formally charge someone, which is what the blank means.
se: Prosecutors expect to ______ at least five people once the investigation is complete.
charge
Both words mean to formally accuse someone of a crime.

m: originating or naturally existing in a particular place; native
x: We planted only indigenous trees in the garden because they need less water.
The company now makes its packaging from indigenous plant fibres grown by local farmers.
Her thesis examines the indigenous languages spoken in the Chittagong Hill Tracts.
The government has promised to protect the land rights of indigenous communities.
He felt a deep pride in the indigenous traditions his grandmother had taught him.
tc: Unlike the eucalyptus, which was brought from Australia, the banyan is ______ to the region.
The contrast with a tree 'brought from Australia' shows the blank means native.
se: Conservationists are trying to protect ______ wildlife from invasive species.
native
Both words mean naturally belonging to the area, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: angry because of something that seems unfair or insulting
x: The customer was indignant when the shop refused to refund a clearly broken kettle.
Several employees wrote an indignant letter after being left out of the bonus scheme.
Students were indignant at the sudden rise in tuition fees halfway through the year.
Indignant residents protested outside city hall after the park was sold to developers.
She was indignant that her brother had read her diary without asking.
tc: Accused of cheating in an exam she had studied for weeks, the student was understandably ______.
Being wrongly accused is unfair treatment, which naturally makes someone angry in this way.
se: The passengers were ______ when the airline cancelled the flight without offering any compensation.
outraged
Both words describe anger at being treated unfairly.

m: absolutely necessary; impossible to do without
x: For anyone who cooks every day, a sharp knife is indispensable.
Within a year, she had made herself indispensable to the marketing team.
A good dictionary is indispensable for students learning to write academic English.
Volunteers have become indispensable to the relief effort in flood-hit districts.
After thirty years of marriage, they had become indispensable to each other.
tc: Far from being an optional extra, a reliable internet connection is ______ for anyone working from home.
'Far from being an optional extra' shows the blank means absolutely necessary.
se: Her years of experience made her ______ to the project.
vital
Both words mean the project could not succeed without her.

m: to persuade someone to do something, or to cause something to happen
x: Nothing could induce my grandmother to eat at a fast-food restaurant.
The company offered generous bonuses to induce experienced staff to stay.
In the experiment, researchers used a mild electric current to induce muscle contractions.
Some medicines can induce drowsiness, so avoid driving after taking them.
She tried every argument she could think of to induce him to apologise to his father.
tc: No amount of money could ______ him to betray his oldest friend.
'No amount of money' implies an attempt to persuade him, which he resisted.
se: The government is offering tax breaks to ______ foreign companies to invest in the region.
persuade
Both words mean to lead someone to act, so the meaning stays the same.

m: never wrong or never failing
x: My father thinks his sense of direction is infallible, which is why we always get lost.
No forecasting model is infallible, so we always plan for the worst-case scenario.
Students should remember that even textbooks are not infallible and sometimes contain errors.
The scandal shattered the public's belief that forensic evidence is infallible.
As a child, she saw her mother as infallible, but adulthood taught her otherwise.
tc: Even the most experienced surgeons are not ______; they too sometimes make mistakes.
'Sometimes make mistakes' describes the opposite of the blank, which must mean never wrong.
se: She trusted her instincts as if they were ______, and was shocked when they let her down.
unerring
Both words mean never making mistakes.

m: to reach a conclusion from evidence or reasoning rather than from direct statements
x: From the empty fridge, I inferred that my flatmates had raided it again.
We can infer from the sales figures that the new campaign is working.
Readers are expected to infer the narrator's feelings from small details in the text.
From the satellite images, scientists inferred that the glacier had retreated by several kilometres.
She inferred from his silence that he was still upset about the argument.
tc: The author never states the character's age directly, but readers can ______ it from her memories of the war.
Since the age is 'never stated directly', readers must work it out from clues.
se: From the tone of his email, I could ______ that he was unhappy with the decision.
gather
Both words mean to work out a conclusion from indirect evidence.

m: to secretly enter or join a group or place, usually to gain information or cause harm
x: Somehow ants managed to infiltrate the sealed jar of sugar in our kitchen.
The company discovered that a competitor had tried to infiltrate its research team.
The study shows how cancer cells infiltrate nearby healthy tissue.
Police officers spent two years infiltrating a gang that smuggled drugs across the border.
He felt his sister's new boyfriend was trying to infiltrate the family circle a little too quickly.
tc: To gather evidence without arousing suspicion, the journalist posed as a supporter in order to ______ the extremist group.
Posing as a supporter 'without arousing suspicion' describes secretly entering a group.
se: Hackers managed to ______ the bank's computer network and steal customer data.
penetrate
Both words mean to get secretly into the network.

m: to break a law or agreement, or to limit someone's rights
x: Playing loud music at midnight infringes on the neighbours' right to a quiet night.
The startup was sued for infringing a rival's patent on battery technology.
Copying large parts of another author's work without permission may infringe copyright.
Civil liberties groups argue that the new surveillance law infringes citizens' privacy.
She felt that her parents' constant questions infringed on her independence.
tc: The court ruled that the ban did not ______ freedom of speech, since people could still express their views in other ways.
Because people could still speak freely, the ban did not violate that right.
se: Any company that uses the logo without permission will ______ the trademark.
violate
Both words mean to break the legal protection of the trademark.

m: clever, original, and inventive
x: My uncle came up with an ingenious way to keep mosquitoes out of the bedroom using an old fan.
The team found an ingenious solution that cut delivery times in half.
Her thesis proposed an ingenious method for measuring air pollution with cheap sensors.
Engineers designed an ingenious system of floating gardens to cope with seasonal floods.
He planned an ingenious surprise for her birthday, hiding clues all over the city.
tc: Lacking proper tools, the stranded sailors devised ______ ways to catch fish using only wire and plastic bottles.
Managing with only wire and bottles shows the blank means cleverly inventive.
se: The engineer's ______ design allowed the bridge to be built in half the usual time.
inventive
Both words describe a clever, original design.

m: firmly fixed and difficult to change, especially of habits or beliefs
x: The habit of checking my phone first thing in the morning is deeply ingrained.
Changing an ingrained company culture takes far longer than changing its logo.
Researchers found that gender stereotypes become ingrained in children by the age of six.
Corruption is so ingrained in the system that reforms keep failing.
Her ingrained fear of disappointing her parents made it hard for her to change careers.
tc: The prejudice was so ______ in the village that even a generation of education failed to remove it.
Failing to remove it after a generation shows the prejudice was firmly fixed.
se: It is hard to break habits that have become ______ over many years.
entrenched
Both words describe habits that are firmly established and hard to change.

m: existing as a natural, permanent, or essential part of something
x: There are risks inherent in buying a used car from a stranger.
Some stress is inherent in any job that involves tight deadlines.
The professor explained the limitations inherent in using surveys to study behaviour.
Critics say the plan has an inherent flaw: it depends on oil prices staying high.
She believed in the inherent goodness of people, even after being betrayed.
tc: Danger is ______ in mountaineering; no amount of preparation can remove it completely.
If no preparation can remove it, the danger is a built-in part of the sport.
se: The ______ weakness of the plan is that it relies entirely on volunteers.
intrinsic
Both words describe a weakness that is part of the plan's basic nature.

m: to hold back, restrain, or prevent an action or process
x: The loud music in the café inhibited any serious conversation between us.
Fear of criticism can inhibit employees from sharing new ideas.
This enzyme inhibits the growth of bacteria in the lab samples.
High interest rates tend to inhibit investment by small businesses.
Shyness inhibited him from telling her how he really felt.
tc: Instead of encouraging debate, the professor's harsh comments tended to ______ it.
'Instead of encouraging' signals that the blank means to hold back.
se: The new drug is designed to ______ the spread of the virus within the body.
curb
Both words mean to restrain or limit the spread.

m: present from birth; natural rather than learned
x: My little sister has an innate talent for making friends wherever she goes.
Good managers have an innate sense of when to step in and when to step back.
Linguists debate whether the ability to learn grammar is innate or acquired.
Scientists believe that some fears, such as the fear of snakes, may be innate in humans.
His innate kindness made it impossible for him to stay angry with anyone for long.
tc: Mozart's musical gift seemed ______ rather than learned, since he composed pieces before he could properly read.
'Rather than learned' and composing as a small child show the gift was present from birth.
se: Some psychologists argue that a sense of fairness is ______ in children rather than taught.
inborn
Both words mean present from birth rather than learned.

m: unable to pay one's debts
x: After losing his job, he was nearly insolvent and had to sell his motorbike.
Our main supplier went insolvent, leaving us without spare parts for three months.
The professor's research shows how quickly small banks can become insolvent during a crisis.
Regulators shut down the insurer last month after declaring it insolvent.
She was embarrassed to admit to her family that her business was insolvent.
tc: With debts far exceeding its assets and no lenders willing to help, the airline was declared ______.
Debts exceeding assets with no outside help means the airline cannot pay what it owes.
se: The firm was ______ by the end of the year and had to close its doors.
bankrupt
Both words mean unable to pay debts, so the meaning is the same.

m: to start or provoke something, especially trouble or an official process
x: My cousin always instigates the pillow fights and then blames everyone else.
The new director instigated a review of all overtime payments.
The university instigated an inquiry after allegations of plagiarism in several doctoral theses.
Police say a small group instigated the violence at the end of the march.
She suspected that her mother-in-law had instigated the family quarrel.
tc: Although he claimed to be a peacemaker, he had secretly tried to ______ a riot by spreading false rumours.
Spreading false rumours, in contrast to being a peacemaker, is an attempt to provoke trouble.
se: Shareholders voted to ______ legal proceedings against the former chairman.
initiate
Both words mean to start a formal process.

m: refusing to obey orders or show respect to those in authority
x: Our teenage son has grown insubordinate and now ignores almost every rule we set at home.
The employee was fired for being insubordinate after refusing to follow his supervisor's instructions.
Students who are insubordinate in class may be sent to the headteacher's office.
The general dismissed two insubordinate officers who had questioned his orders in public.
Her father saw her decision to marry for love as insubordinate rather than brave.
tc: The soldier was court-martialled for ______ conduct after openly refusing to carry out his commander's orders.
'Openly refusing to carry out orders' defines disobedient conduct.
se: The crew grew increasingly ______, ignoring the captain's commands.
defiant
Both words describe people openly refusing to obey authority.

m: a person who fights against a government or authority, often with weapons
x: In the film, a young farmer becomes an insurgent after soldiers burn his village.
Before the trip, the security firm warned staff that insurgents had attacked several convoys on that road.
Her dissertation examines how insurgents use social media to recruit young men.
Government forces claimed to have killed dozens of insurgents in the mountain region.
He refused to believe that his gentle younger brother had joined the insurgents.
tc: Every ______ captured by the army claimed to be fighting to overthrow the corrupt government.
Fighting to overthrow the government identifies someone who rebels against authority.
se: The government offered an amnesty to any ______ who laid down his weapons.
rebel
Both words mean a person fighting against the government.

m: the quality of being honest and having strong moral principles
x: The cashier showed real integrity when she returned the extra change I had given her.
Our team leader is a man of integrity who never takes credit for other people's work.
Academic integrity requires students to cite every source they use.
Voters questioned the integrity of a minister who had hidden his foreign bank accounts.
She admired his integrity more than his looks or his salary.
tc: Though he was offered a large bribe to change the inspection report, his ______ would not allow him to accept it.
Refusing a bribe shows strong moral principles.
se: No one doubted the judge's ______; she had refused bribes throughout her career.
probity
Both words mean honesty and strong moral principles.

m: to step in on someone's behalf, especially to plead for them
x: When my father refused to let me go on the trip, my grandmother interceded on my behalf.
The union asked the director to intercede with the board to save the jobs.
Our supervisor interceded with the department to get our thesis deadline extended.
Religious leaders interceded to secure the release of the kidnapped aid workers.
She begged her older brother to intercede with their parents about her choice of husband.
tc: Facing expulsion, the student asked his favourite professor to ______ with the dean on his behalf.
Speaking to the dean 'on his behalf' means pleading for him.
se: Neighbouring countries offered to ______ in the dispute to prevent a war.
intervene
Both words mean to step into the dispute to help resolve it.

m: temporary; serving for a period until something permanent is arranged
x: We're renting a small flat as an interim solution until our new house is ready.
She agreed to serve as interim manager while the company searched for a permanent replacement.
The research team published an interim report after the first year of the study.
An interim government was formed to run the country until elections could be held.
After the breakup, staying with his parents was only meant to be an interim arrangement.
tc: Until a permanent coach could be appointed, the club named its assistant as the ______ coach.
'Until a permanent coach could be appointed' shows the role was temporary.
se: The court issued ______ orders to protect the forest until the full case could be heard.
temporary
Both words describe orders meant to last only until a final decision.

m: seeming endless; lasting so long that it becomes tiresome
x: We sat through an interminable wedding speech while the food went cold.
The interminable Monday meetings in our department rarely produced a single useful decision.
Students groaned as the lecturer embarked on yet another interminable digression.
Peace talks dragged on through interminable rounds of negotiation.
Waiting for the biopsy results, she found the days almost interminable.
tc: The flight was supposed to last two hours, but delays on the runway made the journey feel ______.
Delays that stretch out a short flight make it feel endless.
se: Passengers complained about the ______ queues at passport control.
endless
Both words describe queues that seem never to finish.

m: to frighten or threaten someone, especially to make them do what one wants
x: Don't let the big dog intimidate you; he's actually very friendly.
Some managers try to intimidate their staff into working unpaid overtime.
First-year students are often intimidated by the length of their reading lists.
Armed men were accused of intimidating voters outside polling stations.
His older brother's success intimidated him for most of his twenties.
