tc: The gang tried to ______ the shopkeeper into silence by smashing his windows at night.
Smashing windows to force silence is an attempt to frighten someone into obeying.
se: The defendant's relatives were accused of trying to ______ witnesses before the trial.
threaten
Both words mean to use fear to pressure the witnesses.

m: very detailed and complicated, with many small connected parts
x: My grandmother's nakshi kantha quilts are covered in intricate embroidery.
The contract contains intricate clauses that only a lawyer could fully understand.
Students spent weeks mapping the intricate network of nerves in the human hand.
Investigators uncovered an intricate web of shell companies used to hide the money.
Their relationship was more intricate than it seemed, shaped by years of shared secrets.
tc: Far from being simple, the watch's mechanism was so ______ that only a master craftsman could repair it.
'Far from being simple' signals the blank means highly complicated.
se: The carpet was decorated with ______ patterns of birds and flowers.
elaborate
Both words describe patterns with many fine, detailed parts.

m: tending to examine one's own thoughts and feelings
x: Long train journeys always make me introspective, staring out of the window and thinking about life.
After losing the contract, the team held an introspective meeting about what had gone wrong.
Her introspective essays about growing up between two cultures won a university prize.
The country entered an introspective mood after the election revealed deep divisions.
He became quiet and introspective in the months after his father's sudden death.
tc: Unlike his outgoing brother, Rafiq was quiet and ______, spending hours writing in his diary about his own motives.
Examining his own motives, in contrast to being outgoing, describes someone who looks inward.
se: The singer's latest album is more ______, focusing on her own doubts and fears.
reflective
Both words describe work that looks inward at one's own thoughts.

m: based on feeling or instinct rather than conscious reasoning
x: She has an intuitive sense of what her guests need before they even ask.
Good salespeople have an intuitive understanding of when to stop talking.
Many great mathematicians describe their first insights as intuitive rather than logical.
Studies suggest that voters often make intuitive judgements about candidates based on their faces.
Their friendship was so close that each had an intuitive grasp of the other's moods.
tc: She never calculated the risks consciously; her decisions were ______, guided by gut feeling rather than analysis.
'Gut feeling rather than analysis' defines the blank as instinctive.
se: Experienced nurses often develop ______ feelings about which patients are about to get worse.
instinctive
Both words describe knowledge that comes from instinct rather than reasoning.

m: to give strength, energy, or new life to someone or something
x: A quick swim before breakfast always invigorates me for the rest of the day.
The new CEO hopes to invigorate the sales team with fresh targets and incentives.
A semester in Japan invigorated her interest in architecture and urban design.
The government plans to invigorate the rural economy by improving roads and internet access.
Their trip to the hills invigorated a marriage that had grown dull and routine.
tc: Instead of tiring the runners, the cool mountain air seemed to ______ them.
'Instead of tiring' signals the blank means to give energy.
se: The new coach managed to ______ a team that had lost ten games in a row.
revitalise
Both words mean to bring new energy and life to the team.

m: impossible to harm, damage, or defeat
x: At nineteen, he drove as if he were invulnerable, ignoring every speed limit.
No company is invulnerable to a cyberattack, however good its security.
The study challenges the idea that elite athletes are invulnerable to depression.
The fortress was once thought invulnerable, but it fell after a three-day siege.
Being in love made her feel invulnerable, as though nothing could hurt her.
tc: The champion had seemed ______, but a young unknown challenger defeated him in straight sets.
'But' contrasts his apparently unbeatable status with his defeat.
se: With high walls and a deep moat, the castle was thought to be ______ to attack.
impervious
Both words mean that attacks could not harm the castle.

m: impossible to prove wrong or deny
x: The chocolate on my son's face was irrefutable proof of who had opened the box.
The auditors presented irrefutable evidence that the figures had been altered.
Her careful experiment provided irrefutable support for a hypothesis others had dismissed.
Scientists say the evidence for human-caused climate change is now irrefutable.
He made an irrefutable case for why they should move closer to her parents.
tc: The defence lawyer had hoped to cast doubt on the video, but the footage was ______ and the jury convicted within an hour.
The quick conviction despite attempts to cast doubt shows the footage could not be disputed.
se: The DNA results provided ______ proof that the man was innocent.
incontrovertible
Both words describe proof that cannot be denied or disputed.

m: tired, bored, or lacking enthusiasm after having too much of something
x: After a month of eating out every night, we felt jaded and longed for simple rice and dal at home.
Even jaded office workers cheered when the boss announced a four-day week.
By their final year, many medical students have become jaded by long hours and endless exams.
Jaded voters stayed at home, convinced that no party would keep its promises.
After three failed relationships, she had grown jaded about romance.
tc: Having travelled to forty countries, the journalist had become so ______ that even the pyramids failed to excite him.
Too much travel leaving him unexcited even by the pyramids shows he was bored from excess.
se: After twenty years in the business, the critic had grown ______ and rarely praised any film.
world-weary
Both words describe someone who has lost enthusiasm after long experience.

m: specialized words used by a profession or group that outsiders find hard to understand
x: My dad asked me what 'cloud storage' meant, so I avoided jargon and compared it to a filing cabinet.
The consultant's report was so full of corporate jargon that nobody in the meeting knew what he was recommending.
Good academic writers define their jargon clearly instead of assuming every reader already knows the field.
Critics say the new tax law is buried in legal jargon that ordinary citizens cannot hope to understand.
When my doctor dropped the medical jargon and spoke plainly, I finally felt less anxious about the diagnosis.
tc: The manual was meant for beginners, yet it was so dense with ______ that only trained engineers could follow it.
'Meant for beginners, yet' signals a contrast: only specialized professional language would make it readable solely by engineers.
se: Patients often feel confused when doctors speak in medical ______ rather than simple words.
terminology
Both 'jargon' and 'terminology' refer to specialized vocabulary that contrasts with 'simple words'.

m: to put something at risk of harm, loss, or failure
x: Skipping breakfast every day can jeopardize your health more than most people realize.
One careless email to the wrong client could jeopardize a deal we've spent six months negotiating.
Students who plagiarize even a single assignment jeopardize their entire academic record.
Environmental groups warn that the new dam will jeopardize the survival of several rare fish species.
He didn't want to jeopardize their friendship by confessing his feelings too soon.
tc: Afraid that one more late submission would ______ her scholarship, she started working on assignments a week early.
'Afraid' and the precaution she takes show that a late submission would put the scholarship at risk.
se: Driving on bald tires during the monsoon will ______ the safety of everyone in the car.
endanger
Both 'jeopardize' and 'endanger' mean to put at risk, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: fond of joking; humorous or playful in manner
x: My uncle's jocular remarks at dinner always keep the conversation light, even when the topic turns serious.
The manager adopted a jocular tone in her email, but everyone knew the deadline was no joke.
Despite the professor's jocular manner, his exams were notoriously difficult.
The mayor's jocular comment about the flooding was widely criticized as insensitive.
She tried to hide her nervousness behind a jocular reply, but her shaking voice gave her away.
tc: Although his words were ______, there was an unmistakable edge of seriousness beneath the jokes.
'Although' sets up a contrast with 'seriousness beneath the jokes', so the blank must mean joking.
se: He greeted his old classmates with ______ remarks about their thinning hair.
humorous
Both 'jocular' and 'humorous' describe remarks meant to amuse, so the meaning stays the same.

m: cheerful, friendly, and good-humored
x: Our jovial neighbor waves at everyone on the street and always has a kind word for the kids.
The new team leader's jovial personality quickly made the long office meetings more bearable.
Even during exam week, the librarian remained jovial and patient with stressed-out students.
Reporters noted that the normally stern judge seemed unusually jovial at the charity dinner.
Grandfather always grew jovial when the cousins arrived for Eid, telling stories and laughing late into the night.
tc: Far from the ______ host we had expected, he was curt and barely smiled all evening.
'Far from' contrasts the expected host with one who was 'curt and barely smiled', so the blank means cheerful and friendly.
se: Everyone at the reunion was ______, laughing and swapping old stories until midnight.
cheerful
Both 'jovial' and 'cheerful' describe a good-humored, happy mood that fits the laughter.

m: feeling or expressing great happiness and triumph
x: My little brother was jubilant when he finally found the kite he had lost on the roof.
The whole team was jubilant when the client signed the contract after months of negotiation.
She sent a jubilant message to her family the moment she received her acceptance letter.
Jubilant fans poured into the streets of Dhaka after Bangladesh won the cricket match.
Scientists were jubilant when the spacecraft sent back its first clear images of the distant planet.
tc: The players, who had been gloomy at halftime, were ______ after scoring three goals in the second half to win the final.
The contrast with 'gloomy' and the victory in the final show the blank means triumphantly happy.
se: The students were ______ when they heard that their exams had been postponed for a week.
elated
Both 'jubilant' and 'elated' mean extremely happy, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to arouse or inspire an emotion, interest, or idea; literally, to set alight
x: We used dry leaves and old newspaper to kindle a small fire at the campsite.
A single inspiring mentor at my first job kindled my interest in data analysis.
The documentary kindled in her a lifelong passion for marine biology.
The leaked report kindled public anger over the government's handling of the crisis.
A chance meeting at a friend's wedding kindled a romance that has now lasted twenty years.
tc: A good teacher does not simply fill students with facts but tries to ______ their curiosity so that they keep learning on their own.
'Not simply fill... but' and 'keep learning on their own' show the blank means to arouse or spark.
se: The coach's speech managed to ______ fresh hope in a team that had lost five games in a row.
spark
Both 'kindle' and 'spark' mean to arouse a feeling, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: a natural skill or talent for doing something well
x: My mother has a knack for making leftover rice and lentils taste like a feast.
Rafiq has a real knack for calming down angry clients on the phone.
Some students have a knack for exams, while others shine in long research projects.
Successful journalists often have a knack for spotting a story where others see nothing.
She has a knack for knowing exactly when a friend needs a phone call.
tc: He never took a single art class, yet he had an uncanny ______ for arranging colors that impressed professional designers.
'Never took a single art class, yet' shows the blank means a natural talent rather than trained skill.
se: She has a real ______ for languages and picked up Spanish in a single summer.
talent
Both 'knack' and 'talent' mean a natural ability, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: lacking energy, brightness, or excitement; dull and mediocre
x: After a lackluster meal at the new restaurant, we decided to cook at home on weekends.
The company blamed its lackluster sales on rising costs and weak demand.
His lackluster essay showed that he had barely engaged with the assigned readings.
Voter turnout was lackluster, with fewer than half of eligible citizens casting a ballot.
She felt their marriage had grown lackluster, so they planned a trip to rekindle the old spark.
tc: Critics had expected an electrifying sequel, but the film turned out to be ______, with flat dialogue and a predictable plot.
'Expected an electrifying sequel, but' and 'flat dialogue' show the blank means dull.
se: The team's ______ performance in the second half cost them the championship.
uninspired
Both 'lackluster' and 'uninspired' describe a dull, energyless performance.

m: to express sorrow, regret, or disappointment about something
x: My grandmother often laments that nobody writes letters by hand anymore.
Managers lament the shortage of skilled workers, yet few are willing to invest in training.
Historians lament the loss of so many ancient manuscripts in the library fire.
Residents lament the loss of the neighborhood park, which was paved over to build a shopping mall.
He still laments the day he let her leave without telling her how he felt.
tc: Rather than celebrate the new highway, many villagers ______ the destruction of the farmland it replaced.
'Rather than celebrate' and 'destruction' signal that the blank means to express sorrow.
se: Older fans often ______ the decline of Test cricket in an age of short, flashy formats.
bemoan
Both 'lament' and 'bemoan' mean to express regret about something, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to publicly mock or ridicule someone or something, especially through satire
x: My brothers love to lampoon my cooking, though they always ask for second helpings.
The office holiday skit lampooned the endless meetings that eat up everyone's week.
The student newspaper lampooned the administration's new dress code in a front-page cartoon.
Late-night comedians regularly lampoon politicians of every party, and audiences seem to love it.
She was hurt when her friends lampooned her poetry in front of people she barely knew.
tc: The satirical magazine was known to ______ anyone in power, from bank chiefs to bishops, with savage cartoons.
'Satirical' and 'savage cartoons' indicate the blank means to mock through satire.
se: Cartoonists were quick to ______ the minister's clumsy attempt to explain the price rise.
satirize
Both 'lampoon' and 'satirize' mean to mock someone publicly through humor.

m: lawful or valid; justified by reason or accepted standards
x: Feeling exhausted after a twelve-hour shift is a perfectly legitimate reason to skip the party.
Before signing, check whether the company is a legitimate business or just a website with a logo.
The professor said that questioning a study's methods was a legitimate part of academic debate.
International observers declared the election free, fair, and legitimate, ending weeks of uncertainty.
She had legitimate concerns about moving abroad, and her husband promised to take them seriously.
tc: The court ruled that, since the contract had been signed under threat, it could not be considered ______.
'Signed under threat' explains why the contract cannot be treated as lawful or valid.
se: Parents have ______ concerns when schools cut science classes to save money.
valid
Both 'legitimate' and 'valid' mean the concerns are reasonable and justified.

m: more merciful or tolerant than expected; not strict in punishing
x: My parents were lenient about curfews as long as I phoned to say where I was.
Our new boss is lenient about working from home, which has made the team much happier.
Some students think Professor Ahmed is lenient in grading, but his final exam proves otherwise.
Victims' families protested what they saw as a lenient sentence for the drunk driver.
She was always lenient with her younger brother, forgiving him even when he broke her camera.
tc: Critics argued that the judge was far too ______, giving a mere warning to a man convicted of repeated fraud.
Giving 'a mere warning' for 'repeated fraud' shows the blank means not strict enough.
se: The new principal was more ______ than her predecessor, rarely punishing students for minor mistakes.
tolerant
Both 'lenient' and 'tolerant' describe someone who is not strict about punishment.

m: legally responsible for something, such as damages, debts, or injuries
x: If your dog bites someone, you could be held liable for their medical bills.
The contract makes the supplier liable for any delays caused by faulty parts.
Universities may be liable if they fail to protect students' personal data.
A court ruled that the factory owners were liable for the pollution of the river.
When we bought the flat together, I didn't realize I would be liable for half of his debts too.
tc: Because the landlord had ignored repeated warnings about the broken stairs, the court found him ______ for the tenant's injuries.
Ignoring repeated warnings explains why the court made him legally responsible.
se: Under the new law, company directors can be held personally ______ for unpaid taxes.
responsible
Both 'liable' and 'responsible' mean legally answerable, so the sentence means the same.

m: a false written or published statement that damages someone's reputation
x: My aunt threatened to sue for libel after a neighbor posted lies about her online.
Our legal team checks every press release to make sure it contains nothing that could count as libel.
In media law class, we studied how courts distinguish libel from honest criticism.
The newspaper was ordered to pay damages for libel after printing false claims about a local businessman.
He never forgave his former partner for the libel that cost him both his job and his marriage.
tc: Because the article's accusations were both false and published in print, the senator's lawyers filed a suit for ______.
'False' and 'published in print' together define written defamation.
se: The tabloid paid a huge settlement to avoid a trial for ______.
defamation
Both 'libel' and 'defamation' refer to damaging someone's reputation with false statements.

m: lacking energy, interest, or enthusiasm
x: The heat was so oppressive that even the children lay listless on the floor all afternoon.
After the layoffs were announced, the office felt listless and quiet for weeks.
By the third hour of the lecture, most students were listless and staring at their phones.
Doctors say that a listless, feverish child should be examined as soon as possible.
Since the breakup, she has been listless, barely eating and rarely leaving her room.
tc: The usually energetic puppy was strangely ______, refusing to play and sleeping most of the day.
The contrast with 'usually energetic' and 'refusing to play' shows the blank means lacking energy.
se: Weeks of poor sleep left him ______ and unable to concentrate at work.
lethargic
Both 'listless' and 'lethargic' mean lacking energy, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: extremely angry; furious
x: Dad was livid when he found out I had dented the car and tried to hide it.
The CEO was livid that confidential sales figures had been leaked to the press.
Our professor was livid when half the class submitted identical answers to the take-home exam.
Commuters were livid after the train company cancelled services without warning for the third day running.
She was livid with her best friend for revealing her secret at the party.
tc: Far from being mildly annoyed, the customer was ______, shouting at the staff and demanding to see the manager.
'Far from being mildly annoyed' and the shouting show the blank means extremely angry.
se: The coach was ______ when his players showed up an hour late for the final.
furious
Both 'livid' and 'furious' mean extremely angry, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: unwilling or reluctant to do something
x: I was loath to leave my warm bed on such a cold winter morning.
The manager was loath to hire anyone new until next year's budget was approved.
Many students are loath to ask questions in class for fear of looking foolish.
Governments are often loath to raise taxes in the months before an election.
She was loath to admit that she still missed him after all these years.
tc: Having been burned by bad investments before, the old farmer was ______ to trust anyone who promised quick profits.
His past bad experience explains why he is unwilling to trust such promises.
se: Most people are ______ to change habits they have followed for decades.
reluctant
Both 'loath' and 'reluctant' mean unwilling, so the sentence means the same.

m: noble, high-minded, or highly ambitious in ideals or aims
x: My lofty plan to read fifty books this year collapsed by February.
The company's lofty mission statement means little if employees are treated badly.
The university's lofty goal is to rank among the top hundred research institutions in the world.
The summit began with lofty promises to cut emissions, but few concrete commitments followed.
He admired her lofty ideals, even when they made her impatient with his more practical choices.
tc: The charter was full of ______ ideals about justice and equality, yet the government that wrote it ignored them in practice.
The contrast between the ideals and 'ignored them in practice' shows the blank means noble or high-minded.
se: Few people doubted the ______ aims of the charity, but many questioned how it spent its money.
noble
Both 'lofty' and 'noble' describe high-minded aims, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: producing a lot of money or profit
x: Selling homemade pickles online turned out to be surprisingly lucrative for my aunt.
He left a lucrative job at an investment bank to start a small nonprofit.
Many graduates chase lucrative careers in finance instead of pursuing research.
Garment exports remain one of Bangladesh's most lucrative sources of foreign income.
Their friendship ended when one of them sold their lucrative business without telling the other.
tc: Although the work was dull and exhausting, it was so ______ that he paid off his student loans in two years.
'Although... dull and exhausting' contrasts with paying off loans quickly, so the blank means highly profitable.
se: Tutoring wealthy students for university entrance exams can be extremely ______.
profitable
Both 'lucrative' and 'profitable' mean earning a lot of money.

m: shocking and sensational, especially in describing violent or scandalous details
x: My mother refused to let us watch the lurid crime shows our classmates talked about.
The HR manager told staff not to spread lurid rumors about why their colleague had resigned.
Victorian novels often used lurid descriptions of crime to attract working-class readers.
Tabloids filled their front pages with lurid details of the celebrity divorce.
He was hurt that his friends repeated lurid gossip about his divorce instead of asking him what happened.
tc: Unlike the tabloids, which printed ______ accounts of the murder, the local paper reported the facts with restraint.
'Unlike' and 'with restraint' show the blank means sensational and shocking.
se: The book's cover promised ______ tales of scandal, but the stories inside were fairly tame.
sensational
Both 'lurid' and 'sensational' describe shocking content that contrasts with 'tame'.

m: a wealthy and powerful person in a particular industry or business
x: Our quiet neighbor turned out to be a shipping magnate who owned dozens of cargo vessels.
The young engineers dreamed of becoming tech magnates by the time they turned forty.
Our business history course examined how nineteenth-century railroad magnates built their fortunes.
A media magnate bought the struggling newspaper and promised not to interfere with its editors.
She fell in love with a property magnate but soon realized his work always came first.
tc: Having started with a single bakery stall, he became the country's leading food ______, controlling chains in every major city.
His rise to controlling chains nationwide shows the blank means a wealthy, powerful business figure.
se: The museum's new wing was funded by a steel ______ who had made his fortune during the boom.
tycoon
Both 'magnate' and 'tycoon' mean a rich, powerful businessperson.

m: a disease or ailment; also, a serious problem affecting a society
x: My grandfather had a mysterious malady that no village doctor could explain.
Burnout has become a common malady among young professionals who never switch off their phones.
Medical students learn to recognize rare maladies that most doctors see only once in a career.
Corruption is a malady that weakens public trust in every institution it touches.
Loneliness, she believed, was a malady that no amount of money could cure.
tc: Doctors were baffled by the ______, which caused high fevers and joint pain but did not match any known infection.
Fevers, joint pain, and comparison to infections show the blank means a disease.
se: The villagers believed that the bitter herb could cure almost any ______.
illness
Both 'malady' and 'illness' mean a sickness, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: the desire or intention to harm or hurt someone
x: I don't think he broke the vase out of malice; he's just clumsy.
Her colleague's comments in the meeting seemed driven more by malice than by honest disagreement.
Literary critics have long debated whether Iago acts from pure malice or from jealousy.
The court found that the fire had been set with malice, not by accident.
Even after the divorce, she spoke of her ex-husband without any trace of malice.
tc: Though his review was harsh, it contained no ______; he simply wanted the author to improve.
'Though... harsh' and 'wanted the author to improve' show the blank means intent to harm.
se: The witness insisted that she had spread the rumor out of ______, not ignorance.
spite
Both 'malice' and 'spite' mean a desire to hurt someone, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to say harmful and untrue things about someone; to speak ill of unfairly
x: It isn't fair to malign the new neighbors before you've even met them.
He felt maligned by colleagues who blamed him for a project failure he had warned against.
Once widely maligned, the theory is now accepted by most physicists as the best explanation available.
Activists say the campaign ads unfairly malign immigrants as criminals.
She refused to malign her former partner, even when friends urged her to tell her side of the story.
tc: Rather than ______ his rivals with false accusations, the candidate chose to focus on his own record.
'False accusations' shows the blank means to speak harmful untruths about someone.
se: Jealous classmates tried to ______ her by spreading false stories about cheating.
defame
Both 'malign' and 'defame' mean to damage someone's reputation with untrue claims.

m: an official order or authority to do something, often given by voters
x: Our building committee has a mandate to fix the lifts before spending money on anything else.
The new CEO arrived with a clear mandate to cut costs and modernize the company.
The research council's mandate is to fund projects that benefit public health.
After winning by a landslide, the party claimed a strong mandate for sweeping reforms.
My parents treated my silence as a mandate to start planning my wedding without asking me.
tc: With barely a third of the vote, the new government could hardly claim a popular ______ for such drastic changes.
'Barely a third of the vote' explains why it lacks authority from the voters.
se: The committee was given the ______ to investigate any department it chose.
authority
Both 'mandate' and 'authority' mean official permission to act.

m: clear or obvious to the eye or mind
x: Her joy was manifest the moment she saw her brother walk through the door.
The flaws in the plan became manifest within the first week of its launch.
The student's lack of preparation was manifest in every answer he gave.
The dangers of the drug became manifest only after thousands of patients had taken it.
His manifest affection for his children touched everyone at the gathering.
tc: Although the risks seemed hidden at first, they soon became ______ to everyone involved.
The contrast with 'hidden' shows the blank means obvious.
se: His nervousness was ______ from the way his hands shook as he spoke.
evident
Both 'manifest' and 'evident' mean clearly visible, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to control or influence someone or something cleverly or unfairly for one's own advantage
x: Children quickly learn how to manipulate their grandparents into buying them sweets.
The finance officer was fired for manipulating the accounts to hide the company's losses.
Researchers who manipulate data to fit their hypothesis undermine trust in the whole field.
Social media algorithms can be used to manipulate public opinion during elections.
She finally realized that he had been manipulating her with guilt for years.
tc: The scam artists did not use force; instead they tried to ______ their victims through flattery and false promises.
'Did not use force; instead' plus 'flattery and false promises' show the blank means to influence deviously.
se: Investigators found that traders had conspired to ______ interest rates for their own profit.
rig
Both 'manipulate' and 'rig' mean to dishonestly control an outcome.

m: minor and not important; small in amount or effect
x: Switching to a cheaper phone plan made only a marginal difference to my monthly bills.
The new software led to marginal improvements in productivity, hardly worth its high price.
The professor dismissed the debate as marginal to the main argument of the book.
Economists expect only a marginal rise in inflation next quarter, despite higher fuel prices.
He felt like a marginal figure in his own family, rarely consulted on any decision.
tc: The drug's benefits were so ______ that regulators questioned whether they justified its serious side effects.
Doubting whether the benefits justify serious side effects shows they were very small.
se: The changes to the exam format had ______ effects on students' scores, hardly worth discussing.
negligible
Both 'marginal' and 'negligible' mean very small, matching 'hardly worth discussing'.

m: to intervene between opposing sides to help them reach an agreement
x: My mother usually mediates when my brother and I argue over the television remote.
HR was asked to mediate a dispute between two department heads.
Our faculty advisor mediated between the student union and the administration over the fee increase.
Neighboring countries offered to mediate peace talks between the warring factions.
Tired of always mediating between her friends, she told them to settle their differences directly.
tc: Since neither the union nor the factory owners trusted each other, a retired judge was invited to ______ the dispute.
The mutual distrust explains the need for a neutral third party to help settle the dispute.
se: The United Nations agreed to ______ between the two governments after direct talks broke down.
intercede
Both 'mediate' and 'intercede' mean to step in between two parties to resolve a conflict.

m: deeply and lastingly sad or thoughtful
x: The steady rain and gray skies put me in a melancholy mood all weekend.
There was a melancholy atmosphere in the office on the day our old manager retired.
Many of the poet's later works have a melancholy tone, reflecting her years in exile.
The documentary paints a melancholy portrait of fishing towns emptied by economic decline.
Looking through old family photographs always makes my father quiet and melancholy.
tc: Though the song's melody is cheerful, its lyrics are deeply ______, telling of lost love and loneliness.
The contrast with 'cheerful' and the themes of loss show the blank means sad.
se: The empty house felt ______ after the children moved away to university.
gloomy
Both 'melancholy' and 'gloomy' describe a sad, somber feeling.

m: dull and repetitive; lacking variety
x: Sitting in the same traffic jam every morning can become painfully monotonous.
Data entry is monotonous work, but someone has to do it accurately.
The lecturer's monotonous voice made it hard to stay awake in the afternoon class.
Studies suggest that monotonous factory jobs can harm workers' mental health.
She left the relationship because their weekends had become monotonous and predictable.
tc: After years of the same ______ tasks, she longed for a job that offered variety and new challenges.
'Longed for... variety' shows the blank means repetitive and dull.
se: Eating rice and boiled potatoes every single day quickly became ______.
tedious
Both 'monotonous' and 'tedious' mean boring because of repetition.

m: a temporary ban or suspension of an activity
x: We've declared a moratorium on phones at the dinner table, and family meals feel much calmer.
Management announced a hiring moratorium until the end of the financial year.
The university imposed a moratorium on new construction while it reviewed its budget.
Several countries have called for a moratorium on deep-sea mining until its effects are better understood.
After one heated argument, my wife and I agreed on a moratorium on discussing politics with her parents.
tc: Until the safety review is complete, the city has placed a temporary ______ on new building permits.
'Temporary' and 'until the safety review is complete' show the blank means a temporary ban.
se: The government announced a two-year ______ on new coal-fired power plants.
freeze
Both 'moratorium' and 'freeze' mean a temporary halt to an activity.

m: to make someone feel deeply embarrassed or ashamed
x: It mortified me when my mother showed my baby photos to my new friends.
He was mortified to discover he had sent his complaint about his boss to his boss.
Forgetting her lines in front of the entire school mortified her for weeks.
The minister was mortified when a live microphone recorded his rude remarks about voters.
I was mortified when I accidentally called my girlfriend by my ex's name.
tc: Afraid that a clumsy speech would ______ her in front of her new colleagues, she rehearsed it a dozen times.
Her fear and repeated rehearsal show the blank means to deeply embarrass.
se: Nothing seemed to ______ him more than being corrected in front of his own students.
embarrass
Both 'mortify' and 'embarrass' mean to make someone feel ashamed, so the meaning stays the same.

m: of many different kinds; very varied and diverse
x: My grandmother's kitchen shelf held multifarious jars of spices, pickles, and homemade remedies.
A project manager juggles multifarious duties, from budgeting to resolving team conflicts.
The course explores the multifarious influences that shaped modern architecture.
Climate change has multifarious effects, from rising seas to shifting farming seasons.
Her multifarious interests, from jazz to beekeeping, made her fascinating company on a first date.
tc: Far from having a single purpose, the old market served ______ functions: bank, post office, theater, and meeting place.
'Far from having a single purpose' and the list of roles show the blank means many and varied.
se: The museum's collection reflects the ______ cultures that have passed through the region.
diverse
Both 'multifarious' and 'diverse' mean of many different kinds.

m: liable to change; changeable
x: Our weekend plans are always mutable, depending on the weather and the kids' moods.
The project's scope proved highly mutable, shifting every time the client called.
Linguists show that the meanings of words are mutable, changing from one generation to the next.
Public opinion is mutable, and a single scandal can reverse a politician's popularity overnight.
Teenage friendships can be mutable, with best friends becoming strangers within months.
tc: Unlike the fixed laws of physics, the rules of fashion are ______, shifting from one season to the next.
The contrast with 'fixed' and the word 'shifting' show the blank means changeable.
se: Our understanding of history is ______, revised whenever new evidence comes to light.
changeable
Both 'mutable' and 'changeable' mean able to change.

m: countless; extremely great in number
x: There are myriad ways to cook lentils, and my mother seems to know every one of them.
New managers face myriad challenges in their first year, from hiring staff to managing budgets.
The archive contains myriad documents that have never been studied by historians.
Coral reefs support myriad species of fish, many of which are found nowhere else on Earth.
She had myriad reasons to leave him, yet she found it hard to let go.
tc: The night sky far from the city lights revealed not a handful but ______ stars, far too many to count.
'Not a handful but' and 'far too many to count' show the blank means countless.
se: The internet offers ______ opportunities for distraction during exam season.
countless
Both 'myriad' and 'countless' mean extremely numerous.

m: the lowest point in the fortunes or condition of someone or something
x: Losing my wallet and missing my flight on the same day was the nadir of that trip.
The company's share price hit its nadir in March before slowly recovering.
Historians often describe that decade as the nadir of the empire's cultural life.
Relations between the two countries reached their nadir after the border clash.
He describes the months after his father's death as the nadir of his life.
tc: After years of steady decline, the team's fortunes reached their ______ last season, when they failed to win a single match.
'Failed to win a single match' after years of decline shows the blank means the lowest point.
se: The economy reached its ______ in the middle of the year and then began a slow recovery.
trough
Both 'nadir' and 'trough' mean the lowest point before a recovery.

m: excessive interest in or admiration of oneself and one's appearance
x: Posting forty selfies a day seems less like confidence and more like narcissism.
His narcissism made him take credit for every success while blaming the team for every failure.
Psychology students learn to distinguish healthy self-esteem from clinical narcissism.
Some commentators argue that social media encourages a culture of narcissism among young people.
She ended the relationship once she realized his narcissism left no room for her needs.
tc: His ______ was so extreme that he could not hold a conversation without steering it back to his own achievements and appearance.
Always steering talk back to his own achievements and looks shows excessive self-admiration.
se: Critics accused the film director of ______, noting that he cast himself as the hero in every movie.
egotism
Both 'narcissism' and 'egotism' mean excessive focus on oneself.

m: to make something necessary as a result or consequence
x: A flat tire on the way to the airport necessitated a very expensive taxi ride.
Rising demand will necessitate hiring at least three more engineers next year.
Changing your thesis topic this late would necessitate a whole new literature review.
The severe flooding necessitated the evacuation of thousands of families from low-lying districts.
Her mother's illness necessitated a move back home, which put a strain on her marriage.
tc: The bridge had grown so unsafe that any further cracks would ______ closing it to traffic.
'So unsafe' explains that further cracks would make closure necessary.
se: Expanding the factory will ______ a large investment in new machinery.
require
Both 'necessitate' and 'require' mean to make something necessary.

m: failing to take proper care in doing something, especially one's duty
x: Leaving the stove on all night was negligent, and we were lucky the house didn't burn down.
The firm dismissed an accountant who had been negligent in checking client records.
Supervisors who are negligent about lab safety put every student at risk.
The hospital was found negligent after a patient was given the wrong medication.
She felt she had been a negligent friend, missing every birthday during her busy final year.
tc: Whereas the first contractor inspected every beam, his successor was so ______ that he never checked the foundations at all.
'Whereas' contrasts careful inspection with a total failure to check, so the blank means careless.
se: The landlord was ______ in failing to repair the broken railing for months.
remiss
Both 'negligent' and 'remiss' mean failing in one's duty to take care.

m: the practice of people in power favoring relatives or friends, especially by giving them jobs
x: Everyone in the family whispered about nepotism when my uncle hired his own son as manager.
The company introduced strict hiring rules to prevent nepotism in promotions.
Researchers found that nepotism in university hiring discouraged talented outsiders from applying.
Protesters accused the ruling elite of nepotism, pointing to relatives appointed to key government posts.
She resented the nepotism that let her cousin climb the ladder while she worked twice as hard.
tc: Although the new director claimed he hired purely on merit, three of his nephews were soon on the payroll, a clear case of ______.
Hiring nephews despite claiming to hire on merit shows favoritism toward relatives.
se: The minister was forced to resign after reports of ______ in government appointments.
favoritism
Both 'nepotism' and 'favoritism' describe unfairly favoring certain people in appointments.

m: a sentimental longing for a happy period in the past
x: The smell of rain on dry earth fills me with nostalgia for my childhood village.
The marketing team used nostalgia for 1990s cartoons to sell its new sneakers.
In her thesis, she argues that nostalgia can distort how communities remember their history.
Political slogans often play on voters' nostalgia for a supposedly simpler era.
Seeing my old school friends again stirred a wave of nostalgia I hadn't expected.
tc: Looking at the faded photographs, the old couple were filled with ______ for the years when they were young and newly married.
Sentimental feelings for their happy early years show the blank means longing for the past.
se: Old songs on the radio filled her with ______ for her university days.
longing
Both 'nostalgia' and 'longing' express a wistful desire for a past time.

m: harmful, poisonous, or very unpleasant
x: We had to open every window after the cleaning product filled the bathroom with noxious fumes.
Workers at the plant complained of headaches caused by noxious chemicals in the air.
The lab requires students to handle noxious substances only under a fume hood.
Brick kilns around the city release noxious smoke that worsens air quality every winter.
She finally cut ties with a friend whose noxious gossip had soured every gathering.
tc: Far from being harmless, the gas leaking from the pipe was ______ enough to make residents dizzy and sick.
'Far from being harmless' and the residents' symptoms show the blank means harmful or poisonous.
se: The factory was fined for releasing ______ waste into the river.
toxic
Both 'noxious' and 'toxic' mean poisonous and harmful.

m: a subtle difference in meaning, expression, tone, or feeling
x: Texting loses the nuance of tone, so jokes are easily mistaken for insults.
A skilled negotiator notices every nuance in the other side's language.
Good translators capture the nuances of the original text, not just its literal meaning.
Critics complained that the televised debate on immigration lacked nuance and relied on slogans.
After years of marriage, he could read every nuance of his wife's silence.
tc: Her performance was praised for its ______, conveying with the slightest glance what other actors would shout.
'The slightest glance' versus shouting shows the blank means subtlety of expression.
se: The translation was accurate but missed every ______ of the poet's humor.
subtlety
Both 'nuance' and 'subtlety' mean a fine shade of meaning.

m: to make legally void or to cancel out the effect of something
x: Eating a giant dessert after the gym seemed to nullify my entire workout.
A single unsigned page could nullify the entire contract, so read everything before you sign.
Contaminated samples can nullify months of careful laboratory work, which is why technicians follow strict cleaning procedures.
The Supreme Court voted to nullify the election results in three districts.
His apology could not nullify the hurt his words had caused her.
tc: Because the referee had blown his whistle before the shot, officials decided to ______ the goal.
The whistle before the shot explains why the goal had to be cancelled.
se: The judge ruled that the forged signature would ______ the will.
invalidate
Both 'nullify' and 'invalidate' mean to make legally void.

m: not expressed directly; indirect
x: My mother made an oblique comment about my messy room instead of simply telling me to clean it.
The manager's oblique reference to 'restructuring' left everyone worried about layoffs.
The novel's oblique style rewards readers who are willing to read between the lines.
The spokesperson gave only oblique answers when asked about the missing funds.
He dropped oblique hints about marriage for months before finally proposing.
tc: Rather than criticize the policy openly, the official made only ______ references to its flaws.
'Rather than... openly' shows the blank means indirect.
se: Her poems approach grief in ______ ways, through images of empty rooms rather than direct statements.
indirect
Both 'oblique' and 'indirect' mean not stated outright, matching the contrast with 'direct statements'.

m: to destroy completely, leaving no trace
x: Heavy rain obliterated the chalk drawings the children had made on the pavement.
A computer crash obliterated three weeks of my unsaved work.
Scientists believe an enormous asteroid impact nearly obliterated life on Earth 66 million years ago.
The cyclone obliterated entire villages along the coast, leaving thousands of families without shelter.
She wished she could obliterate every memory of that humiliating evening.
tc: The fire did more than damage the old library; it managed to ______ every book, leaving nothing but ash.
'More than damage' and 'nothing but ash' signal total destruction.
se: The bombing raids threatened to ______ the historic center of the city.
annihilate
Both 'obliterate' and 'annihilate' mean to destroy completely.

m: the state of being completely forgotten or unknown
x: Old flip phones have slipped into oblivion now that everyone carries a smartphone.
Without a strong marketing campaign, the product faded into oblivion within a year.
The scholar rescued several medieval poets from oblivion by translating their works.
Once-famous film stars can sink into oblivion as new generations forget them.
Their love story would have passed into oblivion if her granddaughter had not found the letters.
tc: Once the toast of the literary world, the novelist died in ______, his books long out of print and his name forgotten.
The contrast with 'toast of the literary world' and 'his name forgotten' show the blank means a state of being forgotten.
se: Without government support, many traditional crafts will slip into ______.
obscurity
Both 'oblivion' and 'obscurity' mean the state of being forgotten or unknown.

m: not aware of or not concerned about what is happening around one
x: Wearing headphones, he crossed the road oblivious to the honking rickshaws.
The manager seemed oblivious to the growing tension between his two senior engineers.
Absorbed in her equations, she was oblivious to the fact that the library had closed.
Many consumers remain oblivious to how much personal data their apps collect.
He was completely oblivious to the fact that his best friend had a crush on him.
tc: So absorbed was the child in his video game that he remained ______ to his mother calling him for dinner.
'So absorbed' explains why he did not notice his mother calling.
se: The tourists seemed ______ of the danger posed by the rising tide.
unaware
Both 'oblivious of' and 'unaware of' mean not noticing the danger.

m: to block or get in the way of something; to hinder progress
x: A fallen tree obstructed the road, so we had to take a long detour.
Bureaucratic delays continue to obstruct the launch of our new product.
The professor was suspended for obstructing an inquiry into research misconduct in his lab.
The official was charged with obstructing justice after destroying key documents.
Her parents tried to obstruct the marriage, but she was determined to follow her heart.
tc: Instead of helping the investigation, the company's lawyers tried to ______ it at every turn by withholding documents.
'Instead of helping' and 'withholding documents' signal the blank means to block or hinder.
se: Parked trucks continued to ______ the entrance to the hospital.
block
Both 'obstruct' and 'block' mean to get in the way physically.
